# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# FTX's Ties To The Bahamian Government

On cross-examination on October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon drew out evidence that Bankman-Fried had a cozy — perhaps even inappropriately cozy — relationship with the Bahamian government, which is not what he was on trial for but probably did not make him look any better to a jury. She asked whether he had made comments about paying off the Bahamian national debt, which he did not recall.

The court then saw an internal FTX group chat called "Project Chinchilla Chatter," in which another member asked who in the Bahamian government they needed to talk to for the project. "His name is Ryan Salame :p," Bankman-Fried replied; Salame was one of FTX's executives. In another part of the chat, Bankman-Fried noted that the Bahamian prime minister was at the FTX arena in FTX seats with his wife.

The jury was also shown a November 9th email from Bankman-Fried to Ryan Pinder, attorney general of the Bahamas, saying "we are deeply grateful" for what the Bahamas had done for FTX, and offering as a token of that gratitude: "We would be more than happy to open up withdrawals for all Bahamian customers on FTX, so that they can, tomorrow, fully withdraw all of their assets, making them fully whole. It's your call whether you want us to do this, but we are more than happy to and would consider it the very least of our duty to the country, and could open it up immediately if you reply saying you want us to. If we don't hear back from you, we are going to go ahead and do it tomorrow." Bankman-Fried did indeed open withdrawals for Bahamian customers.



---


# Reaction To Lewis's Portrayal Of SBF

The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. TechCrunch collected the reaction on 2023-10-02.

The premise is attacked head-on by Dan Held, who on October 2, 2023 quoted Lewis — "They had a great real business. If no one had cast aspersions on the business, if there hadn't been a run on customers deposits, they'd still be making tons of money" — and answered: "That's not true. They are not a bank, they're…", prefacing it with "Shameful that Michael Lewis is defending SBF." Ryan Selkis attacked the framing instead of the balance sheet, writing the same day that "The Michael Lewis interview is infuriating. SBF was a scumbag, and now we need to hear about his 'tragic fall' in the MSM because Sam told them he was an 'effective altruist' and people like Michael Lewis were so far up his ass they couldn't tell truth from fiction." Tobi Lutke attacked the coverage itself: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is still getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world?"

Two qualifications sit against the backlash. Noff is defensive: she believes crypto is no worse than the stock market, which can also be manipulated and mishandled, adding that "Even when you identify corruption, I don't think that means we don't believe in the system in question." And TechCrunch's own reading is that the thing being attacked may not be quite what the critics take it for — Lewis's picture is a little less stark from the looks of the 60 Minutes episode, and it is not that clear at all whether SBF is getting a kicking or a coat of polish in the interview, given Lewis's celebration of SBF's self-proclaimed (yet not quite proven) idealism and the "Bankman-Fried-shaped hold in the world" that exists. The writer's closing point is that this confused message is very apt for cryptocurrency, where the process by which it works is forever murky and often misrepresented, at least to most people.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.

# The Blurred Line Between SEO And Spam

Lily Ray's rebuttal targets Sullivan's premise that the boundary is clean and that Google has not changed. Sullivan had tried to convince the writer that Google was not behaving differently and in fact had not changed its search criteria in any major way for the past 20 years: Google wanted you to make good websites, and that was that; everyone who tried to rank higher by messing with the algorithm would be blocked. Sullivan even insisted that what these rule-breakers did should not be called SEO — he deemed it all "spam," defining spam as "stuff that search engines don't like."

The objection is that the line between strategies that violate Google's terms of service and strategies that do not has always been blurry and inconsistently enforced. "I've never seen this much tension in the industry in terms of, like, what Google says to do and what people are doing and getting away with," Ray said. "If you're gonna tell us that this stuff doesn't work, make it stop working!"

Ray declines to make it a question of individual character. As much as she despises what this kind of SEO has done to the internet, she hesitated to condemn the actual people doing it: "I used to do those types of tactics, so I couldn't hate on anybody personally," she said. "If people have a problem with Google's results, they have to ask themselves, is it the fault of the SEOs? Or is this Google behaving differently than it used to?"

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Disinformation

## Definition

Disinformation is false or misleading content spread online — distinct from the illegal-content category (like terrorism or hate speech) in that, per the corpus's account of EU regulation, disinformation "is not illegal in the EU per se," yet still counts as a *systemic risk* that large platforms must assess and mitigate.

## Context

The corpus's central storyline is the EU's escalating regulatory pressure on X (formerly Twitter) over disinformation tied to the Israel-Hamas war: the Commission's October 2023 warning and formal information request to Musk accused X of being used "to disseminate illegal content and disinformation" following the Hamas attacks, and a EU-commissioned study later found X had "the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts" among major platforms.
Because X is a Digital Services Act (DSA) "very large online platform" (VLOP), the obligation to mitigate disinformation risk is legally binding on it even though the underlying falsehoods are not themselves illegal; the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (which Musk pulled X out of earlier in 2023) is treated by the Commission as a signal of DSA compliance on this exact risk.
Disinformation also surfaces as a generative-AI worry: Suleyman warned DeepMind's ethics board that AI "could lead to an explosion in disinformation," EU commissioner Vera Jourova flagged AI-generated disinformation as an election threat, and early fears that ChatGPT would be used "to generate disinformation on a massive scale" pushed European policymakers toward mandating security assessments of generative AI products.
Real-world examples in the corpus include a video-game clip falsely presented as Hamas missile footage circulating on X, and misinformation described as "rampant on social media" during the Gaza crisis, prompting some users to turn to Snap Map for unmediated, firsthand footage instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **Not illegal per se in the EU** — disinformation is treated as a systemic risk to be mitigated, not content that platforms are legally required to remove the way they must remove illegal content.
- **Distinct from "misinformation" but often paired with it** — the corpus uses both terms (e.g., "mis/disinformation posts," Mozilla's content-policy list of "misinformation" as a harm category), generally without a sharp technical distinction, though disinformation carries a stronger connotation of deliberate falsehood or manipulation (e.g., "Kremlin propaganda").
- **A VLOP systemic-risk obligation** — under the DSA, platforms designated VLOPs (like X) must proactively assess and mitigate disinformation risk, which is what makes an EU formal-information request or investigation possible even absent an illegal-content finding.
- **Measurable and comparable across platforms** — the EU's Code of Practice enabled a pilot study producing "structural indicators" (e.g., how easily disinformation content is found, how much engagement it gets) that let regulators rank X as worst among mainstream platforms.
- **A named risk of generative AI** — beyond social-media falsehoods, the corpus repeatedly frames disinformation as a downstream risk of AI text/image generation (ChatGPT, deepfakes), motivating both EU AI-Act-era safeguards and industry-side labeling commitments.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Cloud Computing

## Definition

Cloud computing, in the corpus, is the named vendor-run industry that Microsoft's OpenAI deal plugged into — when the deal closed in 2019, Microsoft "had a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service" — and that later commentary treats as the historical template for AI-market dynamics like vendor lock-in, market consolidation, and billing norms.

## Context

In the corpus, cloud computing shows up mainly as the historical precedent and infrastructural backbone for the current AI boom, rather than as a subject in its own right.

Commentators reach for the cloud computing industry to explain both OpenAI's near-collapse and the shape of the AI market that followed it: the industry became renowned for locking companies into "centralized, vortex-like silos," which is offered as the reason so many startups panicked and contacted OpenAI's rivals when OpenAI itself looked like it might disintegrate.

The same precedent is used to forecast how the AI market layers will settle: the foundation-model layer is expected to "settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market," and, separately, incumbents in cloud computing (like those in the earlier internet buildout) are said to have kept innovating "until innovation becomes stagnant" — a pattern predicted to repeat for AI incumbents.

Cloud computing also appears as a budget line competing with AI spending — total AI spending has overtaken cloud computing spending even though cloud computing "remains critical" — and as a unit-economics contrast: AI compute is normally metered in raw processing terms (FLOPs) or dollars per day, a different and less mature billing metric than most cloud computing's established consumption pricing.

## Key Characteristics

- **Centralized, provider-hosted delivery** — cloud computing is a vendor's service that a customer builds on top of, illustrated by Microsoft's use of its "cloud computing service" as the integration point for OpenAI's models.
- **Lock-in and the multi-cloud response** — the cloud computing industry is described as having locked customers into single-vendor "silos," which pushed companies toward multi-cloud and hybrid strategies — a dynamic the corpus draws on directly to explain AI startups' current over-reliance on OpenAI.
- **Tendency toward an oligopolistic market structure** — cloud computing is used as the reference case for a market that consolidated around a few large "cloud provider" incumbents, the same structure forecast for the foundation-model layer of the AI stack.
- **Incumbent-innovate-then-stagnate pattern** — cloud computing (alongside the internet) is cited as a precedent where incumbents keep innovating only until the market matures and stagnates, opening room for new entrants.
- **Compute as a metered, regulable resource** — "compute" (processing capacity, measured in floating point operations or FLOPs) is treated as a quantifiable input separate from "cloud computing" as an industry, and it is significant enough that the EU AI Act sets its high-risk regulatory threshold for general-purpose AI models directly on cumulative training compute (10^25 FLOPs).
- **Distinct billing norms from AI compute** — cloud computing has settled consumption-pricing conventions, whereas AI compute costs (e.g., OpenAI's roughly $700,000/day compute spend) are tracked and priced differently, "a very different metric than most cloud computing."

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources — such as networks, servers, storage, applications, and services — that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort (NIST, "NIST Definition of Cloud Computing", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.nist.gov/publications/nist-definition-cloud-computing).

# Celebrity Endorsement

In the corpus, "celebrity endorsements" is named directly only once — listed alongside "campaign trail rallies" as one of several online-campaign tactics that, on their own, are "not enough to engage voters online" — and everywhere else the corpus treats it as a family of concrete cases rather than a defined category: FTX's paid partnerships with athletes, Anna Wintour's sponsorship request to Sam Bankman-Fried, The Epoch Times' political endorsements and CPAC sponsorship, and Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok launch via a Jake Paul endorsement.

## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. (Wikipedia, "Celebrity branding," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_branding)

# Travis Kelce's First Contact Attempt And The Eras Tour Bracelet

The first link between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce was established in 2016 when Kelce played "Kiss, Marry, Kill" on AfterBuzz TV and said he would kiss Swift, and the first real contact attempt came in July 2023, when he tried and failed to give her a friendship bracelet with his number on it at her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

In the 2016 game Kelce — who helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023 — was given the options of Swift, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, and said he would ultimately kill Grande, marry Perry and kiss Swift. That was about six years earlier, but it more recently set tongues wagging as fans wondered how long the plan for them to meet had been in the works.

Seven years on, things started to heat up: in July, speaking on the podcast he shares with his brother, New Heights, Kelce said he intended to give Swift a friendship bracelet with his number on it during her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City. The bracelet never made it to her wrist, nor his digits to her phone. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs she sings," he said. "She doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me, so I took it personal[sic]." At that point any attraction seemed one-sided, but Kelce, exhibiting the tenacity typical of a professional sportsman, remained determined to get her attention — and the Kelce brothers could not stop talking about Swift on the podcast, her name popping up everywhere, including during conversations about facial hair.



---


# Travis Kelce's Comments On Relationship Privacy

Travis Kelce broke his silence on Taylor Swift's Chiefs game attendance on his podcast on 27 September 2023, while saying he would not speak much more about the relationship, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On the game itself, Kelce said: "To see the slow-motion chest bumps, to see the high-fives with Mom, to see how Chiefs Kingdom was all excited that she was there -- that s--- was absolutely hysterical. It's definitely a game I'll remember, that's for damn sure."

He then set the limit, noting that he wants "to respect both of our lives," and drew a distinction between his own exposure and Swift's: "Yeah, my personal life -- that's not so personal. I did this to myself Jason, I know this. What's real is that you know it is my personal life. ... She's not in the media as much as I am doing this show every single week."



---


# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.

# Celebrity Endorsement

In the corpus, "celebrity endorsements" is named directly only once — listed alongside "campaign trail rallies" as one of several online-campaign tactics that, on their own, are "not enough to engage voters online" — and everywhere else the corpus treats it as a family of concrete cases rather than a defined category: FTX's paid partnerships with athletes, Anna Wintour's sponsorship request to Sam Bankman-Fried, The Epoch Times' political endorsements and CPAC sponsorship, and Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok launch via a Jake Paul endorsement.

## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. (Wikipedia, "Celebrity branding," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_branding)

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# Super Bowl

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).
Franchise identity is tied to it retroactively — the Cincinnati Bengals are described as having reached "a Super Bowl appearance in 2021" as the marker of the team's turnaround (doc_0071), and Travis Kelce is introduced as having "helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023" (doc_0044), with the Kansas City Chiefs subsequently referred to simply as "the defending Super Bowl champions" (doc_0059).
A Christmas Day matchup between the 49ers and Ravens is previewed explicitly as a "potential Super Bowl sneak peek" (doc_0003), showing how regular-season games get framed as previews of the eventual championship.

## Key Characteristics

- **Season-defining stakes** — teams and players are described relative to it long after the fact ("defending Super Bowl champions," "two-time Super Bowl MVP") (doc_0059, doc_0003).
- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).
- **Special-event betting draw** — sportsbooks single out "Super Bowl betting lines" alongside World Series odds and March Madness as flagship special-event markets carrying their own promotional bonuses (doc_0072).
- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "Super Bowl" itself — it only reports how teams, players, and betting markets relate to it.
Per Wikipedia, the Super Bowl is "the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), serving as the final game of each NFL season" (Wikipedia, *Super Bowl*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# 2023 NFL Offensive Player Of The Year: Hill The Favorite, Lamb The Longshot

Tyreek Hill was the current favorite for 2023 NFL Offensive Player of the Year and CeeDee Lamb the longshot, and Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that Lamb could steal the award if Hill faded down the stretch.

There was a good reason why Hill was such a heavy favorite: the Dolphins wide receiver was on track to become the first player with 2,000-plus receiving yards in a single season. But Sporting News saw a solid chance he would not hit that mark, because of Miami's five remaining opponents, four had pass defenses ranked in the league's top eight. If he slowed down, someone like Lamb could catch up.

The Lamb case rests on his trajectory. Based on his current season average, Lamb was on track for close to 1,600 yards, but based on his production over the last seven games he could finish with closer to 1,800. He would probably need Hill to fade down the stretch to have a shot — but if Hill did and Lamb continued to produce, Lamb could steal OPOY from Hill.

# Most Valuable Player (MVP)

## Definition

In the corpus, MVP (Most Valuable Player) names the player judged most valuable to a team's or league's success, and the term surfaces at several distinct scopes: a formal season-long league award (NFL MVP, NBA MVP), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or cross-sport label applied by media, players, and coaches.

## Context

At the league-season level, the NFL MVP and NBA MVP are formal annual awards contested among a small pool of star players. Sporting News's Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece had Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott, and Jalen Hurts as the current NFL MVP favorites after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff as the longshot cases. Separately, Yardbarker's Dec. 24, 2023 Christmas Day preview framed the Ravens-49ers game explicitly as "the decisive clash for the MVP Award," with Brock Purdy the heavy favorite (-230) and Lamar Jackson — the 2019 MVP — holding the second-shortest odds (+525). At the single-game level, MVP denotes a game-specific honor, as with Patrick Mahomes's two Super Bowl MVPs. At the team level, MVP is used informally by outlets like Yardbarker to name each team's most indispensable player at a season's midpoint — a designation that need not track the league-wide award and can go to a non-quarterback, as when Miami's Tyreek Hill or New England's Jabrill Peppers is named team MVP. The same informal usage crosses sports, as when an MLS goalkeeper calls forward Luciano Acosta "the MVP" of FC Cincinnati. MVP is also a standard sports-betting futures market: bettors wager on which player will win the season MVP award well before or during the season, alongside markets like Rookie of the Year and Offensive/Defensive Player of the Year.

## Background (external)

Beyond this corpus's sports-betting and news coverage, Wikipedia describes an MVP award more generally as an honor bestowed on the individual (or individuals, in case of a tie) "whose individual performance is the greatest in an entire league, for a particular competition, or on a specific team," recognizing one player's contribution within a team effort. (Source: Wikipedia, "Most valuable player," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_valuable_player, accessed 2026-09-02.)

## Key Characteristics

- **Multiple scopes** — the same "MVP" language covers a formal season-long league award (NFL, NBA), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or sport-crossing designation used by media and players alike.
- **Voting-panel awards lack fixed criteria** — the NBA MVP, for instance, is chosen by a panel of sportswriters and broadcasters (format since 1980, weighted 5/3/1 points for first/second/third-place votes) with no set selection rulebook, which is why outcomes are notoriously hard to predict and can produce "upset" winners.
- **Quarterback bias in NFL MVP framing** — corpus coverage repeatedly frames the NFL MVP as typically going to a quarterback from a top-seeded team, to the point that a non-quarterback like Christian McCaffrey is described as facing long odds "if the MVP wasn't a quarterback-driven award."
- **Betting futures market** — MVP odds are a standing futures category at sportsbooks (alongside moneylines, spreads, and other award markets), bet on well ahead of the outcome and repriced as the season's results accumulate.
- **Team-level MVP is unofficial** — team MVP picks (e.g., Yardbarker's AFC team-by-team roundup) are editorial judgments, not sanctioned awards, and can diverge sharply from who is in the league MVP conversation.

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# Taylor Swift's First Chiefs Game Appearance On 24 September 2023

Taylor Swift took Travis Kelce up on his offer and attended the Chiefs' Week 3 game against the Chicago Bears on 24 September 2023, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

Swift was dressed on theme and watched intently, cheering and even chest bumping someone during big plays; she was especially thrilled to see Kelce get in the end zone on a three-yard catch that put the Chiefs up 41-0, and Kansas City went on to win 41-10 to improve to 2-1. She sat next to Donna Kelce in the box, the two seen talking and laughing as the game went along.

The postgame press conference seemed more about Swift and Kelce than about the actual game, with the media wanting any insight into the relationship and how Swift ended up at Arrowhead. "He told me at the last minute," Patrick Mahomes said when asked if he knew Swift was coming. "There's some things with Trav where he kind of just says it and you don't know if it's true or not. He says it so calmly. ... Friday he was like, 'Yeah, I think she's coming to the game this weekend,' and then moved about his business." Head coach Andy Reid, asked about his star tight end's supposed relationship, quipped, "I set them up."

Afterwards the two were photographed together for the first time, walking side by side, Kelce fittingly wearing an outfit with "1989" in the title and Swift wearing a Chiefs zip-up; they were then spotted leaving in a convertible with the tight end driving, and Kelce reportedly rented out a restaurant for a private party with Swift and his teammates. A source told Entertainment Tonight that "Taylor Swift likes that Travis Kelce 'pursued her' and the two are having a 'great time getting to know each other,'" adding that "'Taylor wants a guy that's into his career, does his own thing, but is also supportive and understands her,'" and "'Travis fits those qualities.'"
