# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Litigation Hold

## Definition

In the corpus, a litigation hold is the obligation the DOJ says Google was subject to during its antitrust trial — the obligation the DOJ accused Google of breaching by auto-deleting internal chat messages. What such a hold requires in general is given in Background (external) below, not in the cited corpus document.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the obligation Google was under during the DOJ's antitrust trial, and it is what makes Google's chat-deletion practice controversial rather than merely an ordinary retention policy: during Pichai's testimony the DOJ "touched on Google's policy of deleting internal chat messages, despite being subject to a litigation hold"; earlier, in February, the DOJ had accused Google of "systematically destroying chats through its history-off option, which deletes messages every 24 hours unless a user manually changed the setting."
Pichai's own account ties the hold directly to a change in Google's product defaults: he said he took action against the history-off default for chat in February specifically "to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold," and, when confronted with a 2021 message asking for history to be turned off in a group chat, said that exchange concerned a personnel matter and "had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with."

## Key Characteristics

- **The deletion dispute is the whole point** — the litigation hold is what turns Google's default chat auto-deletion (its "history-off" setting, deleting messages every 24 hours) from an ordinary retention policy into the DOJ's accusation of destroying material Google was obliged to keep.
- **Tied to the specific litigation** — the corpus frames the hold as arising from the DOJ's antitrust suit against Google, not as a general corporate record-keeping rule.
- **Distinguishes intentional destruction from routine practice** — the DOJ's accusation frames Google's chat auto-deletion as destruction of material Google was already obliged to preserve, not an ordinary retention decision.
- **Compliance is asserted, not self-evident** — Pichai maintained he "takes great care to comply with" the hold even while defending a 2021 request to turn off chat history, showing the same conduct can be read either as compliant or as evasive depending on intent.

## Background (external)

The corpus establishes that Google was subject to a litigation hold and disputes whether its conduct complied with it, but does not define the obligation itself. A litigation hold (also called a legal hold) is a process an organization initiates to preserve all forms of relevant information when litigation is reasonably anticipated, so that potentially relevant evidence is not lost, destroyed, or altered before or during a legal proceeding (Wikipedia, *Litigation Hold*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

Source: "Major League Baseball," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball

# Most Valuable Player (MVP)

## Definition

In the corpus, MVP (Most Valuable Player) names the player judged most valuable to a team's or league's success, and the term surfaces at several distinct scopes: a formal season-long league award (NFL MVP, NBA MVP), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or cross-sport label applied by media, players, and coaches.

## Context

At the league-season level, the NFL MVP and NBA MVP are formal annual awards contested among a small pool of star players. Sporting News's Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece had Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott, and Jalen Hurts as the current NFL MVP favorites after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff as the longshot cases. Separately, Yardbarker's Dec. 24, 2023 Christmas Day preview framed the Ravens-49ers game explicitly as "the decisive clash for the MVP Award," with Brock Purdy the heavy favorite (-230) and Lamar Jackson — the 2019 MVP — holding the second-shortest odds (+525). At the single-game level, MVP denotes a game-specific honor, as with Patrick Mahomes's two Super Bowl MVPs. At the team level, MVP is used informally by outlets like Yardbarker to name each team's most indispensable player at a season's midpoint — a designation that need not track the league-wide award and can go to a non-quarterback, as when Miami's Tyreek Hill or New England's Jabrill Peppers is named team MVP. The same informal usage crosses sports, as when an MLS goalkeeper calls forward Luciano Acosta "the MVP" of FC Cincinnati. MVP is also a standard sports-betting futures market: bettors wager on which player will win the season MVP award well before or during the season, alongside markets like Rookie of the Year and Offensive/Defensive Player of the Year.

## Background (external)

Beyond this corpus's sports-betting and news coverage, Wikipedia describes an MVP award more generally as an honor bestowed on the individual (or individuals, in case of a tie) "whose individual performance is the greatest in an entire league, for a particular competition, or on a specific team," recognizing one player's contribution within a team effort. (Source: Wikipedia, "Most valuable player," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_valuable_player, accessed 2026-09-02.)

## Key Characteristics

- **Multiple scopes** — the same "MVP" language covers a formal season-long league award (NFL, NBA), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or sport-crossing designation used by media and players alike.
- **Voting-panel awards lack fixed criteria** — the NBA MVP, for instance, is chosen by a panel of sportswriters and broadcasters (format since 1980, weighted 5/3/1 points for first/second/third-place votes) with no set selection rulebook, which is why outcomes are notoriously hard to predict and can produce "upset" winners.
- **Quarterback bias in NFL MVP framing** — corpus coverage repeatedly frames the NFL MVP as typically going to a quarterback from a top-seeded team, to the point that a non-quarterback like Christian McCaffrey is described as facing long odds "if the MVP wasn't a quarterback-driven award."
- **Betting futures market** — MVP odds are a standing futures category at sportsbooks (alongside moneylines, spreads, and other award markets), bet on well ahead of the outcome and repriced as the season's results accumulate.
- **Team-level MVP is unofficial** — team MVP picks (e.g., Yardbarker's AFC team-by-team roundup) are editorial judgments, not sanctioned awards, and can diverge sharply from who is in the league MVP conversation.

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# Bail

## Definition

Bail is the term the corpus uses for Sam Bankman-Fried's pretrial release from custody: a $250 million bond that let him live under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto instead of in jail while awaiting trial, and which a U.S. judge revoked in August 2023 (doc_0010, doc_0226).

## Context

The corpus's clearest illustration is Sam Bankman-Fried's case: after being arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022 and extradited to the U.S., he was released on a $250 million bail bond and confined to house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto (doc_0010). That release was not permanent — a U.S. judge revoked his bail in August 2023 after he was accused of intimidating former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison by leaking her private diary, leaving him in custody by the time his fraud trial began that October (doc_0010, doc_0226). Bail is also treated as something a court can simply refuse to grant: one recap of the FTX saga notes flatly that "SBF has been denied bail" (doc_0030). The concept resurfaces around Bankman-Fried's co-defendants, where house arrest — the condition often attached to bail — is described as a lighter alternative to imprisonment that cooperating felons like Gary Wang, Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison might still face even without prison time (doc_0121).

## Key Characteristics

- **Conditional, not unconditional freedom** — release on bail came bundled with restrictions (house arrest at a fixed address) rather than free movement (doc_0010).
- **Financially secured** — Bankman-Fried's release required a $250 million bail bond, tying his liberty to a monetary guarantee (doc_0010).
- **Revocable** — a judge can revoke bail mid-proceedings for conduct that violates its terms, as happened after the Ellison intimidation allegations, moving the defendant from house arrest to detention (doc_0010, doc_0226).
- **Discretionary and sometimes denied outright** — courts can decline to grant bail at all, as they did for Bankman-Fried at least once during his case (doc_0030).
- **Distinct from post-conviction outcomes** — bail concerns pretrial release, while house arrest can separately appear as a possible post-conviction alternative to imprisonment for cooperating defendants (doc_0121).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "bail" itself — it only reports how bail applied in Bankman-Fried's case.
Per Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, bail is "the money a defendant pays as a guarantee that they will show up in court at a later date," and release can be "conditioned on certain behavior of the defendant," such as staying away from an alleged victim (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).
A defendant's failure to comply "triggers the bond obligation and allows the court to keep any money given as security" (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Sam Altman's Next Move After The OpenAI Firing

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

On November 20 Altman, Brockman and colleagues announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, with Satya Nadella leaving the door open to other OpenAI staffers and saying they would be given the resources they needed should they choose to join. As reported by The Verge, however, Altman's move to Microsoft was not a done deal — both Altman and Brockman remained open to returning to OpenAI if the remaining board members who initially fired him stepped aside. At the same time, according to The Information, Altman had been telling investors he was planning to launch a new venture, with Brockman expected to join the effort in whatever form it took — possibly an AI chip startup. Altman also posted on X on November 18: "i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you're still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are."

Nadella himself hedged. In a series of interviews he stepped back from earlier reporting that Altman and Brockman were headed to Microsoft, telling CNBC: "Obviously, we want Sam and Greg to have a fantastic home if they're not going to be in OpenAI," and saying he was "open" to them settling at Microsoft or returning to OpenAI should the board and employees support the move.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.

# User-Generated Content

## Definition

User-generated content (UGC), in the corpus, is the term for content that ordinary platform users — rather than the platform itself or a news organization — create and publish, such as Reels, Stories, posts, and streams.
The EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) treats UGC as a defined regulatory object, requiring "social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content" to act on reports of illegal content and disinformation (doc_0025).
Snap itself describes the public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "authentic user-generated content" offering perspectives that traditional news outlets may not reflect (doc_0124).

## Context

The corpus treats UGC primarily as the object of content-moderation obligations and disputes rather than as a neutral technical term: the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) explicitly regulates "how social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content must respond to reports of illegal content," putting X under a legal obligation to act on flagged posts and mitigate disinformation risk (doc_0025).
On Meta's platforms, individual users' Reels and Stories about Palestine became the flashpoint for accusations of moderation bias, with filmmaker Khitam Jabr suspecting that her own Palestine travel Reels were restricted for 24 hours after other users reported them (doc_0106).
On Snapchat, an X user described the crowd-sourced public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who could not get on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" increase in Stories submissions from the region since October 7 (doc_0124).
Mozilla frames the broader problem as one of governance: today's large, advertiser-funded social networks decide how UGC is moderated and monetized, which is part of why it is building a decentralized "fediverse" alternative (doc_0026).
On Twitch, UGC is also an economic asset — streamers' broadcasts are the content being monetized, and disputes over revenue splits and the Partner Plus program center on how creators are compensated for the content they generate (doc_0401).

## Key Characteristics

- **User-originated** — the content is authored and published by ordinary platform users (e.g., Reels, Stories, posts, streams), not by the platform or a newsroom (doc_0106, doc_0124).
- **Subject to platform moderation and reporting** — UGC can be flagged, restricted, or shadowbanned by other users' reports or automated systems, as Jabr suspected happened to her Palestine travel videos (doc_0106).
- **Regulatory trigger** — under the DSA, a platform's responsibility to act on illegal UGC and disinformation is a defined legal obligation, not just a policy choice (doc_0025).
- **Real-time information source** — one X user called Snap Map's crowd-sourced Stories "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who weren't on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" rise in submissions from the region (doc_0124).
- **Monetizable** — UGC is also the basis for creator revenue-sharing arrangements, making its governance a business as well as a moderation issue (doc_0401).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "user-generated content" (UGC) — also called "user-created content" (UCC) — is generally defined as content generated by users of the Internet, such as images, videos, audio, text, testimonials, software, and user interactions (Wikipedia, "User-generated content," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content).

# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Bail

## Definition

Bail is the term the corpus uses for Sam Bankman-Fried's pretrial release from custody: a $250 million bond that let him live under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto instead of in jail while awaiting trial, and which a U.S. judge revoked in August 2023 (doc_0010, doc_0226).

## Context

The corpus's clearest illustration is Sam Bankman-Fried's case: after being arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022 and extradited to the U.S., he was released on a $250 million bail bond and confined to house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto (doc_0010). That release was not permanent — a U.S. judge revoked his bail in August 2023 after he was accused of intimidating former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison by leaking her private diary, leaving him in custody by the time his fraud trial began that October (doc_0010, doc_0226). Bail is also treated as something a court can simply refuse to grant: one recap of the FTX saga notes flatly that "SBF has been denied bail" (doc_0030). The concept resurfaces around Bankman-Fried's co-defendants, where house arrest — the condition often attached to bail — is described as a lighter alternative to imprisonment that cooperating felons like Gary Wang, Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison might still face even without prison time (doc_0121).

## Key Characteristics

- **Conditional, not unconditional freedom** — release on bail came bundled with restrictions (house arrest at a fixed address) rather than free movement (doc_0010).
- **Financially secured** — Bankman-Fried's release required a $250 million bail bond, tying his liberty to a monetary guarantee (doc_0010).
- **Revocable** — a judge can revoke bail mid-proceedings for conduct that violates its terms, as happened after the Ellison intimidation allegations, moving the defendant from house arrest to detention (doc_0010, doc_0226).
- **Discretionary and sometimes denied outright** — courts can decline to grant bail at all, as they did for Bankman-Fried at least once during his case (doc_0030).
- **Distinct from post-conviction outcomes** — bail concerns pretrial release, while house arrest can separately appear as a possible post-conviction alternative to imprisonment for cooperating defendants (doc_0121).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "bail" itself — it only reports how bail applied in Bankman-Fried's case.
Per Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, bail is "the money a defendant pays as a guarantee that they will show up in court at a later date," and release can be "conditioned on certain behavior of the defendant," such as staying away from an alleged victim (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).
A defendant's failure to comply "triggers the bond obligation and allows the court to keep any money given as security" (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# FTX's Cooperating Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).



---


# Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."



---


# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.



---


# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.



---


# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott and Jalen Hurts were the current favorites for 2023 NFL MVP after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff the longshots Sporting News argued bettors should consider, per its Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece.

But by that same logic, Sporting News argued, Jared Goff should be in the conversation: he had played well that season, his Lions were 9-3, described by Sporting News as poised to win the NFC South and in contention for the No. 1 seed in the conference — and compared to the 49ers, Cowboys and Eagles, Goff and the Lions may have had the easiest schedule to finish the season.

The case for C.J. Stroud rests on production and value. He led the league in passing yards, was one of four quarterbacks who had started the whole season with a passer rating over 100, and his touchdown-to-interception ratio was the best in the NFL at 4 to 1. As for the value of his play, Stroud had taken one of the worst teams in the NFL — 11 total wins over the previous three seasons — and turned it into a playoff contender and potential division champion.
