# National Basketball Association (NBA)

## Definition

The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the top professional men's basketball league in the United States, grouped in the corpus among "the four major US pro sports leagues" alongside the NFL, MLB, and NHL, and described elsewhere as "the pinnacle of the sport" of basketball.

## Context

In the corpus the NBA appears in three overlapping roles: as a cultural institution with its own holiday tradition, as a subject of sports betting coverage, and as a point of contrast with other basketball leagues.
Its Christmas Day games date back to 1947 and are described as a tradition older than the Super Bowl; last season's slate averaged 4.27 million viewers across platforms — about 200% more than a typical regular-season game — and games are broadcast to over 200 countries in more than 50 languages.
The league is regularly set up as a rival tradition to the NFL's Thanksgiving Day games, with commentary noting the NBA "far outperforms" the NFL in global popularity even though the NFL draws more domestic viewers.
A large share of the corpus's NBA coverage is sports-betting content — moneyline, point-spread, prop, and futures betting sites all use the NBA as their running example, and articles track odds for annual awards such as NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year.
The league is also used as a reference point by Australia's National Basketball League (NBL): NBL recaps describe several players as "ex-NBA" or "NBA hopeful," and note NBL clubs playing exhibition games against NBA opposition, distinguishing the two leagues while linking them through player movement.
Ticket-price reporting places the average 2022 NBA ticket at $94, versus $112 for the NFL, underscoring the NFL's larger domestic commercial scale even as the NBA is framed as more globally popular.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of the "four major" US leagues** — grouped with the NFL, MLB, and NHL as a top-tier US professional sports league.
- **Draft-based player pipeline** — teams acquire young talent through an annual draft, and draft outcomes ("draft misses") are tracked for their long-term effect on team success.
- **Regular season, playoffs, and marquee annual awards** — the league runs a regular season, playoffs, and honors such as the NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year, each with dedicated betting markets and odds coverage.
- **Signature holiday tradition** — Christmas Day games, dating to 1947 and older than the Super Bowl, function as the league's answer to the NFL's Thanksgiving games and are a major global broadcast event.
- **Global broadcast reach** — Christmas Day games alone are broadcast to more than 200 countries and translated into more than 50 languages.
- **Distinct from same-named/similar leagues abroad** — contrasted in the corpus with Australia's NBL, whose rosters and coverage frequently reference NBA-experienced or NBA-aspiring players.
- **A dominant subject of the sports-betting content ecosystem** — used as the default example league across moneyline, spread, prop, and futures betting explainers.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# SEOs Also Say Search Results Have Improved

The strongest challenge to the article's premise is that Sullivan was not the only person insisting search results have improved significantly: out of the dozen-plus SEOs the writer spoke with at length, nearly every single one said search results are way better than they used to be — just objectively more accurate, more useful, more difficult to manipulate.

What gives that testimony force is the absence of an incentive to flatter Google. Except for Sullivan, these were not people with a reason to praise the company; if anything, these were folks who lamented how much harder it had become for them to take advantage of Google.

The effect on the writer was disorientation rather than conviction. This was not what she had been noticing, and certainly not what she had been hearing from friends and journalists and friends who are journalists. Were all of us wrong, or engulfed in some kind of Baader-Meinhof frequency bias delusion? Had she been researching a nonexistent problem? Were Google results actually amazing? # Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

## Context

In the corpus the NBA appears in three overlapping roles: as a cultural institution with its own holiday tradition, as a subject of sports betting coverage, and as a point of contrast with other basketball leagues.
Its Christmas Day games date back to 1947 and are described as a tradition older than the Super Bowl; last season's slate averaged 4.27 million viewers across platforms — about 200% more than a typical regular-season game — and games are broadcast to over 200 countries in more than 50 languages.
The league is regularly set up as a rival tradition to the NFL's Thanksgiving Day games, with commentary noting the NBA "far outperforms" the NFL in global popularity even though the NFL draws more domestic viewers.
A large share of the corpus's NBA coverage is sports-betting content — moneyline, point-spread, prop, and futures betting sites all use the NBA as their running example, and articles track odds for annual awards such as NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year.

- **Regular season, playoffs, and marquee annual awards** — the league runs a regular season, playoffs, and honors such as the NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year, each with dedicated betting markets and odds coverage.

Team props range from which team will score the first bucket to the total points scored in a quarter to which team will lead at halftime, with the selection often robust, especially when high-profile teams play.

Futures bets are bets on events that will happen in the future, and Rookie of the Year is only one of them: legal online sportsbooks carry a wide selection of NBA futures. # Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

## Key Characteristics

- **Contender framing** — press describes a film as "Oscar bait" or "Oscar-baity" when its subject matter, cast, or pedigree seems engineered to attract Academy attention (doc_0094, doc_0192).
- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).
- **Persistent credential** — an Academy Award win or nomination becomes a standing descriptor attached to a person's name in unrelated coverage years or decades later (doc_0165, doc_0587, doc_0177).
- **Multi-category structure** — the season spans many competitive categories beyond lead acting, including Documentary Feature, International Film, Adapted Screenplay, and Animated Feature (doc_0126).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses awards-season vocabulary ("Oscar bait," "tipped to win") without stating when the season runs or how it culminates. Per Wikipedia, the film awards season "usually begins during November or December of the previous year," with the Academy Awards ceremony as its culmination, held "commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees" (Wikipedia, *Academy Awards*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Meta's Moderation During An Earlier Hamas-Israel Conflict

During an earlier Hamas-Israel conflict, the digital-rights organisation 7amleh documented more than 500 reports of Palestinian "digital rights violations" over the 13 days leading up to the ceasefire — including the removal and restriction of content, hashtags and accounts related to the conflict. The figure was recounted to TechCrunch for its 19 October 2023 report on Meta's moderation of Palestinian content.

Meta attributed some of the instances of perceived censorship to technical issues, such as one that prevented users in Palestine and Colombia from posting Instagram Stories. It attributed others to human error, such as blocking the hashtag for Al-Aqsa Mosque — the holy site where Israeli police clashed with Ramadan worshippers — because the name was mistaken for a terrorist organization. The company also blocked journalists in Gaza from WhatsApp without explanation.

Meta committed to implementing policy changes based on the report's recommendations, including updating its keywords associated with dangerous organizations, disclosing government requests to remove content, and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content. 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater added that Meta has improved its response to harassment, at least in comparison to other social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter): although harassment and abuse remain rampant on Instagram and Facebook, he said the company has been responsive to suspending accounts with patterns of targeting other users.

Abukhater's scope condition on all of this is that the improvements do not survive an escalation. "The balance of power is very fixed, in reality, between Israelis and Palestinians," he said. "And this is something that today is reflected heavily on platforms like Meta, even though they have human rights teams releasing reports and trying to improve upon their policies. Whenever an escalation like the one we're experiencing now happens, things just go back to zero."

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.

# Hypothesis: Search Anger Is Really General Internet Malaise

One possibility the writer began to worry about is that all the people who were mad about search results were upset about something that had nothing to do with metrics and everything to do with feelings and vibes — a universal, non-Google-specific resentment and rage about how the internet has made our lives so much worse in so many ways, dividing us and deceiving us and provoking us and making us sadder and lonelier.

The supporting observation is a broader change in mood: decades of American optimism about the wonderful potential of technology, from the Moon landing to personal computers to the iPhone, had finally, in the last few years, broken down into comprehensive chagrin at the petty, pathetic, and violent world enabled by our devices.

The hypothesis is posed as a question about attribution, and what would settle it is whether the anger tracks Google or SEOs at all. Was all that really Google's fault? Or the SEOs? Or was this about something deeper and more human: the will to exploit something so much we destroy it — to muddy it up, as Babin had put it, but while it worked, to make as much money as possible.

# ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

Roughly a year after its release, ChatGPT had 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also revealed that over two million developers use the platform, including more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Two other markers frame that scale. OpenAI hit the one-year anniversary of ChatGPT: what began as a "low-key research preview" evolved into a powerhouse that changed the AI industry forever, and Altman looked back on the night before its launch in a post on X on November 30, 2023 — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…" Meanwhile neither Apple nor Google chose an AI app as its app of the year for 2023, despite the success of ChatGPT's mobile app, which became the fastest-growing consumer application in history before that record was broken by Meta's Threads.

Adoption among the general public is far thinner than the headline numbers suggest. Ongoing polling by Pew Research shows that although ChatGPT is gaining mindshare, only about 18% of Americans have ever actually used it — suggesting the language model is not quite as popular or threatening as some would have you think.



---


# ChatGPT Misuse Fears Versus Observed Abuse

The premise under attack is the set of dire predictions made about ChatGPT's misuse: interestingly — and fortunately — some of them did not come to pass. Some researchers feared the chatbot would be used to generate disinformation on a massive scale, while others sounded the alarm over ChatGPT's phishing email-, spam- and malware-generating potential.

Those concerns had real effects: they pushed policymakers in Europe to mandate security assessments for any products using generative AI systems like ChatGPT, and led over 20,000 signatories — including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak — to sign an open letter calling for the immediate pause of large-scale AI experiments like ChatGPT.

The counter-evidence is observational, and TechCrunch attaches an explicit time limit to it: examples of ChatGPT abuse in the wild have been few and far between — so far.

TechCrunch's framing prediction for 2024, published on 19 December 2023, is that it will be the year when the hype runs full-steam into reality as people reckon with the capabilities and limitations of AI at large.

The premise is the year just ending: 2023 was a banger for AI as the technology went from niche to mainstream about as fast as anything ever has. The proposition would be falsified if that reckoning did not arrive — if capability claims went untested and limitations remained unexamined — and the article sets out a few specific ways the reckoning is expected to play out.

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. # Why Line Shopping Improves Returns

Line shopping is worth a bettor's time because it offers the chance to lay less, win more and improve your chances — and because it need not take long. The grounds start with a feature of how bets settle: when you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted, and if they later change, for better or worse, you are stuck with the odds from when you wagered. That is precisely why the shopping has to happen before the bet, though if significant changes occur afterward you can take more action at the improved odds or more favorable line.

The warrant is that a better price changes outcomes and cash flows, not skill. Getting more points or laying fewer on a typical NFL or NBA point spread might turn a bet you would otherwise lose into a winner, and finding better odds on any bet means dropping fewer dollars when you lose and earning more when you win. Sporting News is explicit about the limit: shopping lines will help you consistently find the best prices, but it will not help you pick more winners — it improves your chances and leads to bigger wins and more affordable losses.

The worked example is a half-point. Suppose you like the Kansas City Chiefs to beat the Cincinnati Bengals in a mid-season NFL game, and three of four licensed online sportsbooks in your state have the Chiefs at -3 while the fourth has them at -2.5. If the Chiefs win by exactly three — a distinct possibility, since a single field goal decides most NFL games — bets at the first three books push, while the fourth is a winner; without shopping you would never have found that half-point and would be stuck with a push instead of a profit.

The effort required is small: a live odds feed makes a basic survey a matter of seconds, and installing multiple licensed online sportsbook apps on your phone allows a more thorough shop in just a few minutes.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

Source: "Major League Baseball," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball

# Super Bowl

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).
Franchise identity is tied to it retroactively — the Cincinnati Bengals are described as having reached "a Super Bowl appearance in 2021" as the marker of the team's turnaround (doc_0071), and Travis Kelce is introduced as having "helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023" (doc_0044), with the Kansas City Chiefs subsequently referred to simply as "the defending Super Bowl champions" (doc_0059).
A Christmas Day matchup between the 49ers and Ravens is previewed explicitly as a "potential Super Bowl sneak peek" (doc_0003), showing how regular-season games get framed as previews of the eventual championship.

## Key Characteristics

- **Season-defining stakes** — teams and players are described relative to it long after the fact ("defending Super Bowl champions," "two-time Super Bowl MVP") (doc_0059, doc_0003).
- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).
- **Special-event betting draw** — sportsbooks single out "Super Bowl betting lines" alongside World Series odds and March Madness as flagship special-event markets carrying their own promotional bonuses (doc_0072).
- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "Super Bowl" itself — it only reports how teams, players, and betting markets relate to it.
Per Wikipedia, the Super Bowl is "the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), serving as the final game of each NFL season" (Wikipedia, *Super Bowl*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# Why Bettors Should Consider NFL Award Longshots — And Bet Them Small

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that with five weeks left in the regular season there was plenty of time for an NFL award longshot to become a contender, so bettors should consider them — but should keep those bets small.

The grounds for taking longshots seriously are that they are easy to overlook because each award has a favorite or favorites: a longshot may be playing well, but other players have commanded the spotlight, making it easier for them to go unnoticed, and whatever the reason, they have not gotten the credit they deserve. The timing argument follows: if you wait too long before placing a bet, your payout will be a lot less than if you were to roll the dice on a longshot right now.

The counterweight, and the warrant for the sizing advice, is that there is always a reason why a player or several players have relatively short odds — they have been the best at their position throughout the season — and consequently there is just as good a reason why longshots have odds as long as they do. So the recommendation is to keep your bets small, or use a bonus bet if one is available, on longshots; if they do go on to win, you can smile all the way to the bank while telling everyone, "I told you so."

# Data Breach

## Definition

A data breach, in the corpus, is an incident in which hackers or unintended exposure let unauthorized parties reach personal or organizational data — spanning the 2017 Equifax hack, the 2023 23andMe breach, an individual's hacked Roblox account, and, more loosely, TikTok's pre-consent data scraping, which a senator branded a "mass breach of privacy" (doc_0015, doc_0334, doc_0178, doc_0189).

## Context

The corpus uses the term across several registers of the same underlying event. The canonical reference point is the Equifax data breach of 2017, invoked in a discussion of Google's search-revenue deals as the event that made identity-theft-protection services like LifeLock a hot commercial topic (doc_0015). The clearest 2023 instance is 23andMe: hackers first accessed the personal data of about 14,000 users (0.1% of customers), a number the company later acknowledged undercounted the real scope, in a breach it disclosed in October 2023 (doc_0334). The same TechCrunch weekly roundup that covers 23andMe also reports a related but distinct exposure — patient scans and health records "spilling online" through security weaknesses in the decades-old DICOM medical-imaging standard, which made private data accessible on the open web without any hacker having to breach a perimeter at all (doc_0334). At smaller scale, the term extends to individual account compromise: Sarah Michelle Gellar described her son's Roblox account being "hacked," which she treated as serious enough to cancel a linked credit card (doc_0178). The corpus also shows the vocabulary of "breach" stretched to cover non-hacking exposure: Australian coverage of TikTok's tracking pixel, which scraped site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before consent was given, was branded a "mass breach of privacy" by a senator — a data-handling violation rather than an intrusion, but framed with the same breach language (doc_0189).

## Key Characteristics

- **Unauthorized access or exposure, not just data collection** — a breach denotes information reaching parties (or the open web) it was never meant to reach, whether via hacking (doc_0334, doc_0178) or unintentional exposure of insecure infrastructure (doc_0334's DICOM item).
- **Initial disclosures tend to understate scope** — 23andMe first quantified only 0.1% of customers as affected before acknowledging the wider group whose data was exposed (doc_0334).
- **Consequences reach beyond the breached company** — Gellar's response to her son's Roblox account being hacked was to cancel a family credit card, showing breach fallout propagating into unrelated financial accounts (doc_0178).
- **The term is applied loosely** — commentary uses "breach" both for classic hacking incidents (23andMe, Roblox) and for non-consensual data collection practices (TikTok's pixel), even though the latter is a policy/consent violation rather than an intrusion (doc_0189).

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), a data breach is any security incident in which unauthorized parties access sensitive, confidential, or protected information (IBM, "What Is a Data Breach?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.ibm.com/topics/data-breach).

# Why Line Shopping Improves Returns

Line shopping is worth a bettor's time because it offers the chance to lay less, win more and improve your chances — and because it need not take long. The grounds start with a feature of how bets settle: when you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted, and if they later change, for better or worse, you are stuck with the odds from when you wagered. That is precisely why the shopping has to happen before the bet, though if significant changes occur afterward you can take more action at the improved odds or more favorable line.

The warrant is that a better price changes outcomes and cash flows, not skill. Getting more points or laying fewer on a typical NFL or NBA point spread might turn a bet you would otherwise lose into a winner, and finding better odds on any bet means dropping fewer dollars when you lose and earning more when you win. Sporting News is explicit about the limit: shopping lines will help you consistently find the best prices, but it will not help you pick more winners — it improves your chances and leads to bigger wins and more affordable losses.

The worked example is a half-point. Suppose you like the Kansas City Chiefs to beat the Cincinnati Bengals in a mid-season NFL game, and three of four licensed online sportsbooks in your state have the Chiefs at -3 while the fourth has them at -2.5. If the Chiefs win by exactly three — a distinct possibility, since a single field goal decides most NFL games — bets at the first three books push, while the fourth is a winner; without shopping you would never have found that half-point and would be stuck with a push instead of a profit.

The effort required is small: a live odds feed makes a basic survey a matter of seconds, and installing multiple licensed online sportsbook apps on your phone allows a more thorough shop in just a few minutes.

# The SEO Naming Effect On Customer Acquisition

The Verge argued that Thai Food Near Me's name really did help the restaurant — but not through the mechanism its owners intended. The initial SEO "hack" was likely technically ineffective, but it was memorable and funny, and the joke led to many, many, many articles and forum posts about the restaurant's name, which tipped the SEO scales in its favor; all of that content, including The Verge's own story, will help the restaurant's prominence on Google platforms. One SEO trick, the reporter wrote, has eaten another.

The grounds for saying the direct hack failed are a test and a concession. A Google Maps search for "Thai food near me" from the reporter's home in Brooklyn yielded plenty of options literally near her but not Jirapraphanan's business a few miles away. Robert Sampson, a co-owner who handles much of the back-end work including SEO, followed the online discussion about the utility of the name and conceded part of it: "The people who said that [the name is] not such a good idea… I think they're responding more from a national brand campaign. It is true that if you're in California, and you type 'Thai food near me,' you're going to have a little bit of a hard time finding us. But for local search, I think the name works really well." Danny Sullivan's position was that a "near me" name is not a silver bullet for gaming the search algorithm.

The warrant connecting name to durable ranking is the feedback loop that follows a first visit. As with Thai Food Near Me, the most powerful thing an SEO-driven name might be able to do is get customers in the door; from there it is up to the business to give them a good experience, whether that is a great plate of pad see ew or the perfect haircut, and then the cycle continues — happy customers leave good reviews, and good reviews help the business's Google Maps profile rank higher. Felix Silva also uploads high-quality photos and videos to his page and shares updates, another SEO move, since some experts say active profiles can improve a business's rankings.

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# User-Generated Content

## Definition

User-generated content (UGC), in the corpus, is the term for content that ordinary platform users — rather than the platform itself or a news organization — create and publish, such as Reels, Stories, posts, and streams.
The EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) treats UGC as a defined regulatory object, requiring "social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content" to act on reports of illegal content and disinformation (doc_0025).
Snap itself describes the public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "authentic user-generated content" offering perspectives that traditional news outlets may not reflect (doc_0124).

## Context

The corpus treats UGC primarily as the object of content-moderation obligations and disputes rather than as a neutral technical term: the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) explicitly regulates "how social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content must respond to reports of illegal content," putting X under a legal obligation to act on flagged posts and mitigate disinformation risk (doc_0025).
On Meta's platforms, individual users' Reels and Stories about Palestine became the flashpoint for accusations of moderation bias, with filmmaker Khitam Jabr suspecting that her own Palestine travel Reels were restricted for 24 hours after other users reported them (doc_0106).
On Snapchat, an X user described the crowd-sourced public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who could not get on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" increase in Stories submissions from the region since October 7 (doc_0124).
Mozilla frames the broader problem as one of governance: today's large, advertiser-funded social networks decide how UGC is moderated and monetized, which is part of why it is building a decentralized "fediverse" alternative (doc_0026).
On Twitch, UGC is also an economic asset — streamers' broadcasts are the content being monetized, and disputes over revenue splits and the Partner Plus program center on how creators are compensated for the content they generate (doc_0401).

## Key Characteristics

- **User-originated** — the content is authored and published by ordinary platform users (e.g., Reels, Stories, posts, streams), not by the platform or a newsroom (doc_0106, doc_0124).
- **Subject to platform moderation and reporting** — UGC can be flagged, restricted, or shadowbanned by other users' reports or automated systems, as Jabr suspected happened to her Palestine travel videos (doc_0106).
- **Regulatory trigger** — under the DSA, a platform's responsibility to act on illegal UGC and disinformation is a defined legal obligation, not just a policy choice (doc_0025).
- **Real-time information source** — one X user called Snap Map's crowd-sourced Stories "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who weren't on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" rise in submissions from the region (doc_0124).
- **Monetizable** — UGC is also the basis for creator revenue-sharing arrangements, making its governance a business as well as a moderation issue (doc_0401).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "user-generated content" (UGC) — also called "user-created content" (UCC) — is generally defined as content generated by users of the Internet, such as images, videos, audio, text, testimonials, software, and user interactions (Wikipedia, "User-generated content," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content).

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# Regulatory Investigations Into OpenAI In 2023

OpenAI faced regulatory action on several fronts in 2023: Italy ordered ChatGPT blocked over GDPR concerns, Poland opened its own GDPR investigation, China's licensing regime pushed ChatGPT clients out of the App Store, and the FTC was reported to be investigating the chatbot's statements about people.

Italy moved first. Italy's data protection authority ordered OpenAI to stop processing people's data locally with immediate effect, saying it was concerned the ChatGPT maker was breaching the EU's General Data Protection Regulation and opening an investigation; OpenAI began geoblocking access to ChatGPT in Italy. The DPA then laid out what OpenAI needed to do for the order to be lifted, giving OpenAI a deadline of April 30 to complete the regulator's compliance demands, with a slightly more generous timeline of May 15 for a local radio, TV and internet awareness campaign. Poland's authority publicly announced it had opened an investigation regarding ChatGPT, accusing the company of a string of breaches of the GDPR.

In China, multiple generative AI apps were removed from Apple's China App Store ahead of the country's latest generative AI regulations, set to take effect August 15. Apple wrote in a letter to OpenCat, a native ChatGPT client: "As you may know, the government has been tightening regulations associated with deep synthesis technologies (DST) and generative AI services, including ChatGPT. DST must fulfill permitting requirements to operate in China, including securing a license from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Based on our review, your app is associated with ChatGPT, which does not have requisite permits to operate in China."

In the United States, the FTC was reportedly in at least the exploratory phase of an investigation into whether ChatGPT made "false, misleading, disparaging or harmful" statements about people. TechCrunch reporter Devin Coldewey noted that such an investigation does not appear out of thin air — the FTC does not look around and say "That looks suspicious"; generally a lawsuit or formal complaint is brought to its attention and the practices described imply that regulations are being ignored, much as a person suing a supplement company over pills that made them sick can prompt an FTC investigation because there is evidence the company lied about side effects. Separately, FTC chair Lina Khan and fellow commissioners warned House representatives in a congressional hearing that modern AI technologies like ChatGPT could be used to "turbocharge" fraud: "AI presents a whole set of opportunities, but also presents a whole set of risks," Khan said. "And I think we've already seen ways in which it could be used to turbocharge fraud and scams. We've been putting market participants on notice that instances in which AI tools are effectively being designed to deceive people can place them on the hook for FTC action."

# Apple's Privacy Stance Versus Google's Default Payments

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

Bellshaw asked Cue whether Apple believes user privacy is important, to which he said, "Absolutely." She then showed a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies, and Cue readily agreed with them: "We've always thought we had better privacy than Google." He said one provision of the ISA was that Google had to allow people to search without logging in, and that Apple has done things in Safari and around its platforms to make it harder for Google or anyone else to track users. Bellshaw never quite said it, but The Verge read the DOJ's implication as this: Google is a privacy menace anathema to everything Apple believes is important to its users, yet Apple gives it that central place because Google pays so handsomely. She then asked Cue to review some of Apple's financial filings and whether it is true that the ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits. Cue's rebuttal was that this is not how Apple looks at it, because the framing doesn't account for all the work Apple did to make its platform so appealing that an agreement like this could work as well as it does.
