# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# Terms of Service

## Definition

Terms of Service (also called T&Cs or "terms and conditions") is the corpus's label for a platform's or vendor's own rulebook, as distinct from external regulation such as the DSA, which compels how that rulebook must be written and enforced (doc_0024).

The corpus applies the same label to two different domains: platform content-moderation rules — paired with, but not identical to, a separately named "Community Guidelines" document in Discord's warning system (doc_0505) — and the commercial fine print that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Context

In the corpus the term recurs wherever a platform's own rulebook — rather than a law — is the thing being disputed or regulated. The EU's DSA obliges platforms to "clearly communicate their T&Cs to users and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement," which is the legal hook the Commission uses against X over illegal-content handling (doc_0024). Breton's letter to X separately flags a change to X's "public interest policy" — the sub-rule governing when rule-breaking posts stay up for newsworthiness — as having left users "uncertain" about how X applies its own rules, illustrating that ToS content itself, not just its existence, is subject to DSA transparency requirements (doc_0025). On Meta's platforms, the operative rulebook is branded "Community Guidelines": Instagram removed and restricted Palestine-related posts that users say complied with those Guidelines, and Meta's own newsroom statements point back to the Guidelines and an appeals process as the mechanism for contesting enforcement (doc_0106). Snapchat's Community Guidelines are described as prohibiting pornographic, terrorism-advocating, or gratuitously violent content — a similarly-scoped rulebook to Meta's (doc_0124). Discord's new warning system links violators directly to its "Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism," pairing the rulebook with a visible enforcement record (doc_0505). Outside content moderation, "terms and conditions" also names the commercial fine print — wagering requirements, banking limits, expiry windows — that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers, which users must accept before registering (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-authored, not statutory** — the rules originate with the service, distinguishing ToS from the regulations (e.g. the DSA) that constrain how it must be written and enforced.
- **Related but distinct rulebooks share the "terms" label** — "T&Cs" and "terms and conditions" name a platform's or vendor's own rules generally, while Meta and Snap label the content-moderation slice specifically "Community Guidelines"; Discord's warning system links to "Terms of Service," "Community Guidelines," and an appeal mechanism as three separate, companion items rather than one document (doc_0505).
- **Sub-policies can shift independently** — X's "public interest policy" changed without broader ToS changing, showing a rulebook is composed of adjustable sub-rules (doc_0025).
- **Transparency and enforcement is a regulatory target** — the DSA specifically requires clear communication of T&Cs and demonstrable enforcement, not merely that terms exist (doc_0024).
- **Disputed, uneven enforcement is a recurring failure mode** — users on Meta's platforms reported content removed despite compliance with Community Guidelines, and inconsistent enforcement (e.g. across Arabic vs. Hebrew content) became a trust and bias issue (doc_0106).
- **Domain-general usage** — the same "terms and conditions" label also covers non-moderation commercial conditions, such as wagering requirements attached to sportsbook bonuses (doc_0072).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "Terms of Service," "T&Cs," and "terms and conditions" throughout without ever stating a general definition for the term.

More broadly, terms of service — also called terms of use or terms and conditions — are the legal agreement between a service provider and its users: a person must agree to follow them to use the offered service, and for some websites they function simply as a disclaimer (Wikipedia, *Terms of service*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

# Why Bettors Should Consider NFL Award Longshots — And Bet Them Small

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that with five weeks left in the regular season there was plenty of time for an NFL award longshot to become a contender, so bettors should consider them — but should keep those bets small.

The grounds for taking longshots seriously are that they are easy to overlook because each award has a favorite or favorites: a longshot may be playing well, but other players have commanded the spotlight, making it easier for them to go unnoticed, and whatever the reason, they have not gotten the credit they deserve. The timing argument follows: if you wait too long before placing a bet, your payout will be a lot less than if you were to roll the dice on a longshot right now.

The counterweight, and the warrant for the sizing advice, is that there is always a reason why a player or several players have relatively short odds — they have been the best at their position throughout the season — and consequently there is just as good a reason why longshots have odds as long as they do. So the recommendation is to keep your bets small, or use a bonus bet if one is available, on longshots; if they do go on to win, you can smile all the way to the bank while telling everyone, "I told you so."

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# FTX's Marketing And Political Influence

FTX bought mainstream recognition through sports branding and paid celebrity partnerships, while Bankman-Fried separately cultivated political access on both sides of American politics — including, according to Lewis, a contemplated $5 billion offer to keep Donald Trump out of the next presidential race. TechCrunch documented the marketing side on 2023-10-01 and the political side on 2023-10-02.

On the branding side, the company gained somewhat mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships: in 2021 it bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena, it got its name branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos, and it partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, as well as Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal and Naomi Osaka, among others. The 2023-10-02 account puts figures on two of those friendships and lucrative marketing deals: Tom Brady was paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million, to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Even Anna Wintour, the fashion doyenne, was in contact — she reached out over a Zoom meeting to ask SBF, whose preferred get-up was wildly curly hair, t-shirts and cargo shorts, to sponsor her Met Costume Ball.

On the political side, Bankman-Fried had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to. Lewis said that he met with the young crypto king ahead of him seeing Mitch McConnell to discuss how he could fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party — a meeting for which the suit SBF brought was tightly balled up under his arm with his dress shoes falling out of the middle of the bundle. Lewis also claimed that SBF had concocted a plan to buy off Trump, to get him not to run again for president. "Like how much would it take to get an answer?" Lewis recounted; "There was a number that was kicking around… this was $5 billion." Lewis said Sam was never sure whether that figure came directly from Trump, and TechCrunch notes it is not known whether anything was ever wired. The giving was not one-sided: SBF also looked to back candidates on the Democratic side of the aisle.

# Terms of Service

## Definition

Terms of Service (also called T&Cs or "terms and conditions") is the corpus's label for a platform's or vendor's own rulebook, as distinct from external regulation such as the DSA, which compels how that rulebook must be written and enforced (doc_0024).

The corpus applies the same label to two different domains: platform content-moderation rules — paired with, but not identical to, a separately named "Community Guidelines" document in Discord's warning system (doc_0505) — and the commercial fine print that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Context

In the corpus the term recurs wherever a platform's own rulebook — rather than a law — is the thing being disputed or regulated. The EU's DSA obliges platforms to "clearly communicate their T&Cs to users and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement," which is the legal hook the Commission uses against X over illegal-content handling (doc_0024). Breton's letter to X separately flags a change to X's "public interest policy" — the sub-rule governing when rule-breaking posts stay up for newsworthiness — as having left users "uncertain" about how X applies its own rules, illustrating that ToS content itself, not just its existence, is subject to DSA transparency requirements (doc_0025). On Meta's platforms, the operative rulebook is branded "Community Guidelines": Instagram removed and restricted Palestine-related posts that users say complied with those Guidelines, and Meta's own newsroom statements point back to the Guidelines and an appeals process as the mechanism for contesting enforcement (doc_0106). Snapchat's Community Guidelines are described as prohibiting pornographic, terrorism-advocating, or gratuitously violent content — a similarly-scoped rulebook to Meta's (doc_0124). Discord's new warning system links violators directly to its "Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism," pairing the rulebook with a visible enforcement record (doc_0505). Outside content moderation, "terms and conditions" also names the commercial fine print — wagering requirements, banking limits, expiry windows — that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers, which users must accept before registering (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-authored, not statutory** — the rules originate with the service, distinguishing ToS from the regulations (e.g. the DSA) that constrain how it must be written and enforced.
- **Related but distinct rulebooks share the "terms" label** — "T&Cs" and "terms and conditions" name a platform's or vendor's own rules generally, while Meta and Snap label the content-moderation slice specifically "Community Guidelines"; Discord's warning system links to "Terms of Service," "Community Guidelines," and an appeal mechanism as three separate, companion items rather than one document (doc_0505).
- **Sub-policies can shift independently** — X's "public interest policy" changed without broader ToS changing, showing a rulebook is composed of adjustable sub-rules (doc_0025).
- **Transparency and enforcement is a regulatory target** — the DSA specifically requires clear communication of T&Cs and demonstrable enforcement, not merely that terms exist (doc_0024).
- **Disputed, uneven enforcement is a recurring failure mode** — users on Meta's platforms reported content removed despite compliance with Community Guidelines, and inconsistent enforcement (e.g. across Arabic vs. Hebrew content) became a trust and bias issue (doc_0106).
- **Domain-general usage** — the same "terms and conditions" label also covers non-moderation commercial conditions, such as wagering requirements attached to sportsbook bonuses (doc_0072).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "Terms of Service," "T&Cs," and "terms and conditions" throughout without ever stating a general definition for the term.

More broadly, terms of service — also called terms of use or terms and conditions — are the legal agreement between a service provider and its users: a person must agree to follow them to use the offered service, and for some websites they function simply as a disclaimer (Wikipedia, *Terms of service*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# Prediction: AI Agents And Generative Media Mature

TechCrunch predicts that some niche applications of AI models will grow beyond "eh" status in 2024, specifically agent-based models and generative multimedia.

For agents, the reasoning is that if AI is going to help you do more than summarize or make lists of things, it will need access to things like your spreadsheets, ticket buying interfaces and transportation apps. 2023 saw a few tentative attempts at this "agent" approach, but none really caught on, and the prediction is deliberately bounded: no agent is expected to really take off in 2024 either, but agent-based models will show their stuff a little more convincingly than they did the year before, and a few clutch use cases will show up for famously tedious processes such as submitting insurance claims.

For generative media, the prediction is that video and audio will find niches where their shortcomings are not quite so visible. In the hands of skilled creators, a lack of photorealism is not a problem, and AI video will be used in fun and interesting ways; likewise, generative music models will likely make it into a few major productions such as games, again where professional musicians can leverage the tools to create an unending soundtrack.

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Project Hug: Google's Developer Incentive Program, As Characterized By Both Sides

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

context:
# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers for the new system, first introduced in November 2022, and Match, as part of its settlement agreement, will also now take advantage of this option. Epic has declined to use it.

Google's defense of the commission rests on what it says the commission buys. It will argue that its commissions are not just tied to payment processing, but help it develop other features and controls to keep Android users safe and guide them to discovering new applications, as well as helping fund the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google also helps developers reach a broader audience beyond the mobile phone, with support for Android across platforms ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. And it notes that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues — so the headline 30% is the boundary case, not the typical one.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.



---


# Activision, Riot And Supercell's Abandoned Android Store Plans

Asked whether he believes Activision Blizzard really intended to build its own app store, Tim Sweeney said yes — Activision was building a store, with a large team of dozens of engineers building a mobile app store to launch on Android — and said that of the three companies, Riot is the strongest example, while he does not know about Supercell.

For Riot, Sweeney cited the documents in the case: Riot planned to distribute League of Legends directly through its website on mobile, exactly as it does on PC, and stuck to that plan until Google paid it off not to; at a minimum, he said, Google's payoff dissuaded Riot from distributing off Google Play. For Activision, his evidence is partly first-hand and partly documentary. Activision came to Epic and told Epic it was building the store; and after everything went down, Sweeney talked to an Activision employee close to that effort, working with the team building the store, who reported that the entire store team Activision had employed had been disbanded as soon as Activision signed its deal with Google. The Verge appended an editor's note that no such person was heard from at trial and that the interviewer would be eager to speak to them. Sweeney added that Activision was telling Google it was building the store, that Google's internal discussions said Google didn't want Activision building a competing store, and that after signing the deal Google staff were gleeful about having dissuaded perhaps their number one competitor at the time from launching its own store.

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Revenue Split

## Definition

A revenue split, in the corpus, is the percentage pair — such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5 — by which a platform and a counterparty divide proceeds: Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) with Android device makers and carriers, Google's 70/30 app-store split with developers, and Twitch's and Kick's subscription-revenue splits with streamers.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces across three unrelated disputes that share the same underlying mechanic: dividing proceeds between a platform and a counterparty. In the US v. Google antitrust trial, Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) pay Android device makers and wireless carriers like Verizon a cut in exchange for setting Google Search and Chrome as defaults. In the Epic v. Google trial, Epic argued that Google's 70/30 app-store revenue split with developers is likely descended from an arbitrary decision Valve made with Steam two decades earlier, rather than from any principled calculation of the value Google's store provides. On the creator-platform side, Twitch's default subscription revenue split for Partners is 50/50, with a premium 70/30 tier once offered to select streamers before Twitch discontinued it in favor of ad revenue; rival platform Kick instead lures streamers away with a 95/5 split.

## Key Characteristics

- **Expressed as a ratio** — revenue splits are stated as two percentages that sum to 100, such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5, denoting each party's share.
- **Applies across different platform relationships** — the corpus shows the same mechanic governing device-maker default agreements (Google RSAs), app-store developer terms (Google/Epic 70/30), and creator subscription payouts (Twitch, Kick).
- **A lever platforms adjust unilaterally** — Twitch changed its subscription split from a 70/30 deal for select streamers to a 50/50 default, then introduced the Partner Plus program to restore a 70/30 rate for qualifying creators, showing the split is a platform-controlled term rather than a fixed market rate.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. # OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.
