# Class Action Settlement

## Definition

A class action settlement is an agreement that resolves a class-action lawsuit before (or instead of) a full trial verdict, typically trading a payment and/or changed business practices from the defendant for an end to the collective claim, in place of the class-wide monetary and injunctive relief a plaintiff would otherwise seek at trial.

## Context

The corpus shows the pattern most clearly in the Epic v. Google app store litigation: Google settled separately with all 50 U.S. state attorneys general and a number of consumers who had brought parallel antitrust claims, and reached a last-minute settlement with Match Group as well, leaving Epic Games as the only original plaintiff still pursuing trial.
Match's settlement let it take advantage of Google's "User Choice Billing" program — a reduced-commission alternative payment option — rather than continuing to litigate; Epic's CEO Tim Sweeney called Match "an awesome partner" and said he hoped Match "got out of their settlement what they needed to get for their business," contrasting Match's choice to settle with Epic's decision to keep fighting because it viewed cash settlements as insufficient while Google's "Google tax" remained in place.
The Helena World Chronicle class action against Google and Alphabet illustrates what a plaintiff seeks when a settlement has not (yet) been reached: the suit asks for damages plus an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using their data to train AI products, showing the class-wide monetary-and-injunctive relief that a settlement would otherwise substitute for.
The corpus also shows settlements shaping corporate behavior after the fact: Apple's earlier keyboard class-action settlement is cited as a factor that "tipped the scales" toward redesigning the MacBook Pro keyboard and dropping the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Substitutes for trial** — a settlement ends the case without a jury verdict; in the Google app-store litigation, settling with the state AGs, consumers, and Match Group left only Epic to actually go to trial.
- **Terms can stay undisclosed** — the corpus notes it was "not clear" what the AG/consumer settlement included, and Google would not say whether it had offered Epic a settlement.
- **Can substitute non-cash remedies for damages** — Match's settlement gave it access to a reduced-commission billing option rather than (or alongside) a cash payment, illustrating that settlements can trade behavioral/business-practice changes for dropped claims.
- **Not universally accepted by co-plaintiffs** — Epic explicitly declined to settle on cash terms alone, showing settlement is a choice each plaintiff or plaintiff group makes independently even within the same litigation.
- **Downstream business impact** — Apple's keyboard settlement is presented as a cost that influenced a later product redesign decision, showing settlements can have effects beyond the parties strictly bound by them.

# Terms of Service

## Definition

Terms of Service (also called T&Cs or "terms and conditions") is the corpus's label for a platform's or vendor's own rulebook, as distinct from external regulation such as the DSA, which compels how that rulebook must be written and enforced (doc_0024).

The corpus applies the same label to two different domains: platform content-moderation rules — paired with, but not identical to, a separately named "Community Guidelines" document in Discord's warning system (doc_0505) — and the commercial fine print that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Context

In the corpus the term recurs wherever a platform's own rulebook — rather than a law — is the thing being disputed or regulated. The EU's DSA obliges platforms to "clearly communicate their T&Cs to users and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement," which is the legal hook the Commission uses against X over illegal-content handling (doc_0024). Breton's letter to X separately flags a change to X's "public interest policy" — the sub-rule governing when rule-breaking posts stay up for newsworthiness — as having left users "uncertain" about how X applies its own rules, illustrating that ToS content itself, not just its existence, is subject to DSA transparency requirements (doc_0025). On Meta's platforms, the operative rulebook is branded "Community Guidelines": Instagram removed and restricted Palestine-related posts that users say complied with those Guidelines, and Meta's own newsroom statements point back to the Guidelines and an appeals process as the mechanism for contesting enforcement (doc_0106). Snapchat's Community Guidelines are described as prohibiting pornographic, terrorism-advocating, or gratuitously violent content — a similarly-scoped rulebook to Meta's (doc_0124). Discord's new warning system links violators directly to its "Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism," pairing the rulebook with a visible enforcement record (doc_0505). Outside content moderation, "terms and conditions" also names the commercial fine print — wagering requirements, banking limits, expiry windows — that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers, which users must accept before registering (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-authored, not statutory** — the rules originate with the service, distinguishing ToS from the regulations (e.g. the DSA) that constrain how it must be written and enforced.
- **Related but distinct rulebooks share the "terms" label** — "T&Cs" and "terms and conditions" name a platform's or vendor's own rules generally, while Meta and Snap label the content-moderation slice specifically "Community Guidelines"; Discord's warning system links to "Terms of Service," "Community Guidelines," and an appeal mechanism as three separate, companion items rather than one document (doc_0505).
- **Sub-policies can shift independently** — X's "public interest policy" changed without broader ToS changing, showing a rulebook is composed of adjustable sub-rules (doc_0025).
- **Transparency and enforcement is a regulatory target** — the DSA specifically requires clear communication of T&Cs and demonstrable enforcement, not merely that terms exist (doc_0024).
- **Disputed, uneven enforcement is a recurring failure mode** — users on Meta's platforms reported content removed despite compliance with Community Guidelines, and inconsistent enforcement (e.g. across Arabic vs. Hebrew content) became a trust and bias issue (doc_0106).
- **Domain-general usage** — the same "terms and conditions" label also covers non-moderation commercial conditions, such as wagering requirements attached to sportsbook bonuses (doc_0072).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "Terms of Service," "T&Cs," and "terms and conditions" throughout without ever stating a general definition for the term.

More broadly, terms of service — also called terms of use or terms and conditions — are the legal agreement between a service provider and its users: a person must agree to follow them to use the offered service, and for some websites they function simply as a disclaimer (Wikipedia, *Terms of service*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Why Bettors Should Consider NFL Award Longshots — And Bet Them Small

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that with five weeks left in the regular season there was plenty of time for an NFL award longshot to become a contender, so bettors should consider them — but should keep those bets small.

The grounds for taking longshots seriously are that they are easy to overlook because each award has a favorite or favorites: a longshot may be playing well, but other players have commanded the spotlight, making it easier for them to go unnoticed, and whatever the reason, they have not gotten the credit they deserve. The timing argument follows: if you wait too long before placing a bet, your payout will be a lot less than if you were to roll the dice on a longshot right now.

The counterweight, and the warrant for the sizing advice, is that there is always a reason why a player or several players have relatively short odds — they have been the best at their position throughout the season — and consequently there is just as good a reason why longshots have odds as long as they do. So the recommendation is to keep your bets small, or use a bonus bet if one is available, on longshots; if they do go on to win, you can smile all the way to the bank while telling everyone, "I told you so."

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

Source: "Major League Baseball," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# E-E-A-T And The Shift Toward Institutional Authority

SEO Lily Ray's account of why Google results feel different from five or six years ago starts with Google's response to the disinformation panic around the 2016 election, which involved questioning the notion that the most reliable information could be chosen by a form of popularity — meaning how many links a site received from other sites. As a result the algorithm seemed to change its approach to links, especially for news and for sites offering legal, financial, or health advice, and instead paid more attention to what Google came to call E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness.

The relation holds over a restricted range rather than across all queries. Not every search query takes E-E-A-T into account; Google has described heightened concern over sites that could impact safety, happiness, and the ability to be an informed citizen. Within that range the effect is large: "E-E-A-T has had a pretty big impact on what types of results you see," Ray said, and her extensive research on how sites have fared under the new guidelines shows the pattern — Urban Dictionary, down; Mayo Clinic, up. Some people consider E-E-A-T part of what is making results better than ever; others see it as a form of censorship, disproportionately affecting right-wing perspectives.

The structural consequence is a reversal of Google's founding logic: for certain kinds of information Google had undone one of the fundamental elements that made its results appealing from the start, so that instead of wild-west crowdsourcing, search was often reinforcing institutional authority. This felt complicated at best. When it comes to health and wellness, for example, quackery is often in the eye of the beholder, and everyone knows someone who has struggled with the limits of Western medicine; so much of the original draw of the internet was the opportunity for outlier voices to be heard alongside established experts and elites. Looking back on all that had changed around what first attracted people to Google, from the introduction of ads to efforts to keep users within the universe of Google products, this seemed to be the last straw.

Ray herself is a 30-something jet-setter with black-line tattoos and an asymmetrical, dyed blonde pixie cut, caught for lunch in Brooklyn between speaking gigs in Chicago and Berlin, on a day when she was also managing a 35-person team at her digital marketing agency, posting multiple times an hour on social media, dog-sitting a Pomeranian whose "daddies" were at Burning Man, caring for her own mini Australian shepherd, and organizing a house party she expected to be late for because she first had to perform a rooftop DJ set at a different party.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. # Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Board Governance

In this corpus, board governance is illustrated by cases where a board of directors exercises (or conspicuously lacks) the power to oversee and remove a company's CEO: OpenAI's board firing Sam Altman, Flexport's board ousting Dave Clark, and FTX's absence of any board at all.

## Context

The corpus's clearest working example is OpenAI's board, which in November 2023 fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after "a deliberative review process" concluded he was "not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."
That framing treats board governance as a standing check on the CEO: the board's stated justification was not a business or legal failure but a breakdown in the information flow the board needs to do its job.
OpenAI's board itself sits atop a nonprofit structure that "preserved its nonprofit governance structure" even as the startup underneath pursued commercial growth, so the board's authority over the CEO ran through that nonprofit layer rather than ordinary shareholder control.
Board composition determines whose judgment gets exercised: OpenAI's board consisted of chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and three non-employee directors (Adam D'Angelo, Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner), and the subsequent standoff over reinstating Altman turned on negotiating a new board (Bret Taylor, Larry Summers, Adam D'Angelo) as a condition of his return.
The corpus also frames board governance by its absence: Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang testified he was "concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors" before investing anyway, though on cross-examination he said Bankman-Fried told him he didn't want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.
Flexport's board, by contrast, illustrates governance operating through composition rather than absence: a board "made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder" held quarterly meetings on June 1 and Aug. 31 before Clark was forced to resign on Sept. 5.

## Key Characteristics

- **Power to remove or reinstate the CEO** — OpenAI's board fired Altman outright, then negotiated the terms (including its own reconstitution) under which he could return.
- **Grounded in a formal duty to oversee, not just advise** — the board's justification for firing Altman was specifically that his conduct hindered "its ability to exercise its responsibilities," i.e., an oversight duty rather than a performance complaint.
- **Structure shapes authority** — OpenAI's nonprofit board sat above the commercial subsidiary, giving it authority that ordinary shareholder-elected boards would not have over a purely for-profit company.
- **Composition determines outcome** — who sits on the board (employee vs. non-employee directors, investor-aligned vs. independent) is itself a lever contested during crises, as seen in both the OpenAI reinstatement talks and Flexport's investor-heavy board.
- **Its absence is itself notable** — the corpus flags FTX's lack of a board of directors as a specific governance gap investors identified before FTX's collapse, distinguishing "no oversight body" from "an oversight body that failed."

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, corporate governance is generally defined as the mechanisms, processes, and relations by which corporations are directed and controlled by their boards of directors, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders.
The widely cited Cadbury Report formulation puts it more simply: corporate governance is "the system by which companies are directed and controlled."
Source: [Corporate governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_governance), Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02.

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Generative AI Guardrails

## Definition

Generative AI guardrails are the constraints — technical, procedural, or regulatory — that companies and lawmakers put around a generative AI system to keep its outputs within intended bounds, whether that means blocking unsafe content, curbing hallucinations, or preventing misuse.

## Context

The corpus uses "guardrails" for three distinct layers of this idea. At the model layer, guardrails are safety filters meant to stop a chatbot from discussing controversial or dangerous topics: Google's Gemini Pro had such filters, but AI security researchers at Robust Intelligence used an automated prompt-mutation method to make the guardrails fail, getting the model to suggest ways to steal from a charity and to plan an assassination. At the product layer, guardrails are the deployment constraints a company layers on top of a model to fit a specific audience — Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" restricts its generative AI to kid-friendly trivia, sourced from only two vetted partners and generated offline with human-plus-AI review, precisely because "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions." OpenAI likewise announced guardrails meant to stop ChatGPT from generating and amplifying political disinformation, though the Washington Post found in an August report that those guardrails "actually weren't" enforced, with the system readily producing partisan campaign messaging on request. At the regulatory layer, guardrails is the term lawmakers and creative-industry advocates use for rules imposed on AI from outside the company building it: a news-publisher antitrust suit against Google sought court-ordered "guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas," California's CPPA drafted privacy guardrails for automated decisionmaking technology, FTC roundtable participants in the creative industries floated copyright law as a guardrail against training on artists' work without consent, and EU lawmakers agreed to a "two-tier" system of guardrails for general-purpose AI foundation models.

## Key Characteristics

- **Multi-layered** — guardrails appear at the model level (safety filters), the product level (deployment-time content and audience restrictions), and the regulatory level (externally imposed rules), each addressing a different point of failure.
- **Meant to counter specific failure modes** — the corpus ties guardrails directly to named risks: hallucination and inappropriate content for kids (Amazon), political disinformation (OpenAI/ChatGPT), jailbreak-style prompt attacks (Google Gemini Pro), privacy harms from automated decisionmaking (CPPA), and unauthorized use of creative work in training (FTC roundtable).
- **Can fail or go unenforced** — guardrails are not guaranteed to hold: Gemini Pro's guardrails were defeated by an automated jailbreak technique, and OpenAI's disinformation guardrails were found by the Washington Post to not actually be enforced despite being announced.
- **Tiered by risk in regulation** — the EU AI Act's negotiated deal applies a "two-tier" guardrail system to general-purpose AI, with lighter transparency duties for standard foundation models and heavier obligations (model evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting) for "high-impact" models with systemic risk.
- **Sought as external legal remedy** — plaintiffs and regulators use "guardrails" to describe court-ordered or statutory constraints they want imposed on AI companies, as in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit against Google and the CPPA's draft ADMT privacy rules.

# Appeals Process

## Definition

An appeals process is a defined mechanism that lets a party formally challenge a decision — a content-moderation action, a disciplinary penalty, or a court ruling — and have it reconsidered by a different decision-maker, rather than accepting the original ruling as final.

## Context

The corpus shows this same structure recurring across three distinct domains. Social platforms build appeals processes into their content-moderation systems: Meta states "there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it," and separately says it "continue[s] to provide tools for users to appeal our decisions if they think we made a mistake" during its Israel-Hamas war content response, while Discord's new account-standing system "link[s] out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism" whenever it notifies a user of a policy violation and restricts their account. In sports governance, Everton's appeal against a 10-point Premier League deduction "will be heard by a different three-person panel" than the one that issued the penalty — the hallmark of an appeals process, a distinct reconsidering body rather than the original decision-maker revisiting its own call. In litigation, an appeal is the formal next step after a verdict or ruling: Bankman-Fried's defense lawyers were "laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments" during his trial, and Apple's patent-infringement loss triggers an "appeals process" that "can take around 18 months" and can determine whether an import ban stays in effect while the case is contested.

## Key Characteristics

- **Distinct reviewing authority** — an appeal is reheard by a different decision-maker than the one who made the original call, as with Everton's separate three-person panel.
- **Available after an adverse decision** — content removals, disciplinary points deductions, and trial verdicts all trigger the same downstream option to contest the outcome.
- **Can be lengthy** — legal appeals are explicitly time-consuming; Apple's appeal of its Apple Watch import ban "can take around 18 months," during which the underlying decision may still take effect unless a stay is separately granted.
- **Built into platform enforcement systems as a safeguard against error** — Meta frames its appeals process as compensating for moderation mistakes ("we can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process") rather than as an admission the underlying policy is wrong, while Discord links its warning notices out to its own appeal mechanism whenever it restricts a user's account for a policy violation.
- **Does not guarantee reversal** — Everton's manager Dyche urges his players to "forget about the appeal and accept the reality" rather than assume it will succeed, underscoring that lodging an appeal only obtains reconsideration, not a favorable outcome.

# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Bot Detection

Bot detection is the set of technical and policy methods a platform uses to identify automated or fake accounts and unwanted bulk activity — spam, phishing, malware, and inauthentic engagement — and to make running them costly or infeasible.
In the corpus it names both the *identification* problem (telling a bot or bulk sender apart from a genuine user) and the *deterrence* problem (raising the cost of operating one), and platforms pursue the two together rather than treating either as sufficient on its own.

## Context

X gives the corpus's most explicit account: director of engineering Eric Farraro described X's existing detection layer as "traditional heuristics and models to detect fake accounts [and] engagement on the platform," which the company runs alongside newer identity-based friction — payment, phone, and ID verification, plus the $1-per-year fee — because heuristic detection alone was not stopping the platform's bot problem.
Farraro framed the challenge as a moving target: he warned that within a matter of years AI would be able to mimic human interactions, solving CAPTCHAs and generating photos and videos "undetectable by human or AI countermeasures," asking rhetorically, "If you can avoid getting identified as a bot, why can't an intelligent AI do the same?"
Elsewhere in the corpus, detection and deterrence take non-account-verification forms: Gmail's 2023 rules for bulk senders required email authentication, an easy unsubscribe path, and staying under a reported spam-rate threshold, which functions as a spam-detection and deterrence regime for email rather than social accounts.
Google Search's decade-plus SEO fight — the Panda and Penguin algorithm updates aimed at "spammers and marketers" — is the same identify-and-raise-the-cost logic applied to search ranking manipulation instead of fake accounts.
The concern also surfaces prospectively: commentators feared ChatGPT could be used to generate spam, phishing email, and malware at scale, and Apple cited the risk of enabling "unwanted messages, spam, and phishing attacks" as its stated reason for blocking Beeper Mini's iMessage bridge.
The Supreme Court's NetChoice cases touch the same terrain from a policy angle: Senator Ron Wyden — who co-authored Section 230 — argued that the First Amendment lets platforms refuse to host "hateful content, misinformation and spam," tying automated content moderation directly to a platform's ability to police spam.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two complementary strategies** — heuristic/model-based detection (flagging accounts or content algorithmically) and cost-based deterrence (fees, verification, authentication requirements) are run together, not as substitutes; Farraro stated explicitly that "these two things are not mutually exclusive."
- **Economics of deterrence** — the goal critics and X itself describe is not eliminating bots outright but raising the cost of running one; Musk called a bot's cost "a fraction of a penny" and said even a $1 fee would make manipulation "1000x harder," while Farraro's stated aim was to make bot operation "difficult and expensive enough that it's less and less viable."
- **Deterrence is contested, not settled** — critics such as Matt Mullenweg argued that determined spammers already spend far more than $1 per year (buying domains, using stolen credit cards and identities), so a small fee only forces a "short-term drop in bots while the bad guys update their scripts."
- **Detection is an adversarial, moving target** — Farraro's own argument for keeping multiple detection layers was that AI would soon defeat CAPTCHA-style and heuristic bot-catching methods, so any single detection method degrades over time.
- **Applies beyond social accounts** — the same identify-and-deter pattern appears in email (Gmail's bulk-sender authentication and spam-rate rules) and in search (Google's anti-SEO-spam algorithm updates), not only in social-platform bot-catching.
- **Friction has side effects** — verification and fee-based deterrence can also burden or exclude genuine users, which is the objection raised against X's fee (digital-divide concerns) independent of whether it deters bots.
