# ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

Roughly a year after its release, ChatGPT had 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also revealed that over two million developers use the platform, including more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Two other markers frame that scale. OpenAI hit the one-year anniversary of ChatGPT: what began as a "low-key research preview" evolved into a powerhouse that changed the AI industry forever, and Altman looked back on the night before its launch in a post on X on November 30, 2023 — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…" Meanwhile neither Apple nor Google chose an AI app as its app of the year for 2023, despite the success of ChatGPT's mobile app, which became the fastest-growing consumer application in history before that record was broken by Meta's Threads.

Adoption among the general public is far thinner than the headline numbers suggest. Ongoing polling by Pew Research shows that although ChatGPT is gaining mindshare, only about 18% of Americans have ever actually used it — suggesting the language model is not quite as popular or threatening as some would have you think.

# How To Line Shop, Including Futures Markets

The easiest way to line-shop is to find a live odds feed that shows the differences between lines and odds for the same bets at many of the top sportsbooks in the country; it is a one-stop shop and takes just seconds. First, look at such a feed for current opportunities. Second, if you want to go further, perform the task manually — it takes longer but lets you check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds. Third, to do that, download and install more than one of the best sports betting apps on your phone. Fourth, tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan.

Futures deserve their own pass, and this is where the payoff is largest. People tend to bet futures at their favorite online sportsbook, but shopping for better odds on any futures bet is worth the time: most game lines are similar across sportsbooks, whereas the odds in futures markets can vary significantly.

The precondition for those differences is a book's own exposure, and timing governs whether you capture them. Sportsbooks sometimes carry higher liabilities for specific teams and offer better odds on others to lay that off; get the timing right and you can easily take advantage of changes in different futures markets driven by liability. The limit is that the only way to find these opportunities is to shop lines.

# NBA Props And Futures: What They Cover And When To Bet Them

NBA player and team props are growing in popularity, and sportsbooks are providing more NBA props than ever, because it is much easier to focus on a single player and how he will perform than on the entire team. Player props might cover how many points a player scores or how many rebounds he pulls down, typically provided in an over/under format. Team props range from which team will score the first bucket to the total points scored in a quarter to which team will lead at halftime, with the selection often robust, especially when high-profile teams play.

Futures bets are bets on events that will happen in the future, and Rookie of the Year is only one of them: legal online sportsbooks carry a wide selection of NBA futures. They can usually be bet throughout the year, including well before the season starts and through the regular season, and the further away from the event, the more likely you are to find heavier odds in your favor.

Alongside futures, bettors can wager on many NBA markets during the regular season and postseason. Game lines — moneylines, point spreads and totals — are the most popular, but team and player props, parlays and more are also available. The NBA is the second-most popular odds market to bet on in the US, behind NFL betting odds, which means every online betting site always has a great selection of NBA odds.

# Super Bowl

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).
Franchise identity is tied to it retroactively — the Cincinnati Bengals are described as having reached "a Super Bowl appearance in 2021" as the marker of the team's turnaround (doc_0071), and Travis Kelce is introduced as having "helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023" (doc_0044), with the Kansas City Chiefs subsequently referred to simply as "the defending Super Bowl champions" (doc_0059).
A Christmas Day matchup between the 49ers and Ravens is previewed explicitly as a "potential Super Bowl sneak peek" (doc_0003), showing how regular-season games get framed as previews of the eventual championship.

## Key Characteristics

- **Season-defining stakes** — teams and players are described relative to it long after the fact ("defending Super Bowl champions," "two-time Super Bowl MVP") (doc_0059, doc_0003).
- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).
- **Special-event betting draw** — sportsbooks single out "Super Bowl betting lines" alongside World Series odds and March Madness as flagship special-event markets carrying their own promotional bonuses (doc_0072).
- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "Super Bowl" itself — it only reports how teams, players, and betting markets relate to it.
Per Wikipedia, the Super Bowl is "the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), serving as the final game of each NFL season" (Wikipedia, *Super Bowl*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Ecosystem And Unit-Economics Challenge Of Battery Swapping

Battery swapping's promise for consumers is large but its economics and ecosystem requirements are the binding constraint. A recent report jointly created by Bain & Company and Blume Ventures forecast that electric two-wheelers sold without batteries can reduce the upfront cost of vehicles by 40% to 50%, attracting price-sensitive Indian customers — but it also warned that building a battery-swapping ecosystem in India will be challenging in the near term, and suggested maintaining a battery-swapping inventory for top SKUs across manufacturers, identifying customer segments to target, and establishing "walled-garden" partnerships to support swappable-battery systems.

An investor told TechCrunch that to really succeed, the market needs interoperability and standardization in battery swapping, similar to how we have USB-C in phones nowadays. For Gogoro, it is just a start to explore how big a dent it can make in the overall EV market with its available battery-swapping solution.

Gogoro's CEO Horace Luke conceded the scale of the build-out required: "I got an entire ecosystem I need to bring in. It took us a little while to get ready, and it will take us a little while to ramp up. And I'm not fooling anybody that this thing is going to [happen] overnight. India's a huge place. There's a lot of different use cases. The price-performance people ask for is very high . . . So, through making more of the components and making more parts in India, with our Indian suppliers, we'll definitely start, and then more and more localization would certainly help."

The same tension was flagged more generally in TechCrunch's 9 December 2023 roundup: consumer EV battery swapping could usher in freedom for a wide range of people, allowing them to participate in the EV transition in ways that traditional built-in batteries do not, but the challenge is making the unit economics work.

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# Console Hardware

## Definition

In the corpus, "console hardware" refers to physical gaming devices — home consoles like the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and portable or hybrid handhelds like the Nintendo Switch and Valve's Steam Deck — treated as fixed platforms that specific games are tied to, that get revised with mid-cycle refreshes, and that ship with matched first-party controllers.

## Context

In the corpus, console hardware surfaces in two recurring forms: home consoles that plug into a TV (PS5, Xbox Series X/S) and portable or hybrid handhelds (Nintendo Switch, Steam Deck) that can also dock to a screen.
Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is described as a "PS5 exclusive," tying a specific game to specific console hardware, while the "Console Wars" framing pits Xbox and PlayStation hardware against each other directly.
A macOS gaming review notes Lies of P shipping the same day on "PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Windows," using console hardware names as shorthand for distinct target platforms alongside PC.
The Steam Deck OLED coverage treats the device explicitly as console-adjacent hardware: Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais describes enabling the Steam Deck to work as a "hybrid living room console" as a "side goal" of the team, and reviewers compare it functionally to the Wii U as "a portable console to use around the house."
Fan reaction to the Microsoft-Activision deal shows console hardware driving business concerns: fans worried Activision titles like Crash Bandicoot and Spyro, once PlayStation exclusives, could again become tied to a single console's hardware ecosystem.
Controllers are treated as accessories to specific console hardware families — the Xbox Wireless Controller for Xbox Series X/S, the DualSense for PS5, the Switch Pro Controller for Switch — each controller's design and compatibility defined by the console hardware it ships with.

## Key Characteristics

- **Bundled, factory-fixed components** — a console's chip, screen, and battery are packaged together at manufacture, released as a new unit rather than sold as separate upgrades; the Steam Deck OLED combines a die-shrunk AMD APU (same CPU and GPU, just more power-efficient) with a new 7.4-inch HDR OLED screen and a 25 percent larger battery.
- **Mid-cycle hardware refreshes** — manufacturers revise console hardware within a generation without launching a full sequel; the Steam Deck OLED is explicitly "not the Steam Deck 2," described as a die-shrunk chip plus display refresh similar to the Switch OLED update, and paralleled by Sony's PS4 Slim/PS5 Slim revisions.
- **Home vs. portable/hybrid form factors** — PS5 and Xbox Series X/S are TV-connected home consoles, while Switch and Steam Deck are handhelds that can also dock to a television, blurring the line between "portable" and "living room console."
- **Platform-exclusive software ties** — console hardware can gate which games are playable on it, as with Spider-Man 2's PS5 exclusivity and the fan concern that Activision titles could become exclusive to one console family again.
- **Dedicated first-party controllers** — each console hardware line ships with a matched first-party controller (Xbox Wireless Controller, DualSense, Switch Pro Controller) that defines the baseline input experience for that hardware, with third parties building compatible alternatives around it.

## Background (external)

General definition, not corpus-sourced: a video game console is an electronic device that outputs a video signal to display a game, typically played with a controller.
It is distinguished from a PC by shipping with a fixed, manufacturer-preselected set of hardware components rather than user-configurable parts, which lets console makers optimize the design around that fixed hardware and gives developers a stable, unchanging performance target.
Handhelds are consoles that build the display and controls into a single portable unit with a battery, and hybrids (like the Nintendo Switch) combine handheld and home-console use.
(Source: Wikipedia, "Video game console," Wikimedia Foundation, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console)

# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.

# Appeals Process

## Definition

An appeals process is a defined mechanism that lets a party formally challenge a decision — a content-moderation action, a disciplinary penalty, or a court ruling — and have it reconsidered by a different decision-maker, rather than accepting the original ruling as final.

## Context

The corpus shows this same structure recurring across three distinct domains. Social platforms build appeals processes into their content-moderation systems: Meta states "there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it," and separately says it "continue[s] to provide tools for users to appeal our decisions if they think we made a mistake" during its Israel-Hamas war content response, while Discord's new account-standing system "link[s] out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism" whenever it notifies a user of a policy violation and restricts their account. In sports governance, Everton's appeal against a 10-point Premier League deduction "will be heard by a different three-person panel" than the one that issued the penalty — the hallmark of an appeals process, a distinct reconsidering body rather than the original decision-maker revisiting its own call. In litigation, an appeal is the formal next step after a verdict or ruling: Bankman-Fried's defense lawyers were "laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments" during his trial, and Apple's patent-infringement loss triggers an "appeals process" that "can take around 18 months" and can determine whether an import ban stays in effect while the case is contested.

## Key Characteristics

- **Distinct reviewing authority** — an appeal is reheard by a different decision-maker than the one who made the original call, as with Everton's separate three-person panel.
- **Available after an adverse decision** — content removals, disciplinary points deductions, and trial verdicts all trigger the same downstream option to contest the outcome.
- **Can be lengthy** — legal appeals are explicitly time-consuming; Apple's appeal of its Apple Watch import ban "can take around 18 months," during which the underlying decision may still take effect unless a stay is separately granted.
- **Built into platform enforcement systems as a safeguard against error** — Meta frames its appeals process as compensating for moderation mistakes ("we can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process") rather than as an admission the underlying policy is wrong, while Discord links its warning notices out to its own appeal mechanism whenever it restricts a user's account for a policy violation.
- **Does not guarantee reversal** — Everton's manager Dyche urges his players to "forget about the appeal and accept the reality" rather than assume it will succeed, underscoring that lodging an appeal only obtains reconsideration, not a favorable outcome.

# ChatGPT Subscription Tiers And Pricing

ChatGPT is sold in a ladder of paid tiers on top of the free chatbot: ChatGPT Plus at $20 per month, a previewed ChatGPT Business tier, and ChatGPT Enterprise — with the tiers distinguished mainly by data-usage policy, control over end users, and access to the newest models.

The ladder was built in stages. OpenAI first said it was "starting to think about how to monetize ChatGPT" in an announcement on the company's official Discord server, posting a waitlist for a version to be called ChatGPT Professional; the waitlist document listed benefits including no "blackout" windows, no throttling and an unlimited number of messages — "at least 2x the regular daily limit." A month later OpenAI launched a pilot subscription plan, ChatGPT Plus, starting at $20 per month. It then previewed ChatGPT Business, described as "for professionals who need more control over their data as well as enterprises seeking to manage their end users"; OpenAI wrote that "ChatGPT Business will follow our API's data usage policies, which means that end users' data won't be used to train our models by default," and planned to make it available in the coming months. ChatGPT Enterprise followed, able to perform the same tasks as ChatGPT — writing emails, drafting essays, debugging computer code — while adding "enterprise-grade" privacy and data analysis capabilities on top of vanilla ChatGPT, along with enhanced performance and customization options.

Capacity became a binding constraint. Following the Dev Day conference, Sam Altman announced the company was pausing new subscriptions for ChatGPT Plus because of a "surge of usage"; the temporary hold on sign-ups, together with demand for new Plus features such as making custom GPTs, led to a slew of resellers on eBay. On December 13, 2023 Altman announced sign-ups had been re-enabled: "we have re-enabled chatgpt plus subscriptions! thanks for your patience while we found more gpus." The Plus subscription includes access to GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Jury Attentiveness And The Speed Of The Epic Verdict

Tim Sweeney told The Verge that the rapid verdict initially caused "some trepidation," because the conventional wisdom attorneys give is that a fast jury verdict is typically not good for plaintiffs making a complicated case — but the outcome was "a great relief," and in the moment he smiled, shook the Google attorney's hand, and clapped Epic lawyer Bornstein on the back.

Sweeney also said Epic had suspected all along that the jury was following the case carefully: jurors "weren't snoozing off as you might expect with the complexity of these documents," but were looking at the question asker and the witness, taking notes, and reading documents. He took this as evidence "that the justice system works, even with the most complex type of tech antitrust case that you can possibly throw at a jury" — the jury "got it, they got it quickly," and were able to pull the case apart and contrast it with what he called the fiction of the story Google was trying to tell. The Verge added an editor's note that every journalist in the courtroom agreed the jury was attentive, and that most were also surprised by the rapid verdict.

# Data Breach

## Definition

A data breach, in the corpus, is an incident in which hackers or unintended exposure let unauthorized parties reach personal or organizational data — spanning the 2017 Equifax hack, the 2023 23andMe breach, an individual's hacked Roblox account, and, more loosely, TikTok's pre-consent data scraping, which a senator branded a "mass breach of privacy" (doc_0015, doc_0334, doc_0178, doc_0189).

## Context

The corpus uses the term across several registers of the same underlying event. The canonical reference point is the Equifax data breach of 2017, invoked in a discussion of Google's search-revenue deals as the event that made identity-theft-protection services like LifeLock a hot commercial topic (doc_0015). The clearest 2023 instance is 23andMe: hackers first accessed the personal data of about 14,000 users (0.1% of customers), a number the company later acknowledged undercounted the real scope, in a breach it disclosed in October 2023 (doc_0334). The same TechCrunch weekly roundup that covers 23andMe also reports a related but distinct exposure — patient scans and health records "spilling online" through security weaknesses in the decades-old DICOM medical-imaging standard, which made private data accessible on the open web without any hacker having to breach a perimeter at all (doc_0334). At smaller scale, the term extends to individual account compromise: Sarah Michelle Gellar described her son's Roblox account being "hacked," which she treated as serious enough to cancel a linked credit card (doc_0178). The corpus also shows the vocabulary of "breach" stretched to cover non-hacking exposure: Australian coverage of TikTok's tracking pixel, which scraped site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before consent was given, was branded a "mass breach of privacy" by a senator — a data-handling violation rather than an intrusion, but framed with the same breach language (doc_0189).

## Key Characteristics

- **Unauthorized access or exposure, not just data collection** — a breach denotes information reaching parties (or the open web) it was never meant to reach, whether via hacking (doc_0334, doc_0178) or unintentional exposure of insecure infrastructure (doc_0334's DICOM item).
- **Initial disclosures tend to understate scope** — 23andMe first quantified only 0.1% of customers as affected before acknowledging the wider group whose data was exposed (doc_0334).
- **Consequences reach beyond the breached company** — Gellar's response to her son's Roblox account being hacked was to cancel a family credit card, showing breach fallout propagating into unrelated financial accounts (doc_0178).
- **The term is applied loosely** — commentary uses "breach" both for classic hacking incidents (23andMe, Roblox) and for non-consensual data collection practices (TikTok's pixel), even though the latter is a policy/consent violation rather than an intrusion (doc_0189).

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), a data breach is any security incident in which unauthorized parties access sensitive, confidential, or protected information (IBM, "What Is a Data Breach?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.ibm.com/topics/data-breach).

# Console Hardware

## Definition

In the corpus, "console hardware" refers to physical gaming devices — home consoles like the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, and portable or hybrid handhelds like the Nintendo Switch and Valve's Steam Deck — treated as fixed platforms that specific games are tied to, that get revised with mid-cycle refreshes, and that ship with matched first-party controllers.

## Context

In the corpus, console hardware surfaces in two recurring forms: home consoles that plug into a TV (PS5, Xbox Series X/S) and portable or hybrid handhelds (Nintendo Switch, Steam Deck) that can also dock to a screen.
Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is described as a "PS5 exclusive," tying a specific game to specific console hardware, while the "Console Wars" framing pits Xbox and PlayStation hardware against each other directly.
A macOS gaming review notes Lies of P shipping the same day on "PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Windows," using console hardware names as shorthand for distinct target platforms alongside PC.
The Steam Deck OLED coverage treats the device explicitly as console-adjacent hardware: Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais describes enabling the Steam Deck to work as a "hybrid living room console" as a "side goal" of the team, and reviewers compare it functionally to the Wii U as "a portable console to use around the house."
Fan reaction to the Microsoft-Activision deal shows console hardware driving business concerns: fans worried Activision titles like Crash Bandicoot and Spyro, once PlayStation exclusives, could again become tied to a single console's hardware ecosystem.
Controllers are treated as accessories to specific console hardware families — the Xbox Wireless Controller for Xbox Series X/S, the DualSense for PS5, the Switch Pro Controller for Switch — each controller's design and compatibility defined by the console hardware it ships with.

## Key Characteristics

- **Bundled, factory-fixed components** — a console's chip, screen, and battery are packaged together at manufacture, released as a new unit rather than sold as separate upgrades; the Steam Deck OLED combines a die-shrunk AMD APU (same CPU and GPU, just more power-efficient) with a new 7.4-inch HDR OLED screen and a 25 percent larger battery.
- **Mid-cycle hardware refreshes** — manufacturers revise console hardware within a generation without launching a full sequel; the Steam Deck OLED is explicitly "not the Steam Deck 2," described as a die-shrunk chip plus display refresh similar to the Switch OLED update, and paralleled by Sony's PS4 Slim/PS5 Slim revisions.
- **Home vs. portable/hybrid form factors** — PS5 and Xbox Series X/S are TV-connected home consoles, while Switch and Steam Deck are handhelds that can also dock to a television, blurring the line between "portable" and "living room console."
- **Platform-exclusive software ties** — console hardware can gate which games are playable on it, as with Spider-Man 2's PS5 exclusivity and the fan concern that Activision titles could become exclusive to one console family again.
- **Dedicated first-party controllers** — each console hardware line ships with a matched first-party controller (Xbox Wireless Controller, DualSense, Switch Pro Controller) that defines the baseline input experience for that hardware, with third parties building compatible alternatives around it.

## Background (external)

General definition, not corpus-sourced: a video game console is an electronic device that outputs a video signal to display a game, typically played with a controller.
It is distinguished from a PC by shipping with a fixed, manufacturer-preselected set of hardware components rather than user-configurable parts, which lets console makers optimize the design around that fixed hardware and gives developers a stable, unchanging performance target.
Handhelds are consoles that build the display and controls into a single portable unit with a battery, and hybrids (like the Nintendo Switch) combine handheld and home-console use.
(Source: Wikipedia, "Video game console," Wikimedia Foundation, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console)

# Hardware Device

## Definition

A hardware device, in this corpus, is a physical consumer electronics product — a smart speaker, handheld game console, smart glasses, or similar standalone gadget — that a company designs, manufactures, and sells as a distinct unit, as opposed to software or a service.

## Context

The corpus covers hardware devices from two angles: unveilings/reviews and retail deals. Google's annual "hardware event" is where the company unveils an entire slate of new devices at once — the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro phones, the Pixel Fold, Pixel Buds, and the Pixel Watch 2 — showing that "hardware" in this reporting names the physical product line a company ships, distinct from the software layered on top (Android 14, Bard, Google Assistant) that runs on it.

Retail-deal roundups organize hardware devices into shopping categories — Amazon's Cyber Monday guide lists separate sections for Echo/Fire TV/Kindle devices, speakers, headphones, tablets, and gaming gear — treating "speaker" as one device sub-category among several, not a synonym for hardware in general.

Smart glasses form a recurring device category: the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses combine a camera, open-ear audio, and a voice assistant, while Amazon's Echo Frames center on giving hands-free access to Alexa, and both trace the category back to the Google Glass Explorer Edition as its 2013 origin point.

Handheld gaming hardware is treated the same way: the Steam Deck OLED is discussed as a physical device with its own chip, screen, and battery specifications, refreshed mid-cycle the way a phone or headphone line would be.

## Key Characteristics

- **Physical and purchasable** — a hardware device is a standalone unit with a price and a retail listing (the Echo Frames at $314.99, the Ray-Ban Meta glasses at $299, the Steam Deck OLED at $549), not a subscription or app.
- **Distinct from the software it runs** — Google's hardware event unveils devices (Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Watch 2) separately from the software updates (Android 14, Bard) that ship alongside them.
- **Organized into device sub-categories** — retail guides split hardware into categories such as Echo/Fire TV/Kindle, speakers, headphones, tablets, and gaming, each reviewed and discounted on its own terms.
- **Defined by internal components** — reviews describe a device's identity through its chip, screen, and battery (the Steam Deck OLED's die-shrunk APU, 7.4-inch OLED panel, and 50Whr battery), the specs that distinguish one hardware generation from the next.
- **Ambiguous surface form** — "speaker" in the corpus denotes both an audio hardware device (a smart speaker) and the office of Speaker of the House; only the device sense belongs to this concept.

# Sweeney's Lightning Round: Fortnite Skins And The Steam Deck

In a lightning round closing The Verge's post-verdict interview, Tim Sweeney named Jellie — the jellyfish, "you know, the big tentacles" — as his favourite Fortnite skin, answered a question about ever announcing Unreal Tournament 3 X with "Forever in motion, the future is," and explained that Fortnite is still not playable on Steam Deck because of the Linux problem and a shortage of programmers.

On the Steam Deck he was complimentary: he loves the hardware, said Valve has done an amazing job, and wished it would reach tens of millions of users, at which point supporting it would actually make sense. Asked whether Epic is in the "aggressive pursuit model" the company internally floated in October 2019 for the Epic Games Store — aggressively paying more for exclusive games to pull in more users — he said no, Epic is in a different model called the "Ridiculously aggressive pursuit model": if it's a 10-slide deck, that's on slide 11. Asked whether he got a bingo on his Verge bingo card, he said it was almost a complete shutout with only one cell on the entire board missing, and singled out "lick the cookie" as the entry that impressed him, a phrase from the 1999 US v. Microsoft antitrust trial.

# Project Hug: Google's Developer Incentive Program, As Characterized By Both Sides

Project Hug is an initiative that forms part of the Google Games Velocity Program, and it is a second set of agreements Epic will highlight — those between Google and Android app developers themselves, as distinct from Google's agreements with device makers. Its defining feature is contested, and the two characterizations mark the boundary of the concept.

Epic will cite it as an example of where Google paid competitors not to distribute their apps on Android outside of the Play Store, by targeting those developers that were most at risk of attrition from Play and then approaching them with a monetary offer. As an example, Epic will point to Activision Blizzard — the owner of King.com and maker of Candy Crush and Call of Duty — as one developer that wanted to go the route of opening its own app store. Google and Activision Blizzard then entered into a three-year agreement in January 2020, worth approximately $360 million, to keep the developer on Google Play, Epic will argue.

Google, however, will characterize this program as a way to incentivize developers to launch their apps on Android at the same time as they launch on iOS, and plans to dispute Epic's claims that it prevented developers from opening their own app stores.

# Battery Life and Charging

## Definition

Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

## Context

Across the corpus, battery life and charging speed function as headline review criteria and buying-guide sort keys rather than a single defined term: Engadget's Steam Deck OLED review leads with "its battery life is better" as one of the device's core upgrades, and The Verge lists "improved battery life and audio" as a top pro for Amazon's third-gen Echo Frames. The charging half of the pair is increasingly organized around USB-C: Engadget notes that Apple's iPhone 15 line and the second-generation AirPods Pro both moved to USB-C charging, and Polygon's portable-charger guide treats USB-C Power Delivery wattage as the key spec for matching a power bank to a phone, tablet, Steam Deck, or laptop. Capacity for power banks is measured in mAh, per Polygon's guide, while device battery life is reported in hours (the Echo Frames reviewer logged about five hours of media playback and calls before hitting 30 percent) or in minutes of measured playtime (Engadget's Steam Deck OLED testing). Gogoro's battery-swapping business shows the same pair of concerns scaled up to electric vehicles: swapping a depleted battery for a charged one at a station is explicitly framed as a way to cut "charging time" relative to plugging in.

## Key Characteristics

- **Duration is measured empirically, not just claimed** — Engadget timed the Steam Deck OLED at four hours 23 minutes playing Hades versus two hours 42 minutes on the original LCD model under identical settings, a 62 percent gain that beat Valve's own 30-to-50-percent claim.
- **Charging speed is a distinct spec from capacity** — Valve advertises the Steam Deck OLED going from 20 to 80 percent in 45 minutes, a speed claim separate from its 50Whr battery capacity; Polygon likewise separates a power bank's mAh capacity from its wattage-based recharge speed.
- **USB-C is displacing proprietary connectors as the charging standard** — Apple's iPhone 15 and USB-C AirPods Pro, and the iPad's shift off Lightning to USB-C on its 10th-generation model, are all cited by Engadget as part of a single connector transition.
- **Power Delivery (PD) wattage governs compatibility between chargers and devices** — Polygon's guide notes that only power banks supporting the PD 3.0 spec can recharge a Steam Deck at its fastest rate, and that a laptop needs PD 3.1 and a compatible cable to reach 140 W charging.
- **Battery swapping is an alternative to plug-in charging at the vehicle scale** — Gogoro's network lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a station instead of waiting to charge in place, which TechCrunch frames as a way to reduce charging time for EV adopters.

# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.

# The SEO Naming Effect On Customer Acquisition

The Verge argued that Thai Food Near Me's name really did help the restaurant — but not through the mechanism its owners intended. The initial SEO "hack" was likely technically ineffective, but it was memorable and funny, and the joke led to many, many, many articles and forum posts about the restaurant's name, which tipped the SEO scales in its favor; all of that content, including The Verge's own story, will help the restaurant's prominence on Google platforms.
