# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.

# E-E-A-T And The Shift Toward Institutional Authority

SEO Lily Ray's account of why Google results feel different from five or six years ago starts with Google's response to the disinformation panic around the 2016 election, which involved questioning the notion that the most reliable information could be chosen by a form of popularity — meaning how many links a site received from other sites. As a result the algorithm seemed to change its approach to links, especially for news and for sites offering legal, financial, or health advice, and instead paid more attention to what Google came to call E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness.

The relation holds over a restricted range rather than across all queries. Not every search query takes E-E-A-T into account; Google has described heightened concern over sites that could impact safety, happiness, and the ability to be an informed citizen. Within that range the effect is large: "E-E-A-T has had a pretty big impact on what types of results you see," Ray said, and her extensive research on how sites have fared under the new guidelines shows the pattern — Urban Dictionary, down; Mayo Clinic, up. Some people consider E-E-A-T part of what is making results better than ever; others see it as a form of censorship, disproportionately affecting right-wing perspectives.

The structural consequence is a reversal of Google's founding logic: for certain kinds of information Google had undone one of the fundamental elements that made its results appealing from the start, so that instead of wild-west crowdsourcing, search was often reinforcing institutional authority. This felt complicated at best. When it comes to health and wellness, for example, quackery is often in the eye of the beholder, and everyone knows someone who has struggled with the limits of Western medicine; so much of the original draw of the internet was the opportunity for outlier voices to be heard alongside established experts and elites. Looking back on all that had changed around what first attracted people to Google, from the introduction of ads to efforts to keep users within the universe of Google products, this seemed to be the last straw.

Ray herself is a 30-something jet-setter with black-line tattoos and an asymmetrical, dyed blonde pixie cut, caught for lunch in Brooklyn between speaking gigs in Chicago and Berlin, on a day when she was also managing a 35-person team at her digital marketing agency, posting multiple times an hour on social media, dog-sitting a Pomeranian whose "daddies" were at Burning Man, caring for her own mini Australian shepherd, and organizing a house party she expected to be late for because she first had to perform a rooftop DJ set at a different party.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."

# Why Line Shopping Improves Returns

Line shopping is worth a bettor's time because it offers the chance to lay less, win more and improve your chances — and because it need not take long. The grounds start with a feature of how bets settle: when you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted, and if they later change, for better or worse, you are stuck with the odds from when you wagered. That is precisely why the shopping has to happen before the bet, though if significant changes occur afterward you can take more action at the improved odds or more favorable line.

The warrant is that a better price changes outcomes and cash flows, not skill. Getting more points or laying fewer on a typical NFL or NBA point spread might turn a bet you would otherwise lose into a winner, and finding better odds on any bet means dropping fewer dollars when you lose and earning more when you win. Sporting News is explicit about the limit: shopping lines will help you consistently find the best prices, but it will not help you pick more winners — it improves your chances and leads to bigger wins and more affordable losses.

The worked example is a half-point. Suppose you like the Kansas City Chiefs to beat the Cincinnati Bengals in a mid-season NFL game, and three of four licensed online sportsbooks in your state have the Chiefs at -3 while the fourth has them at -2.5. If the Chiefs win by exactly three — a distinct possibility, since a single field goal decides most NFL games — bets at the first three books push, while the fourth is a winner; without shopping you would never have found that half-point and would be stuck with a push instead of a profit.

The effort required is small: a live odds feed makes a basic survey a matter of seconds, and installing multiple licensed online sportsbook apps on your phone allows a more thorough shop in just a few minutes.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Google's Denial That Ad Keyword Matching Affects Organic Results

Google's official search liaison Danny Sullivan rebutted the allegation that Google manipulates search to maximise ad revenue by denying the causal link it depends on: in a post on X, he said ad systems do not affect the organic results — the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored.

"Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads," Sullivan said. "A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query." He also defended query interpretation on its own terms: "It's no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning… If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that's not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren't even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help." The Age noted the claim being answered comes from Megan Gray, herself a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google; she admits she may have misinterpreted the evidence but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. The paper granted that some search queries result in more ads than others and that which ads you get can vary wildly by request — the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads — but noted Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.



---


# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse](ftx_collapse_mechanism.md)
- [Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership](sbf_and_ellison_relationship_and_alameda_leadership.md)



---


# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# Why Bettors Should Consider NFL Award Longshots — And Bet Them Small

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that with five weeks left in the regular season there was plenty of time for an NFL award longshot to become a contender, so bettors should consider them — but should keep those bets small.

The grounds for taking longshots seriously are that they are easy to overlook because each award has a favorite or favorites: a longshot may be playing well, but other players have commanded the spotlight, making it easier for them to go unnoticed, and whatever the reason, they have not gotten the credit they deserve. The timing argument follows: if you wait too long before placing a bet, your payout will be a lot less than if you were to roll the dice on a longshot right now.

The counterweight, and the warrant for the sizing advice, is that there is always a reason why a player or several players have relatively short odds — they have been the best at their position throughout the season — and consequently there is just as good a reason why longshots have odds as long as they do. So the recommendation is to keep your bets small, or use a bonus bet if one is available, on longshots; if they do go on to win, you can smile all the way to the bank while telling everyone, "I told you so."

# National Basketball Association (NBA)

## Definition

The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the top professional men's basketball league in the United States, grouped in the corpus among "the four major US pro sports leagues" alongside the NFL, MLB, and NHL, and described elsewhere as "the pinnacle of the sport" of basketball.

## Context

In the corpus the NBA appears in three overlapping roles: as a cultural institution with its own holiday tradition, as a subject of sports betting coverage, and as a point of contrast with other basketball leagues.
Its Christmas Day games date back to 1947 and are described as a tradition older than the Super Bowl; last season's slate averaged 4.27 million viewers across platforms — about 200% more than a typical regular-season game — and games are broadcast to over 200 countries in more than 50 languages.
The league is regularly set up as a rival tradition to the NFL's Thanksgiving Day games, with commentary noting the NBA "far outperforms" the NFL in global popularity even though the NFL draws more domestic viewers.
A large share of the corpus's NBA coverage is sports-betting content — moneyline, point-spread, prop, and futures betting sites all use the NBA as their running example, and articles track odds for annual awards such as NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year.
The league is also used as a reference point by Australia's National Basketball League (NBL): NBL recaps describe several players as "ex-NBA" or "NBA hopeful," and note NBL clubs playing exhibition games against NBA opposition, distinguishing the two leagues while linking them through player movement.
Ticket-price reporting places the average 2022 NBA ticket at $94, versus $112 for the NFL, underscoring the NFL's larger domestic commercial scale even as the NBA is framed as more globally popular.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of the "four major" US leagues** — grouped with the NFL, MLB, and NHL as a top-tier US professional sports league.
- **Draft-based player pipeline** — teams acquire young talent through an annual draft, and draft outcomes ("draft misses") are tracked for their long-term effect on team success.
- **Regular season, playoffs, and marquee annual awards** — the league runs a regular season, playoffs, and honors such as the NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year, each with dedicated betting markets and odds coverage.
- **Signature holiday tradition** — Christmas Day games, dating to 1947 and older than the Super Bowl, function as the league's answer to the NFL's Thanksgiving games and are a major global broadcast event.
- **Global broadcast reach** — Christmas Day games alone are broadcast to more than 200 countries and translated into more than 50 languages.
- **Distinct from same-named/similar leagues abroad** — contrasted in the corpus with Australia's NBL, whose rosters and coverage frequently reference NBA-experienced or NBA-aspiring players.
- **A dominant subject of the sports-betting content ecosystem** — used as the default example league across moneyline, spread, prop, and futures betting explainers.

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. Maybe you ask a friend."

# ChatGPT's Task Capabilities And Measured Productivity Effects

ChatGPT's skills extend beyond conversation, another likely reason for its staying power. It can complete and debug code, compose music and essays, answer test questions, generate business ideas, write poetry and song lyrics, translate and summarize text, and even emulate a computer running Linux.

The measured effect comes from one study with a specific task set: an MIT study showed that, for tasks like writing cover letters, "delicate" emails and cost-benefit analyses, ChatGPT decreased the amount of time it took workers to complete the tasks by 40% while increasing output quality by 18%, as measured by third-party evaluators.

Ruoxi Shang attributes the breadth to a shift in how such systems are built: "Because [the AI models powering OpenAI] have been trained extensively on vast amounts of data, they [have] shifted focus from training specialized chatbots for specific domains to creating more general-purpose systems that can handle a variety of topics easily through prompting with instructions … [Chatbots like ChatGPT] don't require users to learn any new form of language, as long as they provide a task and some desired output just like how a manager would communicate to an intern."

# Steam Deck OLED Battery Life

Valve says the Steam Deck OLED battery lasts 30 to 50 percent longer than the original's depending on how you play, with an official claim of "three to 12 hours," and Engadget's November 2023 testing measured gains at the top of or above that range.

The original Steam Deck's short battery life was one of its downsides, maxing out at eight hours and only under ideal conditions. The OLED pairs a more-efficient processor with a 25 percent larger battery — 50Whr capacity against the original's 40Whr — and charges faster, going from 20 percent to 80 percent in 45 minutes by Valve's claim. Engadget tested with Hades, its reviewer's most-played game on the original: although Hades does not support HDR it pops on the OLED, with animations looking more fluid than on the LCD version, and the OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes before dying, against two hours and 42 minutes for the original at the same settings of 800p with a 60 fps cap and similar brightness — a 62 percent improvement that surpasses Valve's own estimates. Engadget flags the confound: batteries degrade, and its LCD Steam Deck dated from the device's launch in early 2022, an 18-month-old unit at review time, which explains why its gains were more pronounced. A harsher stress test playing Elden Ring with everything maxed out gave the OLED two hours and 20 minutes, about 40 percent longer than the original. Polygon separately resolved the obvious ambiguity in Valve's 30-50% figure by asking whether the comparison was against a Steam Deck running original firmware, which had poor battery life, or the latest firmware; Valve's answer was the latter, so existing owners should expect the big improvements over their current experience. Polygon's conclusion is that the OLED screen makes for a fancier Steam Deck, but it is the battery life — plus tweaks throughout the design to carve out more of it — that lets the handheld truly deliver on its promise of a portable gaming PC.

# Battery Life and Charging

## Definition

Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

## Context

Across the corpus, battery life and charging speed function as headline review criteria and buying-guide sort keys rather than a single defined term: Engadget's Steam Deck OLED review leads with "its battery life is better" as one of the device's core upgrades, and The Verge lists "improved battery life and audio" as a top pro for Amazon's third-gen Echo Frames. The charging half of the pair is increasingly organized around USB-C: Engadget notes that Apple's iPhone 15 line and the second-generation AirPods Pro both moved to USB-C charging, and Polygon's portable-charger guide treats USB-C Power Delivery wattage as the key spec for matching a power bank to a phone, tablet, Steam Deck, or laptop. Capacity for power banks is measured in mAh, per Polygon's guide, while device battery life is reported in hours (the Echo Frames reviewer logged about five hours of media playback and calls before hitting 30 percent) or in minutes of measured playtime (Engadget's Steam Deck OLED testing). Gogoro's battery-swapping business shows the same pair of concerns scaled up to electric vehicles: swapping a depleted battery for a charged one at a station is explicitly framed as a way to cut "charging time" relative to plugging in.

## Key Characteristics

- **Duration is measured empirically, not just claimed** — Engadget timed the Steam Deck OLED at four hours 23 minutes playing Hades versus two hours 42 minutes on the original LCD model under identical settings, a 62 percent gain that beat Valve's own 30-to-50-percent claim.
- **Charging speed is a distinct spec from capacity** — Valve advertises the Steam Deck OLED going from 20 to 80 percent in 45 minutes, a speed claim separate from its 50Whr battery capacity; Polygon likewise separates a power bank's mAh capacity from its wattage-based recharge speed.
- **USB-C is displacing proprietary connectors as the charging standard** — Apple's iPhone 15 and USB-C AirPods Pro, and the iPad's shift off Lightning to USB-C on its 10th-generation model, are all cited by Engadget as part of a single connector transition.
- **Power Delivery (PD) wattage governs compatibility between chargers and devices** — Polygon's guide notes that only power banks supporting the PD 3.0 spec can recharge a Steam Deck at its fastest rate, and that a laptop needs PD 3.1 and a compatible cable to reach 140 W charging.
- **Battery swapping is an alternative to plug-in charging at the vehicle scale** — Gogoro's network lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a station instead of waiting to charge in place, which TechCrunch frames as a way to reduce charging time for EV adopters.

# AI Hype Meets Reality In 2024

TechCrunch's framing prediction for 2024, published on 19 December 2023, is that it will be the year when the hype runs full-steam into reality as people reckon with the capabilities and limitations of AI at large.

The premise is the year just ending: 2023 was a banger for AI as the technology went from niche to mainstream about as fast as anything ever has. The proposition would be falsified if that reckoning did not arrive — if capability claims went untested and limitations remained unexamined — and the article sets out a few specific ways the reckoning is expected to play out.
