# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# ChatGPT's Launch And Its First Year Of Evolution

ChatGPT, OpenAI's viral AI chatbot, turned one on November 30, 2023. A year earlier OpenAI released it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with AI startup Anthropic. The goal, OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time, was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models.

Initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT would go on to become the company's most popular product ever — and the fastest-growing consumer app in history. Sam Altman marked the anniversary on X: "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…"

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating capabilities via DALL-E 3. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.

# Fake Domain Redirects In The 1990s

One of Daron Babin's signature moves back in the '90s involved fake domain names: "I could make it look like it was somebody else, but it actually redirected to me!" What he and his competitors did was legal but well beyond what the dominant search engine allowed.

The consequences fell on users rather than on him. He never faced any consequences, but in the end internet users at large felt the effects: "It muddied up Yahoo, ultimately," he said, "but while it worked, we banked."

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# National Basketball Association (NBA)

## Definition

The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the top professional men's basketball league in the United States, grouped in the corpus among "the four major US pro sports leagues" alongside the NFL, MLB, and NHL, and described elsewhere as "the pinnacle of the sport" of basketball.

## Context

In the corpus the NBA appears in three overlapping roles: as a cultural institution with its own holiday tradition, as a subject of sports betting coverage, and as a point of contrast with other basketball leagues.
Its Christmas Day games date back to 1947 and are described as a tradition older than the Super Bowl; last season's slate averaged 4.27 million viewers across platforms — about 200% more than a typical regular-season game — and games are broadcast to over 200 countries in more than 50 languages.
The league is regularly set up as a rival tradition to the NFL's Thanksgiving Day games, with commentary noting the NBA "far outperforms" the NFL in global popularity even though the NFL draws more domestic viewers.
A large share of the corpus's NBA coverage is sports-betting content — moneyline, point-spread, prop, and futures betting sites all use the NBA as their running example, and articles track odds for annual awards such as NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year.
The league is also used as a reference point by Australia's National Basketball League (NBL): NBL recaps describe several players as "ex-NBA" or "NBA hopeful," and note NBL clubs playing exhibition games against NBA opposition, distinguishing the two leagues while linking them through player movement.
Ticket-price reporting places the average 2022 NBA ticket at $94, versus $112 for the NFL, underscoring the NFL's larger domestic commercial scale even as the NBA is framed as more globally popular.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of the "four major" US leagues** — grouped with the NFL, MLB, and NHL as a top-tier US professional sports league.
- **Draft-based player pipeline** — teams acquire young talent through an annual draft, and draft outcomes ("draft misses") are tracked for their long-term effect on team success.
- **Regular season, playoffs, and marquee annual awards** — the league runs a regular season, playoffs, and honors such as the NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year, each with dedicated betting markets and odds coverage.
- **Signature holiday tradition** — Christmas Day games, dating to 1947 and older than the Super Bowl, function as the league's answer to the NFL's Thanksgiving games and are a major global broadcast event.
- **Global broadcast reach** — Christmas Day games alone are broadcast to more than 200 countries and translated into more than 50 languages.
- **Distinct from same-named/similar leagues abroad** — contrasted in the corpus with Australia's NBL, whose rosters and coverage frequently reference NBA-experienced or NBA-aspiring players.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# E-E-A-T And The Shift Toward Institutional Authority

SEO Lily Ray's account of why Google results feel different from five or six years ago starts with Google's response to the disinformation panic around the 2016 election, which involved questioning the notion that the most reliable information could be chosen by a form of popularity — meaning how many links a site received from other sites. As a result the algorithm seemed to change its approach to links, especially for news and for sites offering legal, financial, or health advice, and instead paid more attention to what Google came to call E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness.

The relation holds over a restricted range rather than across all queries. Not every search query takes E-E-A-T into account; Google has described heightened concern over sites that could impact safety, happiness, and the ability to be an informed citizen. Within that range the effect is large: "E-E-A-T has had a pretty big impact on what types of results you see," Ray said, and her extensive research on how sites have fared under the new guidelines shows the pattern — Urban Dictionary, down; Mayo Clinic, up. Some people consider E-E-A-T part of what is making results better than ever; others see it as a form of censorship, disproportionately affecting right-wing perspectives.

The structural consequence is a reversal of Google's founding logic: for certain kinds of information Google had undone one of the fundamental elements that made its results appealing from the start, so that instead of wild-west crowdsourcing, search was often reinforcing institutional authority. This felt complicated at best. When it comes to health and wellness, for example, quackery is often in the eye of the beholder, and everyone knows someone who has struggled with the limits of Western medicine; so much of the original draw of the internet was the opportunity for outlier voices to be heard alongside established experts and elites. Looking back on all that had changed around what first attracted people to Google, from the introduction of ads to efforts to keep users within the universe of Google products, this seemed to be the last straw.

Ray herself is a 30-something jet-setter with black-line tattoos and an asymmetrical, dyed blonde pixie cut, caught for lunch in Brooklyn between speaking gigs in Chicago and Berlin, on a day when she was also managing a 35-person team at her digital marketing agency, posting multiple times an hour on social media, dog-sitting a Pomeranian whose "daddies" were at Burning Man, caring for her own mini Australian shepherd, and organizing a house party she expected to be late for because she first had to perform a rooftop DJ set at a different party.

# Bank Run

## Definition

In the corpus, a bank run names the specific event in which rival exchange Binance's withdrawal of its remaining BUSD and FTT holdings "essentially triggered a bank run on FTX," the acute liquidity event that preceded FTX and Alameda's Chapter 11 filings.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the acute phase of FTX's November 2022 collapse: after a leaked Alameda Research balance sheet showed the firm's largest asset was billions of dollars of FTX's own FTT token — more FTT than existed in the entire market — rival exchange Binance began pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, and TechCrunch reports this action "essentially triggered a bank run on FTX." The run was the mechanism that converted a confidence crisis into an immediate liquidity failure, and it directly preceded FTX and Alameda filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in mid-November 2022.

## Key Characteristics

- **Confidence-driven, not solvency-driven at onset** — the run began once the leaked balance sheet destroyed trust in FTX/Alameda, independent of whether the underlying assets were ultimately worthless.
- **Triggered by a large counterparty's exit** — it was Binance's withdrawal of its remaining BUSD and FTT holdings, not a broad retail panic, that set off the run described in the corpus.
- **Fast-moving** — the run happened in the same early-November-2022 window as the balance-sheet leak, ahead of the Chapter 11 filings that followed in mid-November 2022.
- **Terminal for the institution** — in this case the run was followed by Chapter 11 filings for both FTX and Alameda, and Bankman-Fried's resignation.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a bank run is a general banking-system phenomenon: it occurs when many depositors, fearing a bank may fail, rush to withdraw their money at once, and because banks hold only a fraction of deposits as cash, a large enough run can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that drives the institution into sudden insolvency. (Wikipedia, "Bank run," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_run)

# 2023 NFL Comeback Player Of The Year: Hamlin Favored, Wilson The Longshot

Demar Hamlin was the current favorite for 2023 NFL Comeback Player of the Year and Russell Wilson the longshot, and Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that whether Hamlin holds up depends on how vital voters deem playing to be.

The case for Hamlin is that coming back from a life-threatening injury like a cardiac arrest makes him a great candidate to win CPOY. The qualification is that it would be understandable if voters were to look elsewhere, since Hamlin had seldom been active on game day and rarely seen the field.

The case for Wilson rests on the contrast between his two Denver seasons. Wilson was supposed to be the next great franchise quarterback for the Broncos when they acquired him prior to the previous season, but rather than lead the team back to prominence, Wilson was terrible and so was Denver. That season Wilson had played well even when the Broncos had not: he was not producing mind-blowing stat lines, but he was keeping his team competitive, playing efficiently and not making many mistakes. Until his three-interception day the week before, he had the best touchdown-to-interception ratio in the league, and even with those picks his was still second-best.

# National Basketball Association (NBA)

## Definition

The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the top professional men's basketball league in the United States, grouped in the corpus among "the four major US pro sports leagues" alongside the NFL, MLB, and NHL, and described elsewhere as "the pinnacle of the sport" of basketball.

## Context

In the corpus the NBA appears in three overlapping roles: as a cultural institution with its own holiday tradition, as a subject of sports betting coverage, and as a point of contrast with other basketball leagues.
Its Christmas Day games date back to 1947 and are described as a tradition older than the Super Bowl; last season's slate averaged 4.27 million viewers across platforms — about 200% more than a typical regular-season game — and games are broadcast to over 200 countries in more than 50 languages.
The league is regularly set up as a rival tradition to the NFL's Thanksgiving Day games, with commentary noting the NBA "far outperforms" the NFL in global popularity even though the NFL draws more domestic viewers.
A large share of the corpus's NBA coverage is sports-betting content — moneyline, point-spread, prop, and futures betting sites all use the NBA as their running example, and articles track odds for annual awards such as NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year.
The league is also used as a reference point by Australia's National Basketball League (NBL): NBL recaps describe several players as "ex-NBA" or "NBA hopeful," and note NBL clubs playing exhibition games against NBA opposition, distinguishing the two leagues while linking them through player movement.
Ticket-price reporting places the average 2022 NBA ticket at $94, versus $112 for the NFL, underscoring the NFL's larger domestic commercial scale even as the NBA is framed as more globally popular.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of the "four major" US leagues** — grouped with the NFL, MLB, and NHL as a top-tier US professional sports league.
- **Draft-based player pipeline** — teams acquire young talent through an annual draft, and draft outcomes ("draft misses") are tracked for their long-term effect on team success.
- **Regular season, playoffs, and marquee annual awards** — the league runs a regular season, playoffs, and honors such as the NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year, each with dedicated betting markets and odds coverage.
- **Signature holiday tradition** — Christmas Day games, dating to 1947 and older than the Super Bowl, function as the league's answer to the NFL's Thanksgiving games and are a major global broadcast event.
- **Global broadcast reach** — Christmas Day games alone are broadcast to more than 200 countries and translated into more than 50 languages.
- **Distinct from same-named/similar leagues abroad** — contrasted in the corpus with Australia's NBL, whose rosters and coverage frequently reference NBA-experienced or NBA-aspiring players.
- **A dominant subject of the sports-betting content ecosystem** — used as the default example league across moneyline, spread, prop, and futures betting explainers.

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

Source: "Major League Baseball," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

## Definition

Layoffs are the employer-initiated, batch workforce cuts the corpus tracks through 2023's "techwide reckoning" — TechCrunch's running tally puts total tech-industry job losses at more than 240,000 for the year, driven by companies pivoting "from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency" (doc_0049).

## Context

Across the corpus, 2023 is depicted as a "techwide reckoning" year: TechCrunch's running tracker put total tech-industry job losses at more than 240,000 for the year, already 50% above 2022 and still climbing, with cuts driven by the biggest names in tech — Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Yahoo, Meta and Zoom — as well as startups across many sectors (doc_0049).
The phenomenon recurs across very different company situations: a cybersecurity startup that went public but "failed to gain traction" and later shuttered outright, laying off its remaining staff (IronNet, doc_0011); a browser maker cutting 9% of its workforce across departments (Brave Software, doc_0043); a music-streaming giant cutting roughly 1,500 jobs (17% of its workforce) in its third layoff round of the year while its CEO framed the move as "right-sizing" for "productive and efficient" operations (Spotify, doc_0334); and a logistics startup cutting about 20% of its staff (roughly 600 people) under its founder, who returned as CEO after ousting his "hand-picked successor" over alleged overspending (Flexport, doc_0536, doc_0537).
Layoffs also follow directly from an acquired or platform company's takeover events: X's (formerly Twitter's) 2022 change of ownership "saw major layoffs, including in content moderation and human rights," which the corpus ties to the platform's later inability to respond to disinformation reports (doc_0024).
In the video-game industry specifically, layoffs are described as one of three interlocking forces — alongside consolidation and unionization — reshaping the sector: an estimated 9,000-plus video-game jobs were lost in 2023 versus roughly 1,000 in 2022, with layoffs concentrated at recently acquired studios (doc_0050).

## Key Characteristics

- **Batch, employer-driven terminations** — layoffs affect many employees at once (e.g., Brave's 9%, Spotify's 17%, Flexport's 20%), distinguishing them from case-by-case firings (doc_0043, doc_0334, doc_0537).
- **Framed as cost/efficiency correction** — companies in the corpus consistently attribute layoffs to macroeconomic pressure and a shift "from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency," rather than to sectoral collapse (doc_0049).
- **Can accompany full shutdown** — the most severe outcome pairs layoffs with the company ceasing operations entirely, as with IronNet, which "has shuttered and laid off its remaining staff following its collapse" (doc_0011).
- **Recurrent, not one-time** — several companies underwent multiple rounds within the same year (Spotify's third round by December 2023; Flexport cutting 20% in January with "more layoffs expected soon" by October) (doc_0334, doc_0536).
- **Concentrated post-acquisition** — layoffs and closures are described as "the most extreme negative outcomes for an acquired indie studio," recurring after ownership changes (video games) or leadership takeovers (X) (doc_0050, doc_0024).
- **Aggregate scale tracked industry-wide** — outlets maintain running trackers (TechCrunch's tech-layoffs list, Layoffs.fyi, layoffstracker.com) that quantify the year's cuts across sectors (doc_0049, doc_0050).

## Background (external)

Beyond the corpus's 2023 tech-industry usage, Wikipedia defines a layoff generically: "A layoff or downsizing is the temporary suspension or permanent termination of employment of an employee" — extended to a group of employees ("collective layoff") let go together "for business reasons, such as personnel management or downsizing an organization" (Wikipedia, "Layoff," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layoff).

# Appeals Process

## Definition

An appeals process is a defined mechanism that lets a party formally challenge a decision — a content-moderation action, a disciplinary penalty, or a court ruling — and have it reconsidered by a different decision-maker, rather than accepting the original ruling as final.

## Context

The corpus shows this same structure recurring across three distinct domains. Social platforms build appeals processes into their content-moderation systems: Meta states "there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it," and separately says it "continue[s] to provide tools for users to appeal our decisions if they think we made a mistake" during its Israel-Hamas war content response, while Discord's new account-standing system "link[s] out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism" whenever it notifies a user of a policy violation and restricts their account. In sports governance, Everton's appeal against a 10-point Premier League deduction "will be heard by a different three-person panel" than the one that issued the penalty — the hallmark of an appeals process, a distinct reconsidering body rather than the original decision-maker revisiting its own call. In litigation, an appeal is the formal next step after a verdict or ruling: Bankman-Fried's defense lawyers were "laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments" during his trial, and Apple's patent-infringement loss triggers an "appeals process" that "can take around 18 months" and can determine whether an import ban stays in effect while the case is contested.

## Key Characteristics

- **Distinct reviewing authority** — an appeal is reheard by a different decision-maker than the one who made the original call, as with Everton's separate three-person panel.
- **Available after an adverse decision** — content removals, disciplinary points deductions, and trial verdicts all trigger the same downstream option to contest the outcome.
- **Can be lengthy** — legal appeals are explicitly time-consuming; Apple's appeal of its Apple Watch import ban "can take around 18 months," during which the underlying decision may still take effect unless a stay is separately granted.
- **Built into platform enforcement systems as a safeguard against error** — Meta frames its appeals process as compensating for moderation mistakes ("we can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process") rather than as an admission the underlying policy is wrong, while Discord links its warning notices out to its own appeal mechanism whenever it restricts a user's account for a policy violation.
- **Does not guarantee reversal** — Everton's manager Dyche urges his players to "forget about the appeal and accept the reality" rather than assume it will succeed, underscoring that lodging an appeal only obtains reconsideration, not a favorable outcome.

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# The GPT-4 Demonstration To Bill Gates

Over dinner, Bill Gates told Sam Altman and Greg Brockman that he doubted large language models could work, and said he would stay sceptical until the technology performed a task that required critical thinking, such as passing an Advanced Placement biology test. Five months later, on 24 August 2022, Altman and Brockman returned and brought along an OpenAI researcher named Chelsea Voss, who had been a medallist in an international biology Olympiad as a high schooler; Satya Nadella and other Microsoft executives were there too.

On a huge digital display on a stand outside Gates' living room, the OpenAI crew presented a technology called GPT-4. Brockman gave the system a multiple-choice advanced biology test and Voss graded the answers. The first question involved polar molecules, groups of atoms with a positive charge at one end and a negative charge at the other; the system answered correctly and explained its choice. "It was only trained to provide an answer," Brockman said. "The conversational nature kind of fell out, almost magically." In other words, it was doing things they hadn't really designed it to do.

# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.

# Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS)

## Definition

Daily fantasy sports (DFS) is the corpus's term for the weekly, single-slate NFL lineups that outlets like Sporting News build each week for operators such as DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, distinct from a season-long fantasy league roster (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331).

## Context

The corpus treats DFS as the distinct alternative to season-long fantasy football leagues, most explicitly in DraftKings' Week 14 picks column: "Most season-long fantasy leagues are entering their final week of the regular season in Week 14, and if your team isn't going to qualify for the postseason, then welcome to the DFS side of things, where every week is a new season" (doc_0331) — DFS is framed as the format you turn to once season-long fantasy is decided, because it does not carry any of a season-long league's injury reports, trades, or bad-matchup risk from week to week. The dominant DFS operators named across the corpus are DraftKings, FanDuel and SuperDraft, each running weekly "GPP tournament" lineups on a main slate (doc_0056, doc_0276, doc_0331). The corpus also shows DFS as the historical root of today's sportsbook industry: DraftKings is described as "known as a daily fantasy sports operator before becoming a renowned sportsbook" (doc_0062), and CBS Sports likewise reports that DraftKings' Kentucky sportsbook rewards program "caters especially to those who are daily fantasy sports players" (doc_0071), showing that the same companies and customer base carried over from DFS into legal sports betting.

## Key Characteristics

- **Short, fixed contest windows** — a DFS lineup is drafted for a single week's slate rather than an entire season, so a bad week does not carry forward (doc_0331).
- **Salary-cap roster construction** — DraftKings and FanDuel DFS contests assign each player a price against a fixed budget (e.g. a $50,000 budget on DraftKings, $60,000 on FanDuel for the Sunday main slate), forcing owners to balance expensive stars against cheaper "value" plays (doc_0331, doc_0056).
- **Operator-specific scoring rules** — the same players score differently depending on the DFS site: DraftKings uses full-point PPR with three-point yardage bonuses, while FanDuel uses half-point PPR with no such bonuses, and both use four-point passing touchdowns (doc_0331, doc_0056, doc_0276).
- **GPP tournament structure** — DFS lineups compete in "GPP tournaments" against the whole entry field for that slate, distinct from head-to-head season-long league play (doc_0056, doc_0331).
- **Budget-allocation strategy** — winning a large-field DFS tournament ("the milli-maker") depends on rostering cheap sleepers and value plays to free up salary for elite players elsewhere, rather than simply drafting the best players regardless of price (doc_0544).
- **Historical link to sports betting** — major DFS operators such as DraftKings later expanded into licensed sportsbooks, carrying their DFS-era branding and rewards programs into sports wagering (doc_0062, doc_0071).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, daily fantasy sports is generally defined as a subset of fantasy sports in which participants assemble a roster of professional athletes under a salary cap and score points based on those athletes' real-game performance, with contests run over a short period — a single week or even a single day — rather than a full season; contests are typically split into cash games (head-to-head or 50-50 formats) and guaranteed prize pools (GPP) with tiered payouts, and the operator retains a cut of entry fees as rake (Wikipedia, "Daily fantasy sports," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_fantasy_sports).

# National Basketball Association (NBA)

## Definition

The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the top professional men's basketball league in the United States, grouped in the corpus among "the four major US pro sports leagues" alongside the NFL, MLB, and NHL, and described elsewhere as "the pinnacle of the sport" of basketball.

## Context

In the corpus the NBA appears in three overlapping roles: as a cultural institution with its own holiday tradition, as a subject of sports betting coverage, and as a point of contrast with other basketball leagues.
Its Christmas Day games date back to 1947 and are described as a tradition older than the Super Bowl; last season's slate averaged 4.27 million viewers across platforms — about 200% more than a typical regular-season game — and games are broadcast to over 200 countries in more than 50 languages.
The league is regularly set up as a rival tradition to the NFL's Thanksgiving Day games, with commentary noting the NBA "far outperforms" the NFL in global popularity even though the NFL draws more domestic viewers.
A large share of the corpus's NBA coverage is sports-betting content — moneyline, point-spread, prop, and futures betting sites all use the NBA as their running example, and articles track odds for annual awards such as NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year.
The league is also used as a reference point by Australia's National Basketball League (NBL): NBL recaps describe several players as "ex-NBA" or "NBA hopeful," and note NBL clubs playing exhibition games against NBA opposition, distinguishing the two leagues while linking them through player movement.
Ticket-price reporting places the average 2022 NBA ticket at $94, versus $112 for the NFL, underscoring the NFL's larger domestic commercial scale even as the NBA is framed as more globally popular.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of the "four major" US leagues** — grouped with the NFL, MLB, and NHL as a top-tier US professional sports league.
- **Draft-based player pipeline** — teams acquire young talent through an annual draft, and draft outcomes ("draft misses") are tracked for their long-term effect on team success.
- **Regular season, playoffs, and marquee annual awards** — the league runs a regular season, playoffs, and honors such as the NBA MVP and NBA Rookie of the Year, each with dedicated betting markets and odds coverage.
- **Signature holiday tradition** — Christmas Day games, dating to 1947 and older than the Super Bowl, function as the league's answer to the NFL's Thanksgiving games and are a major global broadcast event.
- **Global broadcast reach** — Christmas Day games alone are broadcast to more than 200 countries and translated into more than 50 languages.
- **Distinct from same-named/similar leagues abroad** — contrasted in the corpus with Australia's NBL, whose rosters and coverage frequently reference NBA-experienced or NBA-aspiring players.
- **A dominant subject of the sports-betting content ecosystem** — used as the default example league across moneyline, spread, prop, and futures betting explainers.

# NFL Broadcasters' Taylor Swift Lyric References

On 17 September 2023 Travis Kelce scored a touchdown against the Jaguars, prompting CBS announcer Ian Eagle to say "Kelce finds a blank space for the score" — a reference to Swift's 2014 hit Blank Space — and NFL Network's Rich Eisen followed with a slew of lyric references in a preshow, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

The suspicion that Swift and Kelce were spending time together in New York was seemingly confirmed in September when it was reported they had been "quietly hanging out" for months — the first, albeit tentative, confirmation from the media rather than from amateur Swiftie sleuths on social media. It was only a matter of time before the story entered the cultural zeitgeist, and it did so very quickly. Eisen's preshow references included "shake it off", "anti-hero" and "all too well", and Kelce acknowledged the tongue-in-cheek banter, commenting on a montage video of the preshow that Eisen posted to Instagram: "Well played Rich … Well played."

Suddenly football fans and Swifties were living through this surprising collision — Swift lyrics were infiltrating NFL game commentary, and her fans were furiously becoming football experts. All that needed to happen, the timeline says, was for Swift herself to infiltrate a game, determining once and for all whether there was anything to the rumours.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# Reaction To Lewis's Portrayal Of SBF

The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. TechCrunch collected the reaction on 2023-10-02.

The premise is attacked head-on by Dan Held, who on October 2, 2023 quoted Lewis — "They had a great real business. If no one had cast aspersions on the business, if there hadn't been a run on customers deposits, they'd still be making tons of money" — and answered: "That's not true. They are not a bank, they're…", prefacing it with "Shameful that Michael Lewis is defending SBF." Ryan Selkis attacked the framing instead of the balance sheet, writing the same day that "The Michael Lewis interview is infuriating. SBF was a scumbag, and now we need to hear about his 'tragic fall' in the MSM because Sam told them he was an 'effective altruist' and people like Michael Lewis were so far up his ass they couldn't tell truth from fiction." Tobi Lutke attacked the coverage itself: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. Two qualifications sit against the backlash. # Regulatory Investigations Into OpenAI In 2023

OpenAI faced regulatory action on several fronts in 2023: Italy ordered ChatGPT blocked over GDPR concerns, Poland opened its own GDPR investigation, China's licensing regime pushed ChatGPT clients out of the App Store, and the FTC was reported to be investigating the chatbot's statements about people.

Italy moved first. Italy's data protection authority ordered OpenAI to stop processing people's data locally with immediate effect, saying it was concerned the ChatGPT maker was breaching the EU's General Data Protection Regulation and opening an investigation; OpenAI began geoblocking access to ChatGPT in Italy. The DPA then laid out what OpenAI needed to do for the order to be lifted, giving OpenAI a deadline of April 30 to complete the regulator's compliance demands, with a slightly more generous timeline of May 15 for a local radio, TV and internet awareness campaign. Poland's authority publicly announced it had opened an investigation regarding ChatGPT, accusing the company of a string of breaches of the GDPR.

In China, multiple generative AI apps were removed from Apple's China App Store ahead of the country's latest generative AI regulations, set to take effect August 15. Apple wrote in a letter to OpenCat, a native ChatGPT client: "As you may know, the government has been tightening regulations associated with deep synthesis technologies (DST) and generative AI services, including ChatGPT. DST must fulfill permitting requirements to operate in China, including securing a license from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Based on our review, your app is associated with ChatGPT, which does not have requisite permits to operate in China."

In the United States, the FTC was reportedly in at least the exploratory phase of an investigation into whether ChatGPT made "false, misleading, disparaging or harmful" statements about people. TechCrunch reporter Devin Coldewey noted that such an investigation does not appear out of thin air — the FTC does not look around and say "That looks suspicious"; generally a lawsuit or formal complaint is brought to its attention and the practices described imply that regulations are being ignored, much as a person suing a supplement company over pills that made them sick can prompt an FTC investigation because there is evidence the company lied about side effects. Separately, FTC chair Lina Khan and fellow commissioners warned House representatives in a congressional hearing that modern AI technologies like ChatGPT could be used to "turbocharge" fraud: "AI presents a whole set of opportunities, but also presents a whole set of risks," Khan said. "And I think we've already seen ways in which it could be used to turbocharge fraud and scams. We've been putting market participants on notice that instances in which AI tools are effectively being designed to deceive people can place them on the hook for FTC action."
