# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Crypto Contagion After FTX

FTX's collapse did not stay contained to FTX: the crypto industry as a whole suffered, and TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that the collapse "was the first of many." BlockFi filed for Chapter 11 in November 2022, and Genesis Global Trading did the same in January.

The damage was reputational as well as financial. In TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 piece, Ayelet Noff — the CEO and founder of the public relations firm Sliced Brand, which represents a number of cryptocurrency businesses — gave this assessment: "He doesn't come off good at all here. You can tell he had no experience in management or handling such big undertakings. I think he was in way over his head." She continued: "I think he does a disservice to the whole community. He pushed back crypto adoption by at least a year or two. Each time one of these things happens it brings back the whole market. It's two steps forward and one step back."



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. # Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# Data Breach

## Definition

A data breach, in the corpus, is an incident in which hackers or unintended exposure let unauthorized parties reach personal or organizational data — spanning the 2017 Equifax hack, the 2023 23andMe breach, an individual's hacked Roblox account, and, more loosely, TikTok's pre-consent data scraping, which a senator branded a "mass breach of privacy" (doc_0015, doc_0334, doc_0178, doc_0189).

## Context

The corpus uses the term across several registers of the same underlying event. The canonical reference point is the Equifax data breach of 2017, invoked in a discussion of Google's search-revenue deals as the event that made identity-theft-protection services like LifeLock a hot commercial topic (doc_0015). The clearest 2023 instance is 23andMe: hackers first accessed the personal data of about 14,000 users (0.1% of customers), a number the company later acknowledged undercounted the real scope, in a breach it disclosed in October 2023 (doc_0334). The same TechCrunch weekly roundup that covers 23andMe also reports a related but distinct exposure — patient scans and health records "spilling online" through security weaknesses in the decades-old DICOM medical-imaging standard, which made private data accessible on the open web without any hacker having to breach a perimeter at all (doc_0334). At smaller scale, the term extends to individual account compromise: Sarah Michelle Gellar described her son's Roblox account being "hacked," which she treated as serious enough to cancel a linked credit card (doc_0178). The corpus also shows the vocabulary of "breach" stretched to cover non-hacking exposure: Australian coverage of TikTok's tracking pixel, which scraped site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before consent was given, was branded a "mass breach of privacy" by a senator — a data-handling violation rather than an intrusion, but framed with the same breach language (doc_0189).

## Key Characteristics

- **Unauthorized access or exposure, not just data collection** — a breach denotes information reaching parties (or the open web) it was never meant to reach, whether via hacking (doc_0334, doc_0178) or unintentional exposure of insecure infrastructure (doc_0334's DICOM item).
- **Initial disclosures tend to understate scope** — 23andMe first quantified only 0.1% of customers as affected before acknowledging the wider group whose data was exposed (doc_0334).
- **Consequences reach beyond the breached company** — Gellar's response to her son's Roblox account being hacked was to cancel a family credit card, showing breach fallout propagating into unrelated financial accounts (doc_0178).
- **The term is applied loosely** — commentary uses "breach" both for classic hacking incidents (23andMe, Roblox) and for non-consensual data collection practices (TikTok's pixel), even though the latter is a policy/consent violation rather than an intrusion (doc_0189).

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), a data breach is any security incident in which unauthorized parties access sensitive, confidential, or protected information (IBM, "What Is a Data Breach?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.ibm.com/topics/data-breach).

# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.

The 23andMe breach turned out to reach 6.9 million people, far beyond the number the genetic testing company first quantified. On Friday 1 December 2023, 23andMe announced that hackers managed to access the personal data of 0.1% of customers, or about 14,000 individuals, but the company did not initially say how many other users might have been impacted by the breach, which it first disclosed in October.

# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. # Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

# Celebrity Endorsement

In the corpus, "celebrity endorsements" is named directly only once — listed alongside "campaign trail rallies" as one of several online-campaign tactics that, on their own, are "not enough to engage voters online" — and everywhere else the corpus treats it as a family of concrete cases rather than a defined category: FTX's paid partnerships with athletes, Anna Wintour's sponsorship request to Sam Bankman-Fried, The Epoch Times' political endorsements and CPAC sponsorship, and Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok launch via a Jake Paul endorsement.

## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. (Wikipedia, "Celebrity branding," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_branding)

# Independent Research And Reviews Of ChatGPT's Flaws

Independent researchers and advocacy groups repeatedly found ChatGPT and GPT-4 to be flawed in ways OpenAI's own launches did not resolve — on child safety, on toxicity, and on the vision-enabled multimodal model.

An independent review from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit advocacy group, found that ChatGPT could potentially be harmful for younger users, flagging it as potentially unsafe for kids; ChatGPT got an overall three-star rating in the report, with its lowest ratings relating to transparency, privacy, trust and safety. On multimodality, OpenAI announced that GPT-4 with vision would become available alongside the upcoming launch of the GPT-4 Turbo API, but some researchers found that the model remained flawed in several significant and problematic ways.

Two toxicity findings stand out. A Microsoft-affiliated scientific paper examined the "trustworthiness" — and toxicity — of LLMs including GPT-4; because GPT-4 is more likely to follow the instructions of "jailbreaking" prompts, the co-authors claim it can be more easily prompted than other LLMs to spout toxic, biased text. Separately, a study co-authored by scientists at the Allen Institute for AI showed that assigning ChatGPT a "persona" through the ChatGPT API — for example "a bad person," "a horrible person" or "a nasty person" — increases its toxicity sixfold; the co-authors also found that having the chatbot pose as certain historical figures, gendered people and members of political parties increased its toxicity, with journalists, men and Republicans in particular causing the model to say more offensive things than it normally would. That research was conducted using the latest version, but not the model then in preview based on GPT-4.

# Meta's Moderation During An Earlier Hamas-Israel Conflict

During an earlier Hamas-Israel conflict, the digital-rights organisation 7amleh documented more than 500 reports of Palestinian "digital rights violations" over the 13 days leading up to the ceasefire — including the removal and restriction of content, hashtags and accounts related to the conflict. The figure was recounted to TechCrunch for its 19 October 2023 report on Meta's moderation of Palestinian content.

Meta attributed some of the instances of perceived censorship to technical issues, such as one that prevented users in Palestine and Colombia from posting Instagram Stories. It attributed others to human error, such as blocking the hashtag for Al-Aqsa Mosque — the holy site where Israeli police clashed with Ramadan worshippers — because the name was mistaken for a terrorist organization. The company also blocked journalists in Gaza from WhatsApp without explanation.

Meta committed to implementing policy changes based on the report's recommendations, including updating its keywords associated with dangerous organizations, disclosing government requests to remove content, and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content. 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater added that Meta has improved its response to harassment, at least in comparison to other social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter): although harassment and abuse remain rampant on Instagram and Facebook, he said the company has been responsive to suspending accounts with patterns of targeting other users.

Abukhater's scope condition on all of this is that the improvements do not survive an escalation. "The balance of power is very fixed, in reality, between Israelis and Palestinians," he said. "And this is something that today is reflected heavily on platforms like Meta, even though they have human rights teams releasing reports and trying to improve upon their policies. Whenever an escalation like the one we're experiencing now happens, things just go back to zero."

# Recommendation Algorithm

## Definition

Across the corpus, "recommendation algorithm" (and the closely related notion of algorithmic ranking/curation) names the automated mechanism a platform uses to control the visibility of content, products, or posts — and by extension, the mechanism regulators, courts, and users scrutinize when they suspect a platform is suppressing or favoring particular items.
No single corpus document offers a formal definition of the term; instead each shows the mechanism at work in a different dispute: Amazon's marketplace search ranking and "other products you may like" widget, Instagram's Stories/feed visibility, U.S. platforms' content-moderation feed curation, and Google's Featured Snippets extraction.

## Context

The corpus shows the same underlying mechanism operating across very different platform types, and shows regulators and courts converging on it from different angles.
On Amazon's marketplace, the EU's antitrust objections to the iRobot acquisition center on Amazon's ability to foreclose a rival's *algorithmic visibility* — delisting rival products, reducing their ranking in organic and paid results, excluding them from the "other products you may like" widget, or denying them labels like "Amazon's Choice" — since RVC buyers in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain rely on that in-marketplace ranking both for product discovery and for the final purchase decision.
The same document notes that Amazon's marketplace was separately designated a core platform service under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which imposes restrictions on self-preferencing.
On Meta's Instagram, users and digital-rights groups suspect a comparable but content-moderation-flavored version of the same idea — "shadowbanning" — where an algorithmic process silently lowers a post's visibility (e.g., Palestine-related Stories) without an explicit takedown.
In the U.S. Supreme Court's NetChoice cases (challenging Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072), the fight is over whether a platform's curation of what appears in a user's feed — a process now largely conducted algorithmically, generally with light human intervention or oversight — is a First-Amendment-protected editorial act that states cannot compel platforms to individually explain post-by-post.
Google's Featured Snippets, which algorithmically extract answers directly from publishers' web pages into search results, are cited in a news-publisher antitrust suit as a related mechanism: an algorithm that decides what content a user sees without the user visiting the original source, which publishers say siphons off their traffic and ad revenue.

## Key Characteristics

- **Ranking, not binary inclusion** — the algorithm typically operates on relative visibility (higher/lower placement in organic or paid results, inclusion in a "you may like" widget) rather than simple on/off access, which is what makes self-preferencing and shadowbanning hard to prove or disprove.
- **Automated with limited human oversight** — described in the NetChoice case as a process "largely conducted algorithmically now — generally with light human intervention or oversight," which is central to arguments that mandated per-decision human explanations would be impractical at the scale of "millions and millions of pieces of content a day."
- **Commercial leverage point** — on marketplaces, control over the recommendation algorithm doubles as a competitive lever: a platform that also sells its own products can use ranking, delisting, and widget exclusion to foreclose rivals, per the EU's ability-and-incentive theory of harm against Amazon.
- **Contestable but opaque** — content creators and merchants can suspect suppression (shadowbanning, reduced marketplace visibility) but the underlying ranking logic is not published, so claims tend to rely on circumstantial or anecdotal patterns rather than direct evidence.
- **Distinct from explicit content removal** — reduced algorithmic visibility (shadowbanning, lower ranking) is a softer, less visible action than outright delisting or takedown, and is treated differently in both platform policy and legal argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general computer-science term for this kind of system is a "recommender system" (also called a recommendation algorithm, engine, or platform): a type of information filtering system that suggests items most relevant to a particular user, predicting user preferences to help them choose from large sets of options such as products, media, or content.
Source: "Recommender system," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommender_system.

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# User-Generated Content

## Definition

User-generated content (UGC), in the corpus, is the term for content that ordinary platform users — rather than the platform itself or a news organization — create and publish, such as Reels, Stories, posts, and streams.
The EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) treats UGC as a defined regulatory object, requiring "social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content" to act on reports of illegal content and disinformation (doc_0025).
Snap itself describes the public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "authentic user-generated content" offering perspectives that traditional news outlets may not reflect (doc_0124).

## Context

The corpus treats UGC primarily as the object of content-moderation obligations and disputes rather than as a neutral technical term: the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) explicitly regulates "how social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content must respond to reports of illegal content," putting X under a legal obligation to act on flagged posts and mitigate disinformation risk (doc_0025).
On Meta's platforms, individual users' Reels and Stories about Palestine became the flashpoint for accusations of moderation bias, with filmmaker Khitam Jabr suspecting that her own Palestine travel Reels were restricted for 24 hours after other users reported them (doc_0106).
On Snapchat, an X user described the crowd-sourced public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who could not get on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" increase in Stories submissions from the region since October 7 (doc_0124).
Mozilla frames the broader problem as one of governance: today's large, advertiser-funded social networks decide how UGC is moderated and monetized, which is part of why it is building a decentralized "fediverse" alternative (doc_0026).
On Twitch, UGC is also an economic asset — streamers' broadcasts are the content being monetized, and disputes over revenue splits and the Partner Plus program center on how creators are compensated for the content they generate (doc_0401).

## Key Characteristics

- **User-originated** — the content is authored and published by ordinary platform users (e.g., Reels, Stories, posts, streams), not by the platform or a newsroom (doc_0106, doc_0124).
- **Subject to platform moderation and reporting** — UGC can be flagged, restricted, or shadowbanned by other users' reports or automated systems, as Jabr suspected happened to her Palestine travel videos (doc_0106).
- **Regulatory trigger** — under the DSA, a platform's responsibility to act on illegal UGC and disinformation is a defined legal obligation, not just a policy choice (doc_0025).
- **Real-time information source** — one X user called Snap Map's crowd-sourced Stories "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who weren't on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" rise in submissions from the region (doc_0124).
- **Monetizable** — UGC is also the basis for creator revenue-sharing arrangements, making its governance a business as well as a moderation issue (doc_0401).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "user-generated content" (UGC) — also called "user-created content" (UCC) — is generally defined as content generated by users of the Internet, such as images, videos, audio, text, testimonials, software, and user interactions (Wikipedia, "User-generated content," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content).
