## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. # E-E-A-T And The Shift Toward Institutional Authority

SEO Lily Ray's account of why Google results feel different from five or six years ago starts with Google's response to the disinformation panic around the 2016 election, which involved questioning the notion that the most reliable information could be chosen by a form of popularity — meaning how many links a site received from other sites. As a result the algorithm seemed to change its approach to links, especially for news and for sites offering legal, financial, or health advice, and instead paid more attention to what Google came to call E-E-A-T: experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness.

The relation holds over a restricted range rather than across all queries. Not every search query takes E-E-A-T into account; Google has described heightened concern over sites that could impact safety, happiness, and the ability to be an informed citizen. Within that range the effect is large: "E-E-A-T has had a pretty big impact on what types of results you see," Ray said, and her extensive research on how sites have fared under the new guidelines shows the pattern — Urban Dictionary, down; Mayo Clinic, up. Some people consider E-E-A-T part of what is making results better than ever; others see it as a form of censorship, disproportionately affecting right-wing perspectives.

The structural consequence is a reversal of Google's founding logic: for certain kinds of information Google had undone one of the fundamental elements that made its results appealing from the start, so that instead of wild-west crowdsourcing, search was often reinforcing institutional authority. This felt complicated at best. When it comes to health and wellness, for example, quackery is often in the eye of the beholder, and everyone knows someone who has struggled with the limits of Western medicine; so much of the original draw of the internet was the opportunity for outlier voices to be heard alongside established experts and elites. Looking back on all that had changed around what first attracted people to Google, from the introduction of ads to efforts to keep users within the universe of Google products, this seemed to be the last straw.

Ray herself is a 30-something jet-setter with black-line tattoos and an asymmetrical, dyed blonde pixie cut, caught for lunch in Brooklyn between speaking gigs in Chicago and Berlin, on a day when she was also managing a 35-person team at her digital marketing agency, posting multiple times an hour on social media, dog-sitting a Pomeranian whose "daddies" were at Burning Man, caring for her own mini Australian shepherd, and organizing a house party she expected to be late for because she first had to perform a rooftop DJ set at a different party.

# Hardware Device

## Definition

A hardware device, in this corpus, is a physical consumer electronics product — a smart speaker, handheld game console, smart glasses, or similar standalone gadget — that a company designs, manufactures, and sells as a distinct unit, as opposed to software or a service.

## Context

The corpus covers hardware devices from two angles: unveilings/reviews and retail deals. Google's annual "hardware event" is where the company unveils an entire slate of new devices at once — the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro phones, the Pixel Fold, Pixel Buds, and the Pixel Watch 2 — showing that "hardware" in this reporting names the physical product line a company ships, distinct from the software layered on top (Android 14, Bard, Google Assistant) that runs on it.

Retail-deal roundups organize hardware devices into shopping categories — Amazon's Cyber Monday guide lists separate sections for Echo/Fire TV/Kindle devices, speakers, headphones, tablets, and gaming gear — treating "speaker" as one device sub-category among several, not a synonym for hardware in general.

Smart glasses form a recurring device category: the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses combine a camera, open-ear audio, and a voice assistant, while Amazon's Echo Frames center on giving hands-free access to Alexa, and both trace the category back to the Google Glass Explorer Edition as its 2013 origin point.

Handheld gaming hardware is treated the same way: the Steam Deck OLED is discussed as a physical device with its own chip, screen, and battery specifications, refreshed mid-cycle the way a phone or headphone line would be.

## Key Characteristics

- **Physical and purchasable** — a hardware device is a standalone unit with a price and a retail listing (the Echo Frames at $314.99, the Ray-Ban Meta glasses at $299, the Steam Deck OLED at $549), not a subscription or app.
- **Distinct from the software it runs** — Google's hardware event unveils devices (Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Watch 2) separately from the software updates (Android 14, Bard) that ship alongside them.
- **Organized into device sub-categories** — retail guides split hardware into categories such as Echo/Fire TV/Kindle, speakers, headphones, tablets, and gaming, each reviewed and discounted on its own terms.
- **Defined by internal components** — reviews describe a device's identity through its chip, screen, and battery (the Steam Deck OLED's die-shrunk APU, 7.4-inch OLED panel, and 50Whr battery), the specs that distinguish one hardware generation from the next.
- **Ambiguous surface form** — "speaker" in the corpus denotes both an audio hardware device (a smart speaker) and the office of Speaker of the House; only the device sense belongs to this concept.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Barber Shop Near Me And Felix Silva

Felix Silva decided on the name Barber Shop Near Me after considering more than 20 other options for his Coral Springs, Florida, store in 2019. The name is meant to be neutral and memorable — another contender was "The Barber Shop" — but Silva fully leaned into the Google joke: the logo is a red location pin resembling Google's own, with a blue, white, and red barber pole pattern in the middle. "Before we opened, we just had a logo [on an Instagram account]," Silva says. "And we had some clients then tell us, 'Oh, man, before you guys opened we thought Google was coming to town.'"

Like Jirapraphanan of Thai Food Near Me, Silva had seen firsthand how a business's Google presence could help or hurt its chances of success. He frequently searches for keywords like "vegan" to find restaurants, and one time Google returned results for a restaurant that was not vegan but had a customer review containing the keyword, which was highlighted. "It was a light bulb moment… like, 'Okay, this is the path I need to take. I really need to dial in and focus on the online presence, specifically Google, because that is going to be the foundation of the business,'" Silva says.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Disinformation

## Definition

Disinformation is false or misleading content spread online — distinct from the illegal-content category (like terrorism or hate speech) in that, per the corpus's account of EU regulation, disinformation "is not illegal in the EU per se," yet still counts as a *systemic risk* that large platforms must assess and mitigate.

## Context

The corpus's central storyline is the EU's escalating regulatory pressure on X (formerly Twitter) over disinformation tied to the Israel-Hamas war: the Commission's October 2023 warning and formal information request to Musk accused X of being used "to disseminate illegal content and disinformation" following the Hamas attacks, and a EU-commissioned study later found X had "the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts" among major platforms.
Because X is a Digital Services Act (DSA) "very large online platform" (VLOP), the obligation to mitigate disinformation risk is legally binding on it even though the underlying falsehoods are not themselves illegal; the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (which Musk pulled X out of earlier in 2023) is treated by the Commission as a signal of DSA compliance on this exact risk.
Disinformation also surfaces as a generative-AI worry: Suleyman warned DeepMind's ethics board that AI "could lead to an explosion in disinformation," EU commissioner Vera Jourova flagged AI-generated disinformation as an election threat, and early fears that ChatGPT would be used "to generate disinformation on a massive scale" pushed European policymakers toward mandating security assessments of generative AI products.
Real-world examples in the corpus include a video-game clip falsely presented as Hamas missile footage circulating on X, and misinformation described as "rampant on social media" during the Gaza crisis, prompting some users to turn to Snap Map for unmediated, firsthand footage instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **Not illegal per se in the EU** — disinformation is treated as a systemic risk to be mitigated, not content that platforms are legally required to remove the way they must remove illegal content.
- **Distinct from "misinformation" but often paired with it** — the corpus uses both terms (e.g., "mis/disinformation posts," Mozilla's content-policy list of "misinformation" as a harm category), generally without a sharp technical distinction, though disinformation carries a stronger connotation of deliberate falsehood or manipulation (e.g., "Kremlin propaganda").
- **A VLOP systemic-risk obligation** — under the DSA, platforms designated VLOPs (like X) must proactively assess and mitigate disinformation risk, which is what makes an EU formal-information request or investigation possible even absent an illegal-content finding.
- **Measurable and comparable across platforms** — the EU's Code of Practice enabled a pilot study producing "structural indicators" (e.g., how easily disinformation content is found, how much engagement it gets) that let regulators rank X as worst among mainstream platforms.
- **A named risk of generative AI** — beyond social-media falsehoods, the corpus repeatedly frames disinformation as a downstream risk of AI text/image generation (ChatGPT, deepfakes), motivating both EU AI-Act-era safeguards and industry-side labeling commitments.

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

# Shadowbanning

## Definition

Shadowbanning, as TechCrunch describes it, is when a platform "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of" a user's content without the platform notifying the user that anything has been restricted, so the user only discovers it by noticing a drop in views or reach.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the central accusation in the October 2023 controversy over Meta's handling of Palestine-related content: Instagram users accused Meta of shadowbanning their Stories about Palestine, and TechCrunch frames the belief that Meta "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of," such content as longstanding rather than new to that month.
The same allegation is cited beyond Meta's own platforms as a driver of platform choice: users turned to Snapchat's Snap Map for firsthand Gaza content specifically because accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content on Instagram and Facebook had eroded their trust in those platforms.
Meta's official response did not deny that reach had dropped; it denied the mechanism, attributing the reduced Story reach specifically to a global, content-neutral bug in Stories that re-shared Reels or Feed posts, and separately attributed a different global bug — one that had prevented some users from going live — to technical error rather than deliberate suppression tied to subject matter.

## Key Characteristics

- **Covert, not disclosed** — the defining feature reporters and users pointed to is that visibility drops silently, with no notification to the affected account; Bella Hadid described being "immediately shadowbanned" and her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million" with no explanation from the platform.
- **Detected by comparison, not confirmation** — users inferred shadowbanning by comparing engagement across their own posts (e.g., a user whose Stories fell from "100s of views to zero or a handful" and rebounded only after posting unrelated content like a cat photo), since the platform provided no direct evidence of restriction.
- **Contested mechanism** — Meta disputed that the effect was shadowbanning-by-design, attributing the reduced Story reach to a bug that "affected accounts equally around the globe" and "had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content," rather than confirming intentional visibility limits.
- **Trust-eroding beyond the platform itself** — the accusation pushed users toward alternative platforms (Snap Map) even though the accused conduct occurred on Instagram and Facebook, showing shadowbanning claims can shift audience behavior across platforms, not just within one.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

# Bail

## Definition

Bail is the term the corpus uses for Sam Bankman-Fried's pretrial release from custody: a $250 million bond that let him live under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto instead of in jail while awaiting trial, and which a U.S. judge revoked in August 2023 (doc_0010, doc_0226).

## Context

The corpus's clearest illustration is Sam Bankman-Fried's case: after being arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022 and extradited to the U.S., he was released on a $250 million bail bond and confined to house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto (doc_0010). That release was not permanent — a U.S. judge revoked his bail in August 2023 after he was accused of intimidating former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison by leaking her private diary, leaving him in custody by the time his fraud trial began that October (doc_0010, doc_0226). Bail is also treated as something a court can simply refuse to grant: one recap of the FTX saga notes flatly that "SBF has been denied bail" (doc_0030). The concept resurfaces around Bankman-Fried's co-defendants, where house arrest — the condition often attached to bail — is described as a lighter alternative to imprisonment that cooperating felons like Gary Wang, Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison might still face even without prison time (doc_0121).

## Key Characteristics

- **Conditional, not unconditional freedom** — release on bail came bundled with restrictions (house arrest at a fixed address) rather than free movement (doc_0010).
- **Financially secured** — Bankman-Fried's release required a $250 million bail bond, tying his liberty to a monetary guarantee (doc_0010).
- **Revocable** — a judge can revoke bail mid-proceedings for conduct that violates its terms, as happened after the Ellison intimidation allegations, moving the defendant from house arrest to detention (doc_0010, doc_0226).
- **Discretionary and sometimes denied outright** — courts can decline to grant bail at all, as they did for Bankman-Fried at least once during his case (doc_0030).
- **Distinct from post-conviction outcomes** — bail concerns pretrial release, while house arrest can separately appear as a possible post-conviction alternative to imprisonment for cooperating defendants (doc_0121).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "bail" itself — it only reports how bail applied in Bankman-Fried's case.
Per Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, bail is "the money a defendant pays as a guarantee that they will show up in court at a later date," and release can be "conditioned on certain behavior of the defendant," such as staying away from an alleged victim (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).
A defendant's failure to comply "triggers the bond obligation and allows the court to keep any money given as security" (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Bankman-Fried's Conduct On Direct Examination

On October 28th, 2023, before the cross-examination had even begun, Judge Lewis Kaplan had already instructed Sam Bankman-Fried to answer the question he was being asked by his own lawyer — which The Verge's reporter called honestly kind of incredible, a man torpedoing his own credibility on direct testimony. The count of "Objection, narrative!" to Bankman-Fried's answers, followed by "Sustained," stood at three; the main thing clear so far, she wrote, was that he really loves the sound of his own voice, and that sometimes when he says "we," he only means himself.

The scolding was a pattern across two days. The day before, during an evidentiary hearing, Bankman-Fried had been repeatedly scolded by Kaplan for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's questions on cross-examination; on this day he was scolded for not answering his own counsel Mark Cohen's questions on direct, and he occasionally interrupted Cohen with "yes" and "yup." Much of the morning went on vocabulary — explaining "Amazon Web Services" and "database" was a bit too detail-oriented — and when Bankman-Fried tried to define "market manipulation," Kaplan told the jury that he, the judge, was the final authority on that.

In fairness, the reporter added, he was clearer and much easier to understand than at the evidentiary hearing the day before, with a minimum of word salad; she could not tell whether he was more relaxed or simply more rehearsed, and said she would be watching to see whether he became much less coherent once Sassoon got him on cross. The jury watched all of it intently.

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# Can Sun's Testimony On Fabricated Justifications

Former FTX lawyer Can Sun testified that during the days in November when the exchange imploded, Bankman-Fried — then trying to raise money from the private equity group Apollo, which wanted an explanation for what had happened — came to him and asked him to come up with justifications for the missing funds. That request, Sun said, "basically confirmed my suspicions that had been rising all day" that Bankman-Fried had purloined the funds.

Sun ran Bankman-Fried through possible explanations, including a margin loan program, and explained that none of them could fit the actual situation — for instance, Alameda had borrowed more from FTX than had ever been in the margin loan program. He said Bankman-Fried acknowledged their conversation with a "yup, yup": "I was expecting a bigger response, but it was very muted." After that, Sun testified, Singh spilled the beans that Alameda had withdrawn assets that included the customer funds. Sun quit the next day, and, like Yedidia, testified with immunity.

The jury then saw the fabrication deployed in public: a Good Morning America appearance by Bankman-Fried on December 1st, 2022, in which he tried to justify the missing funds through the margin loan program. The Verge's reporter called it such a flimsy excuse that even George Stephanopoulos could see through it, and described Sun's testimony as brief and explosive.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. # Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.
