The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. # Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."

# Why Bettors Should Consider NFL Award Longshots — And Bet Them Small

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that with five weeks left in the regular season there was plenty of time for an NFL award longshot to become a contender, so bettors should consider them — but should keep those bets small.

The grounds for taking longshots seriously are that they are easy to overlook because each award has a favorite or favorites: a longshot may be playing well, but other players have commanded the spotlight, making it easier for them to go unnoticed, and whatever the reason, they have not gotten the credit they deserve. The timing argument follows: if you wait too long before placing a bet, your payout will be a lot less than if you were to roll the dice on a longshot right now.

The counterweight, and the warrant for the sizing advice, is that there is always a reason why a player or several players have relatively short odds — they have been the best at their position throughout the season — and consequently there is just as good a reason why longshots have odds as long as they do. So the recommendation is to keep your bets small, or use a bonus bet if one is available, on longshots; if they do go on to win, you can smile all the way to the bank while telling everyone, "I told you so."

# 2023/24 Champions League Group Stage Overview

The UEFA Champions League reached the end of its group stage with 16 precious places in the first knockout round claimed, per Sporting News on Dec. 12, 2023.

Manchester City were looking to go back-to-back after their triumph in the previous season's Champions League, potentially becoming the first English club since Nottingham Forest in 1980 to successfully defend the trophy. The likes of Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Barcelona had also enjoyed strong group-stage campaigns and would surely be in the mix towards the sharp end of the competition, while Atletico Madrid and Real Sociedad completed the Spanish contingent in the next round.

# SEOs Also Say Search Results Have Improved

The strongest challenge to the article's premise is that Sullivan was not the only person insisting search results have improved significantly: out of the dozen-plus SEOs the writer spoke with at length, nearly every single one said search results are way better than they used to be — just objectively more accurate, more useful, more difficult to manipulate.

What gives that testimony force is the absence of an incentive to flatter Google. Except for Sullivan, these were not people with a reason to praise the company; if anything, these were folks who lamented how much harder it had become for them to take advantage of Google.

The effect on the writer was disorientation rather than conviction. This was not what she had been noticing, and certainly not what she had been hearing from friends and journalists and friends who are journalists. Were all of us wrong, or engulfed in some kind of Baader-Meinhof frequency bias delusion? Had she been researching a nonexistent problem? Were Google results actually amazing? Truly, she had lost the plot — was the premise of the piece completely off, and was she the asshole who deserved to be attacked by an alligator?

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# Epic Games' 2023 Layoffs And Overspending

Epic Games fired roughly 830 people in 2023, about 16 percent of its staff, including significant job cuts at Mediatonic, the Fall Guys studio Epic purchased in 2021.

CEO Tim Sweeney gave the reason in his note about the layoffs: "For a while now, we've been spending way more money than we earn," adding, "I had long been optimistic that we could power through this transition without layoffs, but in retrospect I see that this was unrealistic." Asked separately by The Verge whether app store restrictions had shaped Epic's plans, Sweeney said not directly, describing a really broad strategy of building games and technology and huge success in recent years with Unreal Engine gaining adoption among all kinds of industries even beyond games. He also acknowledged the company's own financial limitations: "we expanded the company to nine times the size we were before Fortnite took off," and Epic is "just trying to forge the strategy where we're living within our means and doing everything we absolutely can."

# The ChatGPT "Winter Break" Laziness Hypothesis

The "winter break hypothesis" proposes that ChatGPT gets worse in December because the model "learned" to do less work over the holidays — an explanation offered by users for a drop in output quality they began noticing in November 2023.

Starting in November, ChatGPT users noticed that the chatbot felt "lazier" than normal, citing instances of simpler answers and of the model refusing to complete requested tasks. Some users think this plays into the winter break hypothesis; others wonder whether the chatbot is simulating seasonal depression. OpenAI confirmed it was aware of the issue but was not sure why it was happening.

What would bear on the hypothesis is whether the model itself changed. OpenAI's ChatGPT account posted on December 8, 2023: "we've heard all your feedback about GPT4 getting lazier! we haven't updated the model since Nov 11th, and this certainly isn't intentional. model behavior can be unpredictable, and we're looking into fixing it." That the weights were unchanged since November 11 and that the behavior is unintentional are the facts against which any seasonal explanation has to be tested.

# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

# The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

# NFL Broadcasters' Taylor Swift Lyric References

On 17 September 2023 Travis Kelce scored a touchdown against the Jaguars, prompting CBS announcer Ian Eagle to say "Kelce finds a blank space for the score" — a reference to Swift's 2014 hit Blank Space — and NFL Network's Rich Eisen followed with a slew of lyric references in a preshow, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

The suspicion that Swift and Kelce were spending time together in New York was seemingly confirmed in September when it was reported they had been "quietly hanging out" for months — the first, albeit tentative, confirmation from the media rather than from amateur Swiftie sleuths on social media. It was only a matter of time before the story entered the cultural zeitgeist, and it did so very quickly. Eisen's preshow references included "shake it off", "anti-hero" and "all too well", and Kelce acknowledged the tongue-in-cheek banter, commenting on a montage video of the preshow that Eisen posted to Instagram: "Well played Rich … Well played."

Suddenly football fans and Swifties were living through this surprising collision — Swift lyrics were infiltrating NFL game commentary, and her fans were furiously becoming football experts. All that needed to happen, the timeline says, was for Swift herself to infiltrate a game, determining once and for all whether there was anything to the rumours.

# Acquisition

## Definition

Across the corpus, "acquisition" denotes one company buying another and taking ownership and control of it — whether framed as an all-cash purchase of a target's shares (Amazon–iRobot), an outright corporate purchase (OpenAI–Global Illumination, Microsoft–Activision Blizzard King, Palo Alto Networks–Talon/Dig), or referred to interchangeably as a "merger," "buy," or "deal."

## Context

The corpus uses "acquisition" (and its synonyms "purchase," "buy," "merger," "deal") across a wide range of industries and deal sizes, from an AI startup's first tuck-in purchase to a $69 billion mega-deal, showing the term denotes a general transaction type rather than one specific event.
Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot was priced as an all-cash offer, later cut by 15% during a lengthy EU antitrust review, illustrating how the announced acquisition price can move before a deal closes.
OpenAI's purchase of Global Illumination was described as the company's "first public acquisition," showing the term applies equally to small, non-controversial tuck-ins as to headline-grabbing mega-deals.
Microsoft's $69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard and King — the largest acquisition in video game history — took nearly two years to clear antitrust review before completing, and the corpus notes Microsoft's prior $26 billion purchase of LinkedIn as an earlier acquisition of comparable scale.
In cybersecurity, Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Talon Cyber Security and Dig Security for roughly $1 billion combined is framed as one of several "mega deals" and smaller tuck-ins (CrowdStrike–Bionic, IBM–Polar, Cisco–Splunk) that the corpus groups together as an industry-wide acquisition trend driven by consolidation pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Change of ownership and control** — the acquirer gains control of the target's assets, operations, or equity; in the iRobot case the EU's concern was specifically that Amazon would gain the ability and incentive to influence competitive outcomes on its marketplace once it controlled iRobot.
- **A negotiated price that can shift** — the iRobot deal's price fell 15% from its original $1.7 billion all-cash offer as the target took on more debt during a delayed close, showing acquisition price is not fixed until the deal actually closes.
- **Regulatory review as a gating step** — both the Amazon–iRobot deal (EU statement of objections, in-depth probe) and the Microsoft–Activision Blizzard deal (nearly two years of antitrust review before an October 2023 approval) show large acquisitions routinely require competition-authority clearance before completion.
- **Ranges from tuck-ins to mega-deals** — the same term covers OpenAI's small, low-profile purchase of Global Illumination and Microsoft's $69 billion Activision Blizzard purchase, differentiated by disclosed deal size and public scrutiny rather than by transaction mechanics.
- **Driven by consolidation dynamics** — in cybersecurity, acquisitions cluster as companies buy up specialized startups (e.g., Palo Alto pursuing Talon and Dig) partly in reaction to competitors' own acquisitions, a pattern the corpus explicitly attributes to a "swing" toward large all-in-one platforms.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "acquisition" is a standard mergers-and-acquisitions term: it occurs when one entity takes ownership of another entity's share capital, equity interests, or assets, as distinct from a merger, which combines two entities into a single new legal entity. (Source: Wikipedia, "Mergers and acquisitions," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Battery Life and Charging

## Definition

Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

## Context

Across the corpus, battery life and charging speed function as headline review criteria and buying-guide sort keys rather than a single defined term: Engadget's Steam Deck OLED review leads with "its battery life is better" as one of the device's core upgrades, and The Verge lists "improved battery life and audio" as a top pro for Amazon's third-gen Echo Frames. The charging half of the pair is increasingly organized around USB-C: Engadget notes that Apple's iPhone 15 line and the second-generation AirPods Pro both moved to USB-C charging, and Polygon's portable-charger guide treats USB-C Power Delivery wattage as the key spec for matching a power bank to a phone, tablet, Steam Deck, or laptop. Capacity for power banks is measured in mAh, per Polygon's guide, while device battery life is reported in hours (the Echo Frames reviewer logged about five hours of media playback and calls before hitting 30 percent) or in minutes of measured playtime (Engadget's Steam Deck OLED testing). Gogoro's battery-swapping business shows the same pair of concerns scaled up to electric vehicles: swapping a depleted battery for a charged one at a station is explicitly framed as a way to cut "charging time" relative to plugging in.

## Key Characteristics

- **Duration is measured empirically, not just claimed** — Engadget timed the Steam Deck OLED at four hours 23 minutes playing Hades versus two hours 42 minutes on the original LCD model under identical settings, a 62 percent gain that beat Valve's own 30-to-50-percent claim.
- **Charging speed is a distinct spec from capacity** — Valve advertises the Steam Deck OLED going from 20 to 80 percent in 45 minutes, a speed claim separate from its 50Whr battery capacity; Polygon likewise separates a power bank's mAh capacity from its wattage-based recharge speed.
- **USB-C is displacing proprietary connectors as the charging standard** — Apple's iPhone 15 and USB-C AirPods Pro, and the iPad's shift off Lightning to USB-C on its 10th-generation model, are all cited by Engadget as part of a single connector transition.
- **Power Delivery (PD) wattage governs compatibility between chargers and devices** — Polygon's guide notes that only power banks supporting the PD 3.0 spec can recharge a Steam Deck at its fastest rate, and that a laptop needs PD 3.1 and a compatible cable to reach 140 W charging.
- **Battery swapping is an alternative to plug-in charging at the vehicle scale** — Gogoro's network lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a station instead of waiting to charge in place, which TechCrunch frames as a way to reduce charging time for EV adopters.

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.

# FTX's Marketing And Political Influence

FTX bought mainstream recognition through sports branding and paid celebrity partnerships, while Bankman-Fried separately cultivated political access on both sides of American politics — including, according to Lewis, a contemplated $5 billion offer to keep Donald Trump out of the next presidential race. TechCrunch documented the marketing side on 2023-10-01 and the political side on 2023-10-02.

On the branding side, the company gained somewhat mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships: in 2021 it bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena, it got its name branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos, and it partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, as well as Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal and Naomi Osaka, among others. The 2023-10-02 account puts figures on two of those friendships and lucrative marketing deals: Tom Brady was paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million, to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Even Anna Wintour, the fashion doyenne, was in contact — she reached out over a Zoom meeting to ask SBF, whose preferred get-up was wildly curly hair, t-shirts and cargo shorts, to sponsor her Met Costume Ball.

On the political side, Bankman-Fried had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to. Lewis said that he met with the young crypto king ahead of him seeing Mitch McConnell to discuss how he could fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party — a meeting for which the suit SBF brought was tightly balled up under his arm with his dress shoes falling out of the middle of the bundle. Lewis also claimed that SBF had concocted a plan to buy off Trump, to get him not to run again for president. "Like how much would it take to get an answer?" Lewis recounted; "There was a number that was kicking around… this was $5 billion." Lewis said Sam was never sure whether that figure came directly from Trump, and TechCrunch notes it is not known whether anything was ever wired. The giving was not one-sided: SBF also looked to back candidates on the Democratic side of the aisle.

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.

# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

Source: "Major League Baseball," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball

# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Chapter 11 (Bankruptcy)

## Definition

Chapter 11 is the U.S. bankruptcy filing that insolvent companies in the corpus use to seek protection from creditors, and it does not guarantee a company survives: some filers are restructured under new leadership, while others wind down anyway once inside it.

## Context

In the corpus, Chapter 11 is the recurring endpoint for companies whose finances collapsed in 2022–2023. FTX and its trading-firm affiliate Alameda Research filed for Chapter 11 in the U.S. in mid-November 2022, after a published Alameda balance sheet exposed a huge FTT-token shortfall and a Binance-triggered bank run wiped out FTX's liquidity; the filing coincided with Sam Bankman-Fried's resignation as CEO and the appointment of Enron turnaround veteran John J. Ray III in his place. The same collapse pulled other crypto firms into Chapter 11: BlockFi filed in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading followed in January, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse. Outside crypto, WeWork filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in November 2023, listing over $18.6 billion of debt; TechCrunch's Week in Review opened its coverage of the filing with "as predicted," without stating when or on what basis it had made that prediction. SmileDirectClub took the same route but did not come back from it: the company shut down three months after its Chapter 11 filing, citing $900 million of debt — showing that a Chapter 11 filing in this corpus can precede either continued operation under new leadership (FTX) or an eventual full shutdown (SmileDirectClub).

## Key Characteristics

- **Used by companies of very different scale and sector** — from a $32-billion crypto exchange (FTX) to a flexible-office-space firm carrying $18.6 billion of debt (WeWork) to a smaller consumer startup (SmileDirectClub).
- **Often accompanies a leadership change** — FTX's filing came with Bankman-Fried's resignation and Ray's appointment as the new CEO to run the estate.
- **Does not guarantee the company continues operating** — SmileDirectClub shut down three months after filing, despite having gone through Chapter 11.
- **Can spread across a sector after one high-profile filing** — BlockFi's and Genesis Global Trading's Chapter 11 filings followed FTX's within months, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse.
- **Distinct from Chapter 7**, the other U.S. bankruptcy chapter appearing in the same corpus's 2023 tech-layoffs list, which cybersecurity startup IronNet filed as it ceased all business activities.

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly names "Chapter 11" as the filing route without stating what the chapter itself legally entails. Chapter 11, formally Chapter 11 of Title 11 of the U.S. Code, is the reorganization bankruptcy: it lets a debtor continue operating as a "debtor in possession" while it develops a plan to restructure its debts and pay creditors, rather than immediately liquidating its assets — which is the province of Chapter 7 instead (United States Courts, *Chapter 11 - Bankruptcy Basics*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# OpenAI Board Negotiations Over Altman Reinstatement

Over the weekend that followed Sam Altman's firing, OpenAI's board held on-and-off talks about bringing him back as CEO; the talks repeatedly stalled, and at one point it was confirmed that Altman would not return and that new leadership would take hold.

The sequence ran roughly as follows. Investors — reportedly furious at the turn of events — exerted pressure on OpenAI's board to reinstate Altman, going so far as to recruit Microsoft, with Satya Nadella said to be sympathetic. On November 18 The Verge reported that the board had agreed in principle to resign and to allow Altman and Brockman to return, but it waffled, missing a deadline by which many OpenAI staffers were set to leave the company; Altman was said to be ambivalent about coming back and to be asking for "significant" governance changes. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the matter, reported that the board was in talks with Altman about returning as CEO as soon as that week, with discussions involving Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one current board member, and possibly other directors. On November 19 The Information reported that Altman was expected to meet at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters as executives pushed to have him reinstated, with Brockman invited to join though it was unclear whether he would.

Negotiations then hit a snag: Bloomberg reported that Brad Lightcap and Mira Murati, among others, were pushing the board to reinstate Altman, but the directors resisted, and as of midday Sunday the board had not resigned out of concern over who could replace them and was vetting candidates — one possible new addition being Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor. Later, according to The Information citing an internal memo sent by Sutskever, Altman would not be returning as CEO, and OpenAI appointed Emmett Shear, the co-founder of video streaming site Twitch, as interim CEO, replacing Murati. A number of investors and OpenAI employees had tried to bring Altman back after the sudden firing, but following a weekend of negotiations it was confirmed that he would not return; what that meant for ChatGPT's future and for the OpenAI DevDay announcements remained to be seen.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Key Characteristics

- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).

- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "Super Bowl" itself — it only reports how teams, players, and betting markets relate to it.
Per Wikipedia, the Super Bowl is "the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), serving as the final game of each NFL season" (Wikipedia, *Super Bowl*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Layoffs

## Definition

Layoffs are the employer-initiated, batch workforce cuts the corpus tracks through 2023's "techwide reckoning" — TechCrunch's running tally puts total tech-industry job losses at more than 240,000 for the year, driven by companies pivoting "from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency" (doc_0049).

## Context

Across the corpus, 2023 is depicted as a "techwide reckoning" year: TechCrunch's running tracker put total tech-industry job losses at more than 240,000 for the year, already 50% above 2022 and still climbing, with cuts driven by the biggest names in tech — Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Yahoo, Meta and Zoom — as well as startups across many sectors (doc_0049).
The phenomenon recurs across very different company situations: a cybersecurity startup that went public but "failed to gain traction" and later shuttered outright, laying off its remaining staff (IronNet, doc_0011); a browser maker cutting 9% of its workforce across departments (Brave Software, doc_0043); a music-streaming giant cutting roughly 1,500 jobs (17% of its workforce) in its third layoff round of the year while its CEO framed the move as "right-sizing" for "productive and efficient" operations (Spotify, doc_0334); and a logistics startup cutting about 20% of its staff (roughly 600 people) under its founder, who returned as CEO after ousting his "hand-picked successor" over alleged overspending (Flexport, doc_0536, doc_0537).
Layoffs also follow directly from an acquired or platform company's takeover events: X's (formerly Twitter's) 2022 change of ownership "saw major layoffs, including in content moderation and human rights," which the corpus ties to the platform's later inability to respond to disinformation reports (doc_0024).
In the video-game industry specifically, layoffs are described as one of three interlocking forces — alongside consolidation and unionization — reshaping the sector: an estimated 9,000-plus video-game jobs were lost in 2023 versus roughly 1,000 in 2022, with layoffs concentrated at recently acquired studios (doc_0050).

## Key Characteristics

- **Batch, employer-driven terminations** — layoffs affect many employees at once (e.g., Brave's 9%, Spotify's 17%, Flexport's 20%), distinguishing them from case-by-case firings (doc_0043, doc_0334, doc_0537).
- **Framed as cost/efficiency correction** — companies in the corpus consistently attribute layoffs to macroeconomic pressure and a shift "from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency," rather than to sectoral collapse (doc_0049).
- **Can accompany full shutdown** — the most severe outcome pairs layoffs with the company ceasing operations entirely, as with IronNet, which "has shuttered and laid off its remaining staff following its collapse" (doc_0011).
- **Recurrent, not one-time** — several companies underwent multiple rounds within the same year (Spotify's third round by December 2023; Flexport cutting 20% in January with "more layoffs expected soon" by October) (doc_0334, doc_0536).
- **Concentrated post-acquisition** — layoffs and closures are described as "the most extreme negative outcomes for an acquired indie studio," recurring after ownership changes (video games) or leadership takeovers (X) (doc_0050, doc_0024).
- **Aggregate scale tracked industry-wide** — outlets maintain running trackers (TechCrunch's tech-layoffs list, Layoffs.fyi, layoffstracker.com) that quantify the year's cuts across sectors (doc_0049, doc_0050).

## Background (external)

Beyond the corpus's 2023 tech-industry usage, Wikipedia defines a layoff generically: "A layoff or downsizing is the temporary suspension or permanent termination of employment of an employee" — extended to a group of employees ("collective layoff") let go together "for business reasons, such as personnel management or downsizing an organization" (Wikipedia, "Layoff," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layoff).

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.
