# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. # The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." # Terms of Service

## Definition

Terms of Service (also called T&Cs or "terms and conditions") is the corpus's label for a platform's or vendor's own rulebook, as distinct from external regulation such as the DSA, which compels how that rulebook must be written and enforced (doc_0024).

The corpus applies the same label to two different domains: platform content-moderation rules — paired with, but not identical to, a separately named "Community Guidelines" document in Discord's warning system (doc_0505) — and the commercial fine print that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Context

In the corpus the term recurs wherever a platform's own rulebook — rather than a law — is the thing being disputed or regulated. The EU's DSA obliges platforms to "clearly communicate their T&Cs to users and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement," which is the legal hook the Commission uses against X over illegal-content handling (doc_0024). Breton's letter to X separately flags a change to X's "public interest policy" — the sub-rule governing when rule-breaking posts stay up for newsworthiness — as having left users "uncertain" about how X applies its own rules, illustrating that ToS content itself, not just its existence, is subject to DSA transparency requirements (doc_0025). On Meta's platforms, the operative rulebook is branded "Community Guidelines": Instagram removed and restricted Palestine-related posts that users say complied with those Guidelines, and Meta's own newsroom statements point back to the Guidelines and an appeals process as the mechanism for contesting enforcement (doc_0106). Snapchat's Community Guidelines are described as prohibiting pornographic, terrorism-advocating, or gratuitously violent content — a similarly-scoped rulebook to Meta's (doc_0124). Discord's new warning system links violators directly to its "Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism," pairing the rulebook with a visible enforcement record (doc_0505). Outside content moderation, "terms and conditions" also names the commercial fine print — wagering requirements, banking limits, expiry windows — that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers, which users must accept before registering (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-authored, not statutory** — the rules originate with the service, distinguishing ToS from the regulations (e.g. the DSA) that constrain how it must be written and enforced.
- **Related but distinct rulebooks share the "terms" label** — "T&Cs" and "terms and conditions" name a platform's or vendor's own rules generally, while Meta and Snap label the content-moderation slice specifically "Community Guidelines"; Discord's warning system links to "Terms of Service," "Community Guidelines," and an appeal mechanism as three separate, companion items rather than one document (doc_0505).
- **Sub-policies can shift independently** — X's "public interest policy" changed without broader ToS changing, showing a rulebook is composed of adjustable sub-rules (doc_0025).
- **Transparency and enforcement is a regulatory target** — the DSA specifically requires clear communication of T&Cs and demonstrable enforcement, not merely that terms exist (doc_0024).
- **Disputed, uneven enforcement is a recurring failure mode** — users on Meta's platforms reported content removed despite compliance with Community Guidelines, and inconsistent enforcement (e.g. across Arabic vs. Hebrew content) became a trust and bias issue (doc_0106).

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# The SEO Naming Effect On Customer Acquisition

The Verge argued that Thai Food Near Me's name really did help the restaurant — but not through the mechanism its owners intended. The initial SEO "hack" was likely technically ineffective, but it was memorable and funny, and the joke led to many, many, many articles and forum posts about the restaurant's name, which tipped the SEO scales in its favor; all of that content, including The Verge's own story, will help the restaurant's prominence on Google platforms. One SEO trick, the reporter wrote, has eaten another.

The grounds for saying the direct hack failed are a test and a concession. A Google Maps search for "Thai food near me" from the reporter's home in Brooklyn yielded plenty of options literally near her but not Jirapraphanan's business a few miles away. Robert Sampson, a co-owner who handles much of the back-end work including SEO, followed the online discussion about the utility of the name and conceded part of it: "The people who said that [the name is] not such a good idea… I think they're responding more from a national brand campaign. It is true that if you're in California, and you type 'Thai food near me,' you're going to have a little bit of a hard time finding us. But for local search, I think the name works really well." Danny Sullivan's position was that a "near me" name is not a silver bullet for gaming the search algorithm.

The warrant connecting name to durable ranking is the feedback loop that follows a first visit. As with Thai Food Near Me, the most powerful thing an SEO-driven name might be able to do is get customers in the door; from there it is up to the business to give them a good experience, whether that is a great plate of pad see ew or the perfect haircut, and then the cycle continues — happy customers leave good reviews, and good reviews help the business's Google Maps profile rank higher. Felix Silva also uploads high-quality photos and videos to his page and shares updates, another SEO move, since some experts say active profiles can improve a business's rankings.

# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# OpenAI Board Negotiations Over Altman Reinstatement

Over the weekend that followed Sam Altman's firing, OpenAI's board held on-and-off talks about bringing him back as CEO; the talks repeatedly stalled, and at one point it was confirmed that Altman would not return and that new leadership would take hold.

The sequence ran roughly as follows. Investors — reportedly furious at the turn of events — exerted pressure on OpenAI's board to reinstate Altman, going so far as to recruit Microsoft, with Satya Nadella said to be sympathetic. On November 18 The Verge reported that the board had agreed in principle to resign and to allow Altman and Brockman to return, but it waffled, missing a deadline by which many OpenAI staffers were set to leave the company; Altman was said to be ambivalent about coming back and to be asking for "significant" governance changes. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the matter, reported that the board was in talks with Altman about returning as CEO as soon as that week, with discussions involving Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one current board member, and possibly other directors. On November 19 The Information reported that Altman was expected to meet at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters as executives pushed to have him reinstated, with Brockman invited to join though it was unclear whether he would.

Negotiations then hit a snag: Bloomberg reported that Brad Lightcap and Mira Murati, among others, were pushing the board to reinstate Altman, but the directors resisted, and as of midday Sunday the board had not resigned out of concern over who could replace them and was vetting candidates — one possible new addition being Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor. Later, according to The Information citing an internal memo sent by Sutskever, Altman would not be returning as CEO, and OpenAI appointed Emmett Shear, the co-founder of video streaming site Twitch, as interim CEO, replacing Murati. A number of investors and OpenAI employees had tried to bring Altman back after the sudden firing, but following a weekend of negotiations it was confirmed that he would not return; what that meant for ChatGPT's future and for the OpenAI DevDay announcements remained to be seen.

# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. This bug affected accounts equally around the globe and had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content — and we fixed it as quickly as possible." Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Meta's representative did not address the other accusations of censorship beyond Story visibility and did not respond to TechCrunch's follow-up questions; Meta initially did not respond to follow-up requests for comment. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Board Governance

In this corpus, board governance is illustrated by cases where a board of directors exercises (or conspicuously lacks) the power to oversee and remove a company's CEO: OpenAI's board firing Sam Altman, Flexport's board ousting Dave Clark, and FTX's absence of any board at all.

## Context

The corpus's clearest working example is OpenAI's board, which in November 2023 fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after "a deliberative review process" concluded he was "not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."
That framing treats board governance as a standing check on the CEO: the board's stated justification was not a business or legal failure but a breakdown in the information flow the board needs to do its job.
OpenAI's board itself sits atop a nonprofit structure that "preserved its nonprofit governance structure" even as the startup underneath pursued commercial growth, so the board's authority over the CEO ran through that nonprofit layer rather than ordinary shareholder control.
Board composition determines whose judgment gets exercised: OpenAI's board consisted of chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and three non-employee directors (Adam D'Angelo, Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner), and the subsequent standoff over reinstating Altman turned on negotiating a new board (Bret Taylor, Larry Summers, Adam D'Angelo) as a condition of his return.
The corpus also frames board governance by its absence: Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang testified he was "concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors" before investing anyway, though on cross-examination he said Bankman-Fried told him he didn't want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.
Flexport's board, by contrast, illustrates governance operating through composition rather than absence: a board "made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder" held quarterly meetings on June 1 and Aug. 31 before Clark was forced to resign on Sept. 5.

## Key Characteristics

- **Power to remove or reinstate the CEO** — OpenAI's board fired Altman outright, then negotiated the terms (including its own reconstitution) under which he could return.
- **Grounded in a formal duty to oversee, not just advise** — the board's justification for firing Altman was specifically that his conduct hindered "its ability to exercise its responsibilities," i.e., an oversight duty rather than a performance complaint.
- **Structure shapes authority** — OpenAI's nonprofit board sat above the commercial subsidiary, giving it authority that ordinary shareholder-elected boards would not have over a purely for-profit company.
- **Composition determines outcome** — who sits on the board (employee vs. non-employee directors, investor-aligned vs. independent) is itself a lever contested during crises, as seen in both the OpenAI reinstatement talks and Flexport's investor-heavy board.
- **Its absence is itself notable** — the corpus flags FTX's lack of a board of directors as a specific governance gap investors identified before FTX's collapse, distinguishing "no oversight body" from "an oversight body that failed."

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, corporate governance is generally defined as the mechanisms, processes, and relations by which corporations are directed and controlled by their boards of directors, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders.
The widely cited Cadbury Report formulation puts it more simply: corporate governance is "the system by which companies are directed and controlled."
Source: [Corporate governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_governance), Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Nishad Singh's Backdated Revenue And Political Donations

Nishad Singh testified that he spruced up FTX's balance sheet with backdated transactions in December 2021 to push FTX's revenue "over the line" to $1 billion. By the time he found out about the use of customer money, in 2022, he was already compromised.

The falsification was not confined to the books. In Singh's case, The Verge reported on October 26th, 2023, it was also the American political system: by coordinating with Gabe Bankman-Fried, Singh had funneled money to a number of political causes, and that money came from "loans" that were not really loans, since he had not signed any term sheets.

Bankman-Fried's account on the stand distanced him from the backdating. He testified that he definitely did not know that Singh, his employee, had backdated interest payments to get FTX over the line to $1 billion — he had merely asked his employees to check whether there was any source of funds that was missing to get to $1 billion. The Verge's reporter described this testimony as especially rambling.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# ChatGPT Mobile App Launches And Revenue

ChatGPT's mobile apps, launched for iOS in May 2023 and Android in July 2023, topped 110 million combined installs and reached nearly $30 million in consumer spending, according to a market analysis by data.ai.

The rollout was staged by geography. OpenAI launched the ChatGPT app for iOS free to use, free from ads and allowing voice input, but initially limited to U.S. users; the app syncs history across devices so it knows what a user previously searched via the web interface, and it is integrated with Whisper, OpenAI's open source speech recognition system, for voice input. Within six days it topped 500,000 downloads. OpenAI then announced the app was available on iOS in the U.S., Europe, South Korea and New Zealand, and added 11 more countries — Albania, Croatia, France, Germany, Ireland, Jamaica, Korea, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria and the UK. The app was later expanded to more than 30 further countries: Algeria, Argentina, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Estonia, Ghana, India, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Lithuania, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mexico, Morocco, Namibia, Nauru, Oman, Pakistan, Peru, Poland, Qatar, Slovenia, Tunisia and the United Arab Emirates. A new version brought native iPad support with full-screen mode optimized for the tablet interface, support for using the chatbot with Siri and Shortcuts, and drag and drop for pulling individual messages from ChatGPT into other apps. On Android, OpenAI first put up a "pre-order" page on Google Play and days later released the app live in the US, India, Bangladesh and Brazil; the Android app looks more or less identical to the iOS one in functionality, getting most if not all of the web version's features and syncing conversations and preferences across devices.

Revenue is large but not dominant, and growth has slowed. In September, OpenAI amassed 15.6 million downloads and nearly $4.6 million in gross revenue across its iOS and Android apps worldwide — a record $4.58 million month for the mobile app — but revenue growth dropped from 30% to 20% in September according to market intelligence firm Appfigures. OpenAI's chatbot app far outpaces all others on mobile devices in terms of downloads, yet it is surprisingly not the top AI app by revenue: several other AI chatbots, such as "Chat & Ask AI" and "ChatOn — AI Chat Bot Assistant," make more money than ChatGPT.

# Cloud Computing

## Definition

Cloud computing, in the corpus, is the named vendor-run industry that Microsoft's OpenAI deal plugged into — when the deal closed in 2019, Microsoft "had a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service" — and that later commentary treats as the historical template for AI-market dynamics like vendor lock-in, market consolidation, and billing norms.

## Context

In the corpus, cloud computing shows up mainly as the historical precedent and infrastructural backbone for the current AI boom, rather than as a subject in its own right.

Commentators reach for the cloud computing industry to explain both OpenAI's near-collapse and the shape of the AI market that followed it: the industry became renowned for locking companies into "centralized, vortex-like silos," which is offered as the reason so many startups panicked and contacted OpenAI's rivals when OpenAI itself looked like it might disintegrate.

The same precedent is used to forecast how the AI market layers will settle: the foundation-model layer is expected to "settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market," and, separately, incumbents in cloud computing (like those in the earlier internet buildout) are said to have kept innovating "until innovation becomes stagnant" — a pattern predicted to repeat for AI incumbents.

Cloud computing also appears as a budget line competing with AI spending — total AI spending has overtaken cloud computing spending even though cloud computing "remains critical" — and as a unit-economics contrast: AI compute is normally metered in raw processing terms (FLOPs) or dollars per day, a different and less mature billing metric than most cloud computing's established consumption pricing.

## Key Characteristics

- **Centralized, provider-hosted delivery** — cloud computing is a vendor's service that a customer builds on top of, illustrated by Microsoft's use of its "cloud computing service" as the integration point for OpenAI's models.
- **Lock-in and the multi-cloud response** — the cloud computing industry is described as having locked customers into single-vendor "silos," which pushed companies toward multi-cloud and hybrid strategies — a dynamic the corpus draws on directly to explain AI startups' current over-reliance on OpenAI.
- **Tendency toward an oligopolistic market structure** — cloud computing is used as the reference case for a market that consolidated around a few large "cloud provider" incumbents, the same structure forecast for the foundation-model layer of the AI stack.
- **Incumbent-innovate-then-stagnate pattern** — cloud computing (alongside the internet) is cited as a precedent where incumbents keep innovating only until the market matures and stagnates, opening room for new entrants.
- **Compute as a metered, regulable resource** — "compute" (processing capacity, measured in floating point operations or FLOPs) is treated as a quantifiable input separate from "cloud computing" as an industry, and it is significant enough that the EU AI Act sets its high-risk regulatory threshold for general-purpose AI models directly on cumulative training compute (10^25 FLOPs).
- **Distinct billing norms from AI compute** — cloud computing has settled consumption-pricing conventions, whereas AI compute costs (e.g., OpenAI's roughly $700,000/day compute spend) are tracked and priced differently, "a very different metric than most cloud computing."

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources — such as networks, servers, storage, applications, and services — that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort (NIST, "NIST Definition of Cloud Computing", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.nist.gov/publications/nist-definition-cloud-computing).

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

# Expedia's Testimony On Google Ad Costs And Organic Listings

On November 1, 2023, Barry Diller, chair of Expedia and IAC, testified about his concerns that the increasing number of ads in search results was having an impact on organic listings. Quoting a letter he had written to Google back in 2019, per Bloomberg: "I must say I'm on the edge of revolt now that Google's actions are so punitive, not just for Expedia but also for IAC and all the players that depend upon something of a level playing field." Google CEO Sundar Pichai fired back that Google's travel listings was one of the most popular experiences the company built.

Expedia executives also testified about the cost of ads and how increases had no impact on search results. On October 19, 2023, Expedia's former chief operating officer, Jeff Hurst, told the court that the company's ad fees increased tenfold, from $21 million in 2015 to $290 million in 2019, and yet Expedia's traffic from Google did not increase. The implication was that this was due to direct competition from Google itself; Hurst pointed out that Google began sharing its own flight and hotel data in search results in that period, according to The Seattle Times.

# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# AI Startup Defensibility

Startup-focused AI work can be made defensible, but only at the application layer and only on conditions: to prove defensible in the rising climate of AI integration, industry-specific startups that tune generative AI models for a specific niche must prioritize collecting proprietary data, integrating a sophisticated application layer and assuring output accuracy. The claim is made against a market where costs are only one open question — TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of venture capitalists also asked how startups should approach building tools for AI technologies, how defensible startup-focused AI work will prove, and how upstart tech companies should charge for AI-powered tooling.

The grounds are a four-part assessment framework for the defensibility of application layers of AI companies. First, the application must address a real enterprise pain point prioritized by executives. Second, to provide tangible benefits and long-term differentiation, the application should be composed of cutting-edge models that fit the specific and unique needs of the software — it is not enough to simply plug into OpenAI; rather, applications should choose their models intentionally while balancing cost, compute, and performance. Third, the application is only as sophisticated as the data that it is fed: proprietary data is necessary for specific and relevant insights and to ensure others cannot replicate the final product, and to this end, in-house middle-layer capabilities provide a competitive edge while harnessing the power of foundational models. Fourth, due to the inevitable margin of error of generative AI, the niche market must tolerate imprecision, which is inherently found in subjective and ambiguous content, like sales or marketing.

The warrant is that the layer a startup occupies determines whether these conditions can be met at all. Most of the opportunity lies in the application layer, and within that layer the best applications will harness their in-house expertise to build specialized middle-layer tooling and blend them with the appropriate foundational models — "vertically integrated" or "full-stack" applications. For startups this approach means a shorter time-to-market: without negotiating or integrating with external entities, startups can innovate, iterate and deploy solutions at an accelerated pace, and this speed and agility can often be the differentiating factor in capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors. The middle layer alone is a weaker position, since it acts as a conduit connecting the foundational aspects of AI with the refined specialized application layer — model fine-tuning, prompt engineering and agile model orchestration — where the emergence of foundation model providers expanding into middle-layer tools heightens commoditization risks, established market leaders venturing into the space further intensify competition, and despite a surge in startups within this domain, clear winners still need to be discovered.

The incumbent-encroachment objection is answered by historical pattern rather than by denial. LLM observability falls within the middle-layer category, acting as a catalyst for specialized business applications to use foundational models, and incumbents like Datadog, New Relic and Splunk have all produced LLM observability tools and do appear to be putting a lot of R&D dollars behind this, which may curtail the market area in the short term. However, as seen before with the inceptions of the internet and cloud computing, incumbents tend to innovate until innovation becomes stagnant; with AI becoming a household name that finds use cases in every vertical, startups have the chance to come in with innovative solutions that disrupt and reimagine the work of incumbents. It is still too early to say with certainty who the winners will be, as every day reveals new gaps in existing AI frameworks, and therein lie major opportunities for startups. A companion TechCrunch survey of 10 investors on the future of AI and what they believe might be the next big thing touched on the same terrain — where startups still stand a chance, where oligopoly dynamics and first-mover advantages are shaping up, and the value of proprietary data.

# Thai Food Near Me's Customer Experience

For a group The Verge's reporter spoke with at Thai Food Near Me on an evening in August, the SEO plan had — at least practically — the intended effect. One of the diners, Travis, found the restaurant on Yelp when searching for nearby dining options after missing an earlier reservation elsewhere; several people in the group had heard about the restaurant when it went viral in the spring but had not realized it was in New York. The group agreed the food was good, even though they had not known what to expect, and said they would definitely consider coming back if they were in the area.

The channel, though, was not the one the owners planned for. Co-owner Robert Sampson says that for the first several months of being open, most people were coming in after seeing Twitter and Reddit posts, not Google results, while others would walk by outside, do a double take at the sign, and come inside. "After you get that initial bunch, you've got people who enjoyed their dining experience here," he says. "They'll tell all their friends and family if they liked it, and then those people come from word of mouth."

Despite the admittedly silly name, the reporter found it clear that co-owners Jirapraphanan and Sampson care about what they are serving: the restaurant is clean and stylish, and the menu, carefully designed by Jirapraphanan, features original dishes she had not seen at other places; her food was tasty, came out promptly, and she said she too would note the spot if she were in the area again and craving Thai food. Jirapraphanan wants people to come back because they actually like the food — the name is part, but not all, of the branding. "I want to be different from other Thai restaurants," he says. # Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Google Warps The Web It Observes

The article's central claim is that Google, not the SEOs, defined the shape of the modern internet: you cannot be the most powerful observer in the world for two decades and not deeply warp what you are looking at.

The grounds are the structural impossibility built into Google's founding goal. The company started with a noble cause — trying to make the internet easier to navigate at scale — and did accomplish that, but in doing so it inadvertently and profoundly changed how the internet looked. The problem lay in Google trying to be an objective and neutral arbiter of an information landscape that was meant to pretend it did not exist: you cannot design a free, automated system to help people find information without some people trying to game that system.

The warrant that shifts responsibility away from practitioners is a comparison of scale and agency. For the past 25 years the internet as we know it has been almost entirely defined and controlled by Google; what the SEOs do matters for all of us on a daily basis, distorting how we perceive the world in ways we can hardly begin to imagine or understand, yet any money any SEO has made is a fraction of a crumb compared to Google's 10-layer cake. The company brings in hundreds of billions of dollars a year, profits that skew Google's choices and priorities — as Google's founders themselves wrote back in 1997, "we expect that advertising funded search engines will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."

The writer reaches this position by way of Lily Ray, who seemed the most reasonable person she had spoken to — even granting that Ray calls herself a "thought leader" and changed her last name to improve her personal branding by more closely associating herself with her grandmother's uncle, the artist Man Ray. # Celebrity Endorsement

In the corpus, "celebrity endorsements" is named directly only once — listed alongside "campaign trail rallies" as one of several online-campaign tactics that, on their own, are "not enough to engage voters online" — and everywhere else the corpus treats it as a family of concrete cases rather than a defined category: FTX's paid partnerships with athletes, Anna Wintour's sponsorship request to Sam Bankman-Fried, The Epoch Times' political endorsements and CPAC sponsorship, and Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok launch via a Jake Paul endorsement.

## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. (Wikipedia, "Celebrity branding," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_branding)

# Regulatory Investigations Into OpenAI In 2023

OpenAI faced regulatory action on several fronts in 2023: Italy ordered ChatGPT blocked over GDPR concerns, Poland opened its own GDPR investigation, China's licensing regime pushed ChatGPT clients out of the App Store, and the FTC was reported to be investigating the chatbot's statements about people.

Italy moved first. Italy's data protection authority ordered OpenAI to stop processing people's data locally with immediate effect, saying it was concerned the ChatGPT maker was breaching the EU's General Data Protection Regulation and opening an investigation; OpenAI began geoblocking access to ChatGPT in Italy. The DPA then laid out what OpenAI needed to do for the order to be lifted, giving OpenAI a deadline of April 30 to complete the regulator's compliance demands, with a slightly more generous timeline of May 15 for a local radio, TV and internet awareness campaign. Poland's authority publicly announced it had opened an investigation regarding ChatGPT, accusing the company of a string of breaches of the GDPR.

In China, multiple generative AI apps were removed from Apple's China App Store ahead of the country's latest generative AI regulations, set to take effect August 15. Apple wrote in a letter to OpenCat, a native ChatGPT client: "As you may know, the government has been tightening regulations associated with deep synthesis technologies (DST) and generative AI services, including ChatGPT. DST must fulfill permitting requirements to operate in China, including securing a license from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). # The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. # Most Valuable Player (MVP)

## Definition

In the corpus, MVP (Most Valuable Player) names the player judged most valuable to a team's or league's success, and the term surfaces at several distinct scopes: a formal season-long league award (NFL MVP, NBA MVP), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or cross-sport label applied by media, players, and coaches.

## Context

At the league-season level, the NFL MVP and NBA MVP are formal annual awards contested among a small pool of star players. Sporting News's Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece had Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott, and Jalen Hurts as the current NFL MVP favorites after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff as the longshot cases. Separately, Yardbarker's Dec. 24, 2023 Christmas Day preview framed the Ravens-49ers game explicitly as "the decisive clash for the MVP Award," with Brock Purdy the heavy favorite (-230) and Lamar Jackson — the 2019 MVP — holding the second-shortest odds (+525). At the single-game level, MVP denotes a game-specific honor, as with Patrick Mahomes's two Super Bowl MVPs. At the team level, MVP is used informally by outlets like Yardbarker to name each team's most indispensable player at a season's midpoint — a designation that need not track the league-wide award and can go to a non-quarterback, as when Miami's Tyreek Hill or New England's Jabrill Peppers is named team MVP. The same informal usage crosses sports, as when an MLS goalkeeper calls forward Luciano Acosta "the MVP" of FC Cincinnati. MVP is also a standard sports-betting futures market: bettors wager on which player will win the season MVP award well before or during the season, alongside markets like Rookie of the Year and Offensive/Defensive Player of the Year.

## Background (external)

Beyond this corpus's sports-betting and news coverage, Wikipedia describes an MVP award more generally as an honor bestowed on the individual (or individuals, in case of a tie) "whose individual performance is the greatest in an entire league, for a particular competition, or on a specific team," recognizing one player's contribution within a team effort. (Source: Wikipedia, "Most valuable player," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_valuable_player, accessed 2026-09-02.)

## Key Characteristics

- **Multiple scopes** — the same "MVP" language covers a formal season-long league award (NFL, NBA), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or sport-crossing designation used by media and players alike.
- **Voting-panel awards lack fixed criteria** — the NBA MVP, for instance, is chosen by a panel of sportswriters and broadcasters (format since 1980, weighted 5/3/1 points for first/second/third-place votes) with no set selection rulebook, which is why outcomes are notoriously hard to predict and can produce "upset" winners.
- **Quarterback bias in NFL MVP framing** — corpus coverage repeatedly frames the NFL MVP as typically going to a quarterback from a top-seeded team, to the point that a non-quarterback like Christian McCaffrey is described as facing long odds "if the MVP wasn't a quarterback-driven award."
- **Betting futures market** — MVP odds are a standing futures category at sportsbooks (alongside moneylines, spreads, and other award markets), bet on well ahead of the outcome and repriced as the season's results accumulate.
- **Team-level MVP is unofficial** — team MVP picks (e.g., Yardbarker's AFC team-by-team roundup) are editorial judgments, not sanctioned awards, and can diverge sharply from who is in the league MVP conversation.
