# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Mustafa Suleyman, one of the three founders, said "I don't see this as a contradictory position. There are huge benefits to come from these technologies. The goal is not to eliminate them or pause their development. The goal is to mitigate the downsides." Having won over Thiel, Hassabis worked his way into Musk's orbit: about two years later they met at a conference organised by Thiel's investment fund, which had also put money into SpaceX, and Hassabis secured a tour of SpaceX headquarters, after which, with rocket hulls hanging from the ceiling, the two lunched in the cafeteria; Musk explained his plan to colonise Mars to escape overpopulation and other dangers on Earth, and Hassabis replied that the plan would work so long as superintelligent machines didn't follow and destroy humanity on Mars too. Musk was speechless, not having thought about that particular danger, and soon invested in DeepMind alongside Thiel so he could be closer to the creation of the technology.

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Line Of Credit

## Definition

In the corpus, "line of credit" denotes the informal, undocumented facility FTX extended to its affiliated trading firm Alameda Research.

Caroline Ellison testified there was "no contract and no written terms," and that Alameda drew against it in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time to fund trading.

## Context

The corpus uses "line of credit" almost exclusively to describe the Alameda–FTX arrangement at the center of the SBF fraud trial. Gary Wang testified he set the facility up for Alameda and repeatedly raised its ceiling as the firm kept running against its limit — moving from "a few hundred million," to a billion, and eventually to an effectively unlimited figure that reached $65 billion. Caroline Ellison separately testified that Alameda used $14 billion drawn "as a line of credit" to repay debts to third-party lenders, on Bankman-Fried's instruction. Bankman-Fried, for his part, denied on the stand that he knew about the "effectively infinite" line of credit Alameda received from FTX, a denial The Verge's trial coverage called "peculiar," concluding that the CEO of a financial company simply didn't pay attention to finances.

## Key Characteristics

- **Draw-as-needed structure** — funds are accessed incrementally against a ceiling rather than disbursed as one loan, as when Ellison described draws of $100,000 to $10 million at a time.
- **No collateral, no contract** — Ellison testified the $65 billion facility "did not have to post collateral" and had "no contract and no written terms."
- **Escalating limit** — the ceiling was repeatedly raised over time as the borrower kept exceeding it, per Wang's account of the increases from a few hundred million to $65 billion.
- **Invisible to oversight** — the credit line "wasn't visible to FTX's auditors," per Ellison's testimony, despite its size.
- **Exclusivity** — Wang testified the facility was "unmatched by anyone else on FTX," making it a privilege specific to the affiliated firm rather than a standard customer product.

## Background (external)

The corpus illustrates the term through a single, irregular instance rather than defining it as a general banking product. Per Wikipedia, a line of credit is ordinarily a borrowing arrangement from a bank or financial institution that lets a customer access funds up to a set maximum whenever needed, is typically revolving so that repaid amounts can be redrawn without reapplying, and generally charges interest only on the amount actually withdrawn (Wikipedia, *Line of credit*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Alameda–FTX facility described in the corpus departs from that standard model in that it had no written agreement, no collateral requirement, and no independent oversight.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Alameda's $65 Billion Line Of Credit At FTX

Alameda Research held a line of credit at FTX that ultimately reached $65 billion, an effectively unlimited borrowing facility unmatched by anyone else on the exchange and carrying no requirement to post collateral. Caroline Ellison testified that there was no contract and no written terms, and that the credit line was not visible to FTX's auditors; when she raised that with Bankman-Fried, he told her not to worry about it.

The defining features are its size, its informality, and its exclusivity. Gary Wang, who set the line up, testified that it did not start that big: Bankman-Fried asked him to increase it a few times because Alameda kept running into its limits — first "a few hundred million," then a billion, then even that was not enough. It was not clear how Wang arrived at $65 billion specifically, but he said he had discussed the number with Bankman-Fried, and that other customers did not have the same privileges. Ellison said the credit was drawn in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time and was used primarily for trading: the effectively unlimited funds "allowed us to make profitable trades we couldn't have made otherwise."

The boundary case is the source of the capital and Bankman-Fried's disclaimed knowledge of it. Ellison testified that Alameda and FTX were initially "very integrated," run by the same team from the same office, and that when Alameda was scrounging for funds Bankman-Fried told her FTX would be a good source of capital. On the stand, Bankman-Fried denied he knew about the effectively infinite line of credit Alameda received from FTX — an argument The Verge's reporter found peculiar, summarising the take-away as that the CEO of a financial company simply did not pay attention to finances.

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.

# OpenAI Board Negotiations Over Altman Reinstatement

Over the weekend that followed Sam Altman's firing, OpenAI's board held on-and-off talks about bringing him back as CEO; the talks repeatedly stalled, and at one point it was confirmed that Altman would not return and that new leadership would take hold.

The sequence ran roughly as follows. Investors — reportedly furious at the turn of events — exerted pressure on OpenAI's board to reinstate Altman, going so far as to recruit Microsoft, with Satya Nadella said to be sympathetic. On November 18 The Verge reported that the board had agreed in principle to resign and to allow Altman and Brockman to return, but it waffled, missing a deadline by which many OpenAI staffers were set to leave the company; Altman was said to be ambivalent about coming back and to be asking for "significant" governance changes. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the matter, reported that the board was in talks with Altman about returning as CEO as soon as that week, with discussions involving Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one current board member, and possibly other directors. On November 19 The Information reported that Altman was expected to meet at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters as executives pushed to have him reinstated, with Brockman invited to join though it was unclear whether he would.

Negotiations then hit a snag: Bloomberg reported that Brad Lightcap and Mira Murati, among others, were pushing the board to reinstate Altman, but the directors resisted, and as of midday Sunday the board had not resigned out of concern over who could replace them and was vetting candidates — one possible new addition being Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor. Later, according to The Information citing an internal memo sent by Sutskever, Altman would not be returning as CEO, and OpenAI appointed Emmett Shear, the co-founder of video streaming site Twitch, as interim CEO, replacing Murati. A number of investors and OpenAI employees had tried to bring Altman back after the sudden firing, but following a weekend of negotiations it was confirmed that he would not return; what that meant for ChatGPT's future and for the OpenAI DevDay announcements remained to be seen.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# FTX's Ties To The Bahamian Government

On cross-examination on October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon drew out evidence that Bankman-Fried had a cozy — perhaps even inappropriately cozy — relationship with the Bahamian government, which is not what he was on trial for but probably did not make him look any better to a jury. She asked whether he had made comments about paying off the Bahamian national debt, which he did not recall.

The court then saw an internal FTX group chat called "Project Chinchilla Chatter," in which another member asked who in the Bahamian government they needed to talk to for the project. "His name is Ryan Salame :p," Bankman-Fried replied; Salame was one of FTX's executives. In another part of the chat, Bankman-Fried noted that the Bahamian prime minister was at the FTX arena in FTX seats with his wife.

The jury was also shown a November 9th email from Bankman-Fried to Ryan Pinder, attorney general of the Bahamas, saying "we are deeply grateful" for what the Bahamas had done for FTX, and offering as a token of that gratitude: "We would be more than happy to open up withdrawals for all Bahamian customers on FTX, so that they can, tomorrow, fully withdraw all of their assets, making them fully whole. It's your call whether you want us to do this, but we are more than happy to and would consider it the very least of our duty to the country, and could open it up immediately if you reply saying you want us to. If we don't hear back from you, we are going to go ahead and do it tomorrow." Bankman-Fried did indeed open withdrawals for Bahamian customers.

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Acquisition

## Definition

Across the corpus, "acquisition" denotes one company buying another and taking ownership and control of it — whether framed as an all-cash purchase of a target's shares (Amazon–iRobot), an outright corporate purchase (OpenAI–Global Illumination, Microsoft–Activision Blizzard King, Palo Alto Networks–Talon/Dig), or referred to interchangeably as a "merger," "buy," or "deal."

## Context

The corpus uses "acquisition" (and its synonyms "purchase," "buy," "merger," "deal") across a wide range of industries and deal sizes, from an AI startup's first tuck-in purchase to a $69 billion mega-deal, showing the term denotes a general transaction type rather than one specific event.
Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot was priced as an all-cash offer, later cut by 15% during a lengthy EU antitrust review, illustrating how the announced acquisition price can move before a deal closes.
OpenAI's purchase of Global Illumination was described as the company's "first public acquisition," showing the term applies equally to small, non-controversial tuck-ins as to headline-grabbing mega-deals.
Microsoft's $69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard and King — the largest acquisition in video game history — took nearly two years to clear antitrust review before completing, and the corpus notes Microsoft's prior $26 billion purchase of LinkedIn as an earlier acquisition of comparable scale.
In cybersecurity, Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Talon Cyber Security and Dig Security for roughly $1 billion combined is framed as one of several "mega deals" and smaller tuck-ins (CrowdStrike–Bionic, IBM–Polar, Cisco–Splunk) that the corpus groups together as an industry-wide acquisition trend driven by consolidation pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Change of ownership and control** — the acquirer gains control of the target's assets, operations, or equity; in the iRobot case the EU's concern was specifically that Amazon would gain the ability and incentive to influence competitive outcomes on its marketplace once it controlled iRobot.
- **A negotiated price that can shift** — the iRobot deal's price fell 15% from its original $1.7 billion all-cash offer as the target took on more debt during a delayed close, showing acquisition price is not fixed until the deal actually closes.
- **Regulatory review as a gating step** — both the Amazon–iRobot deal (EU statement of objections, in-depth probe) and the Microsoft–Activision Blizzard deal (nearly two years of antitrust review before an October 2023 approval) show large acquisitions routinely require competition-authority clearance before completion.
- **Ranges from tuck-ins to mega-deals** — the same term covers OpenAI's small, low-profile purchase of Global Illumination and Microsoft's $69 billion Activision Blizzard purchase, differentiated by disclosed deal size and public scrutiny rather than by transaction mechanics.
- **Driven by consolidation dynamics** — in cybersecurity, acquisitions cluster as companies buy up specialized startups (e.g., Palo Alto pursuing Talon and Dig) partly in reaction to competitors' own acquisitions, a pattern the corpus explicitly attributes to a "swing" toward large all-in-one platforms.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "acquisition" is a standard mergers-and-acquisitions term: it occurs when one entity takes ownership of another entity's share capital, equity interests, or assets, as distinct from a merger, which combines two entities into a single new legal entity. (Source: Wikipedia, "Mergers and acquisitions," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Terms of Service

## Definition

Terms of Service (also called T&Cs or "terms and conditions") is the corpus's label for a platform's or vendor's own rulebook, as distinct from external regulation such as the DSA, which compels how that rulebook must be written and enforced (doc_0024).

The corpus applies the same label to two different domains: platform content-moderation rules — paired with, but not identical to, a separately named "Community Guidelines" document in Discord's warning system (doc_0505) — and the commercial fine print that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Context

In the corpus the term recurs wherever a platform's own rulebook — rather than a law — is the thing being disputed or regulated. The EU's DSA obliges platforms to "clearly communicate their T&Cs to users and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement," which is the legal hook the Commission uses against X over illegal-content handling (doc_0024). Breton's letter to X separately flags a change to X's "public interest policy" — the sub-rule governing when rule-breaking posts stay up for newsworthiness — as having left users "uncertain" about how X applies its own rules, illustrating that ToS content itself, not just its existence, is subject to DSA transparency requirements (doc_0025). On Meta's platforms, the operative rulebook is branded "Community Guidelines": Instagram removed and restricted Palestine-related posts that users say complied with those Guidelines, and Meta's own newsroom statements point back to the Guidelines and an appeals process as the mechanism for contesting enforcement (doc_0106). Snapchat's Community Guidelines are described as prohibiting pornographic, terrorism-advocating, or gratuitously violent content — a similarly-scoped rulebook to Meta's (doc_0124). Discord's new warning system links violators directly to its "Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism," pairing the rulebook with a visible enforcement record (doc_0505). Outside content moderation, "terms and conditions" also names the commercial fine print — wagering requirements, banking limits, expiry windows — that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers, which users must accept before registering (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-authored, not statutory** — the rules originate with the service, distinguishing ToS from the regulations (e.g. the DSA) that constrain how it must be written and enforced.
- **Related but distinct rulebooks share the "terms" label** — "T&Cs" and "terms and conditions" name a platform's or vendor's own rules generally, while Meta and Snap label the content-moderation slice specifically "Community Guidelines"; Discord's warning system links to "Terms of Service," "Community Guidelines," and an appeal mechanism as three separate, companion items rather than one document (doc_0505).
- **Sub-policies can shift independently** — X's "public interest policy" changed without broader ToS changing, showing a rulebook is composed of adjustable sub-rules (doc_0025).
- **Transparency and enforcement is a regulatory target** — the DSA specifically requires clear communication of T&Cs and demonstrable enforcement, not merely that terms exist (doc_0024).
- **Disputed, uneven enforcement is a recurring failure mode** — users on Meta's platforms reported content removed despite compliance with Community Guidelines, and inconsistent enforcement (e.g. across Arabic vs. Hebrew content) became a trust and bias issue (doc_0106).
- **Domain-general usage** — the same "terms and conditions" label also covers non-moderation commercial conditions, such as wagering requirements attached to sportsbook bonuses (doc_0072).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "Terms of Service," "T&Cs," and "terms and conditions" throughout without ever stating a general definition for the term.

More broadly, terms of service — also called terms of use or terms and conditions — are the legal agreement between a service provider and its users: a person must agree to follow them to use the offered service, and for some websites they function simply as a disclaimer (Wikipedia, *Terms of service*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# How To Open A Sportsbook Account, Download The App, And Place A Bet

The first thing you need before betting on the NBA Rookie of the Year Award, or any other bet, is an account at an online sportsbook — opening one is easy, quick and free, and can be done on a laptop, phone or tablet. The precondition to remember is location: it does not matter which state you live in when you sign up, but you must be within the state lines where sports betting is legal to make wagers, you must meet the legal age requirement (often 21), and you must adhere to all local and federal sports betting regulations. To bet through an app you must be within the state where that app is licensed.

The account steps run in order. Choose a sportsbook available in your state — common options include DraftKings, FanDuel and BetMGM — using trusted sources or official websites for the most reliable links and bonuses. Click "sign up" or "register," which opens a form for your details: first and last name, date of birth, home address, phone number, preferred email address, username and password, and Social Security number. Accept the sportsbook's terms and conditions. Then claim your welcome bonus, which can come in many forms; if a bonus or promo code is needed, enter it at this stage. Read the requirements for any promotion or offer before accepting so you are aware of any restrictions before betting. Make your initial deposit — most apps provide multiple methods such as credit/debit cards, e-wallets like PayPal, or bank transfers — and you are ready to bet. To use an app, download it onto your smartphone or tablet from the App Store for iOS or the Google Play Store for Android; if it is unavailable in your app store, consider downloading it directly from the sportsbook's official website.

Placing the bet is the last step. Browse the app to understand the odds and markets available before placing bets to ensure the best value. For a Rookie of the Year wager specifically, navigate to the basketball section of the sportsbook website, select the NBA, and go to the futures tab, where you will find Rookie of the Year odds, NBA MVP odds and more; select the bet you want, enter the amount, and finalize your bet slip. You can also repeat the process at multiple books — you have to create a new account at each, but you also qualify for new-customer bonuses and promotions at each, so exploring your options and finding the best deal is worth the effort. Always gamble responsibly and stay informed about the regulations specific to your state.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.
