# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Appeals Process

## Definition

An appeals process is a defined mechanism that lets a party formally challenge a decision — a content-moderation action, a disciplinary penalty, or a court ruling — and have it reconsidered by a different decision-maker, rather than accepting the original ruling as final.

## Context

The corpus shows this same structure recurring across three distinct domains. Social platforms build appeals processes into their content-moderation systems: Meta states "there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it," and separately says it "continue[s] to provide tools for users to appeal our decisions if they think we made a mistake" during its Israel-Hamas war content response, while Discord's new account-standing system "link[s] out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism" whenever it notifies a user of a policy violation and restricts their account. In sports governance, Everton's appeal against a 10-point Premier League deduction "will be heard by a different three-person panel" than the one that issued the penalty — the hallmark of an appeals process, a distinct reconsidering body rather than the original decision-maker revisiting its own call. In litigation, an appeal is the formal next step after a verdict or ruling: Bankman-Fried's defense lawyers were "laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments" during his trial, and Apple's patent-infringement loss triggers an "appeals process" that "can take around 18 months" and can determine whether an import ban stays in effect while the case is contested.

## Key Characteristics

- **Distinct reviewing authority** — an appeal is reheard by a different decision-maker than the one who made the original call, as with Everton's separate three-person panel.
- **Available after an adverse decision** — content removals, disciplinary points deductions, and trial verdicts all trigger the same downstream option to contest the outcome.
- **Can be lengthy** — legal appeals are explicitly time-consuming; Apple's appeal of its Apple Watch import ban "can take around 18 months," during which the underlying decision may still take effect unless a stay is separately granted.
- **Built into platform enforcement systems as a safeguard against error** — Meta frames its appeals process as compensating for moderation mistakes ("we can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process") rather than as an admission the underlying policy is wrong, while Discord links its warning notices out to its own appeal mechanism whenever it restricts a user's account for a policy violation.
- **Does not guarantee reversal** — Everton's manager Dyche urges his players to "forget about the appeal and accept the reality" rather than assume it will succeed, underscoring that lodging an appeal only obtains reconsideration, not a favorable outcome.

# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. # Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# Fine / Penalty

In the corpus, a fine or penalty is the recurring instrument through which financial-market, antitrust, data-protection, and platform-governance enforcement is actually made to bite against a confirmed or admitted violation.

## Definition

Fine / Penalty is the label the corpus uses for the monetary sanctions regulators and prosecutors impose on companies and individuals after a confirmed or admitted rule violation — sized as a percentage of global annual turnover under the EU's DSA and CPC regimes, or as a fixed dollar amount tied to a settlement or guilty plea under U.S. agency actions such as the DOJ/Treasury/CFTC resolution with Binance and CZ.

## Context

The corpus shows two dominant penalty designs. First, EU digital regulation ties fines to a percentage of a company's *global annual turnover* rather than a fixed sum: the Digital Services Act (DSA) allows fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover for confirmed breaches, and a separate Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) enforcement track lets national consumer-protection authorities impose fines of up to 4% of global annual turnover for conduct pursued as a consumer-law violation. The Commission invoked the 6% DSA figure against X twice — once as a warning in October 2023 alongside its formal request for information into Israel-Hamas disinformation concerns (before any investigation had been opened), and again in December 2023 when it opened a formal DSA infringement proceeding against X over risk management, content moderation, and deceptive design. Second, U.S. enforcement in the corpus produces fixed-dollar or admission-linked penalties: Binance agreed to pay about $4.3 billion to resolve DOJ, Treasury (FinCEN), OFAC, and CFTC investigations into anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, with CEO Changpeng Zhao separately recommended for a $150 million CFTC fine as part of his guilty plea. Outside the DSA/antitrust cluster, Norway's Datatilsynet used a *daily* fine (up to roughly $100,000 per day) to compel Meta's compliance with a consentless-ad-tracking ban, illustrating that penalties can be structured as recurring pressure rather than a one-time sum. Historical fines also inform present conduct: the corpus notes that Google only invested in improving search quality in Europe after being hit with a €5 billion EU antitrust fine in 2018, and the U.S. government cited that history in the DOJ's antitrust trial to argue Google lacks intrinsic incentive to improve without competitive or regulatory pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Turnover-percentage basis (EU model)** — DSA fines scale with a company's global annual turnover (up to 6%), and the parallel CPC consumer-protection track caps at 4% of the same base, so penalty exposure grows with company size rather than being fixed.
- **Fixed-sum or negotiated basis (US model)** — U.S. agencies in the corpus (DOJ, CFTC, SEC) reach specific dollar penalties, often as part of a guilty plea or settlement, as with Binance's $4.3B resolution and CZ's $150M recommended fine.
- **Recurring/daily penalties** — some regulators (Norway's Datatilsynet against Meta) impose a fine that accrues per day of continued non-compliance, functioning as ongoing coercive pressure rather than a settled sanction.
- **Penalty as leverage before conviction** — the EU explicitly warned X of possible fines and blocking *before* opening a formal investigation, using the threat of a penalty as a compliance-forcing signal.
- **Downstream behavioral effect** — a fine already levied (Google's 2018 EU antitrust fine) can be cited years later as evidence a company's improvements were penalty-driven rather than voluntary.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "fine" and "penalty" as familiar terms without defining them itself. Per the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute (LII), a fine is "a monetary penalty that is issued for failing to comply with one's duties," and it falls under the broader category of penalty, which can be imposed by a court or an administrative agency in either a criminal or a civil context (LII, *Fine*, accessed 2026-09-02). In criminal law a fine may be imposed alongside or instead of incarceration for violating a statute, while in civil law it commonly follows a breach of contract or comparable duty (LII, *Fine*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Ecosystem And Unit-Economics Challenge Of Battery Swapping

Battery swapping's promise for consumers is large but its economics and ecosystem requirements are the binding constraint. A recent report jointly created by Bain & Company and Blume Ventures forecast that electric two-wheelers sold without batteries can reduce the upfront cost of vehicles by 40% to 50%, attracting price-sensitive Indian customers — but it also warned that building a battery-swapping ecosystem in India will be challenging in the near term, and suggested maintaining a battery-swapping inventory for top SKUs across manufacturers, identifying customer segments to target, and establishing "walled-garden" partnerships to support swappable-battery systems.

An investor told TechCrunch that to really succeed, the market needs interoperability and standardization in battery swapping, similar to how we have USB-C in phones nowadays. For Gogoro, it is just a start to explore how big a dent it can make in the overall EV market with its available battery-swapping solution.

Gogoro's CEO Horace Luke conceded the scale of the build-out required: "I got an entire ecosystem I need to bring in. It took us a little while to get ready, and it will take us a little while to ramp up. And I'm not fooling anybody that this thing is going to [happen] overnight. India's a huge place. There's a lot of different use cases. The price-performance people ask for is very high . . . # Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.

# Dangerous Organizations and Individuals Policy

The Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy is the named enforcement category Meta cites when it removes content tied to groups that governments designate as terrorist organizations, most directly Hamas.
In the corpus its practical trigger is Hamas: content praising or supporting Hamas, which governs Gaza and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union, is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms.
Meta tracks enforcement of this policy as its own category, separate from its Violence and Incitement policy, reporting that it removed "seven times as many pieces of content on a daily basis for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy in Hebrew and Arabic alone" in the three days after October 7, 2023, compared with the two months prior.

## Context

In the corpus the policy is the mechanism through which Meta enforces against Hamas-related content during the Israel-Hamas war, and it is the recurring flashpoint in disputes over whether that enforcement is applied evenly.
Meta invokes the policy to justify removing content that praises or supports Hamas — Hamas being "designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union" — and Instagram separately cited a related "Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations" when it denied that a specific violent, threatening comment violated its rules, illustrating that the same policy family both blocks and, in users' eyes, under-enforces depending on the content.
The designation logic recurs beyond Meta's own platform actions: the corpus notes that Hamas is "considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries" in the context of the Web Summit/Cosgrave controversy, and that UNRWA operates "alongside Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other countries designate as a terrorist organization" in Gaza — showing the same underlying designation of Hamas driving both platform moderation policy and geopolitical characterization of the region's governing party.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named, tracked enforcement category** — Meta reports removal volumes specifically "for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy," distinct from its Violence and Incitement policy, letting the company cite a sevenfold daily increase in Hebrew/Arabic enforcement after October 7.
- **Anchored to external terrorist designations** — the policy's practical trigger in the corpus is content supporting Hamas, an organization the U.S., EU and U.K. designate as a terrorist group; the platform rule imports government designations rather than defining "dangerous" independently.
- **Contested in application** — Palestinian users and digital-rights advocates argue the policy (and its Community Guidelines "violence or dangerous organizations" language) is enforced inconsistently, citing a case where a violent, threatening comment was ruled not to violate it, and past instances where the Al-Aqsa Mosque hashtag was blocked after being "mistaken for a terrorist organization."
- **Localized to Arabic and Hebrew content** — the volume Meta cites for this policy is scoped specifically to Hebrew and Arabic content, not platform-wide, reflecting the languages most implicated in Israel-Hamas war content moderation.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Meta's own Community Standards describe the Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy more broadly than the Hamas-specific enforcement described above: it generally bars praise, substantive support, and representation of any individual or organization that Meta designates as dangerous, a designation list that spans terrorist organizations, hate organizations, criminal organizations, and other violence-inducing entities, not just Hamas.
Source: Meta Transparency Center, "Dangerous Organizations and Individuals" Community Standard, accessed 2026-09-02, https://transparency.meta.com/policies/community-standards/dangerous-individuals-organizations/.

# Lars Mapstead And The Discovery Of Early Web Monetization

Lars Mapstead — "Legendary Lars," described by an old contact as "an absolute god in that space" — was tracked down in Northern California, where he was preparing to run for president in 2024 as a Libertarian. He spent the first two years of his life in a Volkswagen van traveling the Pacific coast before his hippie parents settled on a Big Sur property with goats, chickens, and no electricity, and became a tinkerer and autodidact, the guy who reads the instruction manual and fixes everything himself.

He first heard about the World Wide Web in 1993, while working for a company selling computer motherboards, and his reaction was idealistic: "It's like the freedom of information! It's all just about collaborating and bettering mankind!" He learned how to build a website and then how to submit a site to be listed in early search directories like AltaVista, WebCrawler, Infoseek, and Lycos, and how to create chat rooms attracting people spread across the globe, all alone in their homes but together online. It was beautiful, it was exciting, and he saw himself as an explorer in a small but finite kingdom: "I had surfed the entire internet. There wasn't a page I hadn't seen."

Everything changed when a company in New York offered to pay him $2,000 a month to put banner ads on one of his websites. More clicks meant more ad dollars, higher search engine rankings meant more clicks, so whatever it took to get a higher ranking he learned how to do: he bought photographs of women in bikinis and made a 60-page slideshow with banner ads on each page, and he realised most search engines were just listing websites in order of how many times a search term appeared on the site and in its tags, so he focused on stuffing his sites with keywords, resubmitting his URL to the search engines, and waiting for the results to change.

Mapstead started pulling in $25,000–$30,000 a month, working 12- to 14-hour days. "It was how long could I stay awake and how little life could I have because this was more money than I could have ever imagined in my lifetime," he said. "It was like I won the lottery, and I didn't know how long it would last."

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

On November 21, 2023, OpenAI announced that it and Sam Altman had "reached an agreement in principle" for him to return as the company's CEO, alongside a restructured "initial" board of directors.

The new initial board named in the announcement comprised former Salesforce chief executive Bret Taylor as chair, former US Secretary of the Treasury Larry Summers, and Quora founder Adam D'Angelo. OpenAI posted: "We have reached an agreement in principle for Sam Altman to return to OpenAI as CEO with a new initial board of Bret Taylor (Chair), Larry Summers, and Adam D'Angelo. Altman also posted about the deal, saying his decision to join Microsoft on the Sunday "was the best path for me and the team"; since then, the new board's composition and Microsoft's support appeared to have been enough to bring him back to the company he co-founded. On November 29, OpenAI announced that Microsoft would gain representation on the new initial board in the form of a non-voting observer — it was not immediately clear who this observer might be, only that they would not have an official vote in board business.

# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.

# FTX's Ties To The Bahamian Government

On cross-examination on October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon drew out evidence that Bankman-Fried had a cozy — perhaps even inappropriately cozy — relationship with the Bahamian government, which is not what he was on trial for but probably did not make him look any better to a jury. She asked whether he had made comments about paying off the Bahamian national debt, which he did not recall.

The court then saw an internal FTX group chat called "Project Chinchilla Chatter," in which another member asked who in the Bahamian government they needed to talk to for the project. "His name is Ryan Salame :p," Bankman-Fried replied; Salame was one of FTX's executives. In another part of the chat, Bankman-Fried noted that the Bahamian prime minister was at the FTX arena in FTX seats with his wife.

The jury was also shown a November 9th email from Bankman-Fried to Ryan Pinder, attorney general of the Bahamas, saying "we are deeply grateful" for what the Bahamas had done for FTX, and offering as a token of that gratitude: "We would be more than happy to open up withdrawals for all Bahamian customers on FTX, so that they can, tomorrow, fully withdraw all of their assets, making them fully whole. It's your call whether you want us to do this, but we are more than happy to and would consider it the very least of our duty to the country, and could open it up immediately if you reply saying you want us to. # The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Lobbying and Political Donations

Lobbying and political donations, in the corpus, are the practice of routing money to political candidates, parties, or officials to gain influence with regulators and lawmakers.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's use of FTX- and Alameda-linked funds for political spending during his rise, which became a prosecution theme at his fraud trial: TechCrunch reports he "had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to," and that Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" surfaced his "attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president" by discussing with Mitch McConnell how to "fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party." At trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried used stolen customer funds to "donate millions to political candidates," and Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Bankman-Fried, pleaded guilty to charges that included counts "around his political donations." The practice also extended to those around Bankman-Fried: The Verge names "Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap" among the entities caught up in the case.

## Key Characteristics

- **Funding source under dispute** — the prosecution's theory was that the political donations were financed with misappropriated FTX customer deposits, not Bankman-Fried's own money.
- **Instrument of influence, not charity** — donations to candidates and officials are described alongside efforts to buy access (e.g., the reported offer to Trump), distinguishing them from Bankman-Fried's professed effective-altruism philanthropy.
- **Bipartisan reach** — the reporting describes both engagement with Democratic-aligned regulators/officials and an attempt to influence a Republican presidential race, i.e., donations spanning both parties.
- **Legal exposure** — political donations became a distinct criminal count (against Nishad Singh) and a recurring prosecution talking point against Bankman-Fried, showing the practice can carry direct legal consequences when the underlying funds are alleged to be stolen.
- **Family/associate involvement** — the practice was not confined to Bankman-Fried himself; his mother Barbara Fried's PAC, Mind the Gap, is named as part of the same political-spending network.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# X Post-Volume Discrepancy

X CEO Linda Yaccarino's post-volume figure contradicts Elon Musk's: speaking at an event in the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, she claimed X was seeing 500 million posts per day on the platform, whereas in September Musk had said X users were creating 100 million to 200 million posts every day, excluding retweets.

The contradiction attacks the reliability of the platform's own content-volume claims rather than any single argument built on them: two of X's most senior figures, weeks apart, gave figures that differ by a factor of roughly two to five. TechCrunch does not adjudicate between them, closing the item with "So who's right? Beats us." The item also does not state whether Yaccarino's 500 million figure excludes retweets, as Musk's explicitly did — so part of the gap may be definitional and part may not.

# Lars Mapstead And The Discovery Of Early Web Monetization

Lars Mapstead — "Legendary Lars," described by an old contact as "an absolute god in that space" — was tracked down in Northern California, where he was preparing to run for president in 2024 as a Libertarian. He spent the first two years of his life in a Volkswagen van traveling the Pacific coast before his hippie parents settled on a Big Sur property with goats, chickens, and no electricity, and became a tinkerer and autodidact, the guy who reads the instruction manual and fixes everything himself.

He first heard about the World Wide Web in 1993, while working for a company selling computer motherboards, and his reaction was idealistic: "It's like the freedom of information! It's all just about collaborating and bettering mankind!" He learned how to build a website and then how to submit a site to be listed in early search directories like AltaVista, WebCrawler, Infoseek, and Lycos, and how to create chat rooms attracting people spread across the globe, all alone in their homes but together online. It was beautiful, it was exciting, and he saw himself as an explorer in a small but finite kingdom: "I had surfed the entire internet. There wasn't a page I hadn't seen."

Everything changed when a company in New York offered to pay him $2,000 a month to put banner ads on one of his websites. More clicks meant more ad dollars, higher search engine rankings meant more clicks, so whatever it took to get a higher ranking he learned how to do: he bought photographs of women in bikinis and made a 60-page slideshow with banner ads on each page, and he realised most search engines were just listing websites in order of how many times a search term appeared on the site and in its tags, so he focused on stuffing his sites with keywords, resubmitting his URL to the search engines, and waiting for the results to change.

Mapstead started pulling in $25,000–$30,000 a month, working 12- to 14-hour days. "It was how long could I stay awake and how little life could I have because this was more money than I could have ever imagined in my lifetime," he said. "It was like I won the lottery, and I didn't know how long it would last."

# Eddy Cue's Testimony In US V. Google

Eddy Cue took the stand as a witness in US v. Google, the landmark antitrust trial over Google's search business, and arrived with two messages: Apple believes in protecting its users' privacy, and it also believes in Google — whether those two statements can be simultaneously true became the question of the day.

Cue is one of the highest-profile witnesses in the case so far, in part because the deal between Google and Apple, which makes Google the default search engine on all Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year, is central to the US Department of Justice's case against Google. The Verge set the scene in the Washington, DC courtroom, where the screens had briefly malfunctioned and left witnesses with only binders before the tech came back up, showing an image of three iPhones each demonstrating a part of the phone's setup process. Cue, in a dark suit, squinted at the monitor and said, "The resolution on this is terrible. You should get a Mac," drawing laughs in an otherwise staid and quiet courtroom; Judge Amit Mehta, presiding over the case, leaned into his microphone and answered, "If Apple would like to make a donation…", drawing bigger ones, before everybody got back down to business.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. # Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.
