# Accessibility Localisation

Accessibility localisation is the work of adapting a digital product or platform's language coverage — dialects, translation, and rollout scope — to serve users outside the default language, and the gap that opens when that work is incomplete. In the corpus it shows up in two forms: a company's own roadmap for extending a feature beyond one language, and the moderation failures that surface when a platform's language resources are thin relative to the languages and dialects it actually serves.

## Context

Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" generative-AI feature for kids launched on 25 October 2023 available in English only, with internationalization described as "further down the road" — an explicit statement that localisation is a staged rollout, not a launch-day requirement. On the other end of the spectrum, TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 reporting on Meta describes localisation as an unmet obligation rather than a future roadmap item: Meta "struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources," and a third-party report commissioned by Meta after the May 2021 conflict found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, attributing the gap partly to Hebrew being a "more standardized language" and to reviewers lacking competence in less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic. Meta's response to the October 2023 Israel-Hamas war — a special operations center staffed with Hebrew and Arabic speakers that removed or flagged over 795,000 pieces of content in those two languages in three days — is itself evidence of how much moderation capacity a platform must mobilize once it takes multilingual coverage seriously.

## Key Characteristics

- **Staged rollout vs. structural gap** — a company can frame incomplete localisation as a temporary phase (Amazon's "English only… internationalization further down the road") or it can be a longstanding structural deficit that draws external criticism (Meta's under-resourced Arabic-language moderation).
- **Dialect granularity matters** — Arabic's 25+ dialects mean that broad-language coverage is not the same as coverage of a specific dialect (e.g., Palestinian Arabic), and a platform can claim "Arabic support" while still failing specific dialect communities.
- **Localisation gaps have asymmetric enforcement effects** — Meta's own commissioned report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content for the same underlying conduct, tying uneven language resourcing directly to uneven moderation outcomes.
- **Crisis response can expand localisation capacity rapidly** — Meta stood up a dedicated Hebrew/Arabic special operations center and processed hundreds of thousands of pieces of content in those languages within days once the Israel-Hamas war escalated, showing localisation investment is elastic to urgency, not fixed.

# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.

# Film Awards Season

## Definition

Film awards season is the recurring stretch of the film-industry calendar in which press coverage frames new releases as Oscar or Academy Award contenders — flagging some as deliberately positioned to win ("Oscar bait") and speculating on which will actually take home a prize — while a person's past Academy Award wins and nominations continue to be cited as a lasting professional credential.

## Context

In the corpus the season shows up mainly as a lens critics apply to late-2023 releases: Polygon calls Poor Things "the unlikeliest but most effective Oscar bait" and says it is "tipped to win a few real Oscars," and in a separate piece calls Martin Scorsese's The Aviator "the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography" he has made — both using the same vocabulary of prediction and campaign-style positioning ahead of the ceremony.
The corpus also shows the season's residue outside the current release cycle: composer Danny Elfman is described as having earned "four Oscar nominations for Good Will Hunting, Men in Black, Big Fish, and Milk," Eyes Without a Face's score composer Maurice-Alexis Jarre is noted as someone who "would later go on to win an Academy Award for his work on Lawrence of Arabia," and Reese Witherspoon is introduced simply as "the Oscar-winner" in an unrelated parenting interview — in each case the award functions as a durable label attached to the person's name long after the ceremony itself.
A TechCrunch piece on Google's Gemini Pro model uses the prior season's results as a factual benchmark to catch AI errors, listing the actual 2023 winners it got wrong: Brendan Fraser for Best Actor, "Navalny" for Best Documentary Feature, "All Quiet on the Western Front" for Best International Film, "Women Talking" for Best Adapted Screenplay, and "Pinocchio" for Best Animated Feature Film.

## Key Characteristics

- **Contender framing** — press describes a film as "Oscar bait" or "Oscar-baity" when its subject matter, cast, or pedigree seems engineered to attract Academy attention (doc_0094, doc_0192).
- **Predictive speculation** — outlets explicitly forecast outcomes ahead of the ceremony, e.g. Poor Things being "tipped to win a few real Oscars" (doc_0094).
- **Persistent credential** — an Academy Award win or nomination becomes a standing descriptor attached to a person's name in unrelated coverage years or decades later (doc_0165, doc_0587, doc_0177).
- **Multi-category structure** — the season spans many competitive categories beyond lead acting, including Documentary Feature, International Film, Adapted Screenplay, and Animated Feature (doc_0126).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses awards-season vocabulary ("Oscar bait," "tipped to win") without stating when the season runs or how it culminates. Per Wikipedia, the film awards season "usually begins during November or December of the previous year," with the Academy Awards ceremony as its culmination, held "commonly in late February or early March following the relevant calendar year, and six weeks after the announcement of the nominees" (Wikipedia, *Academy Awards*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Lobbying and Political Donations

Lobbying and political donations, in the corpus, are the practice of routing money to political candidates, parties, or officials to gain influence with regulators and lawmakers.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's use of FTX- and Alameda-linked funds for political spending during his rise, which became a prosecution theme at his fraud trial: TechCrunch reports he "had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to," and that Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" surfaced his "attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president" by discussing with Mitch McConnell how to "fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party." At trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried used stolen customer funds to "donate millions to political candidates," and Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Bankman-Fried, pleaded guilty to charges that included counts "around his political donations." The practice also extended to those around Bankman-Fried: The Verge names "Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap" among the entities caught up in the case.

## Key Characteristics

- **Funding source under dispute** — the prosecution's theory was that the political donations were financed with misappropriated FTX customer deposits, not Bankman-Fried's own money.
- **Instrument of influence, not charity** — donations to candidates and officials are described alongside efforts to buy access (e.g., the reported offer to Trump), distinguishing them from Bankman-Fried's professed effective-altruism philanthropy.
- **Bipartisan reach** — the reporting describes both engagement with Democratic-aligned regulators/officials and an attempt to influence a Republican presidential race, i.e., donations spanning both parties.
- **Legal exposure** — political donations became a distinct criminal count (against Nishad Singh) and a recurring prosecution talking point against Bankman-Fried, showing the practice can carry direct legal consequences when the underlying funds are alleged to be stolen.
- **Family/associate involvement** — the practice was not confined to Bankman-Fried himself; his mother Barbara Fried's PAC, Mind the Gap, is named as part of the same political-spending network.

# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

# Meta's Arabic Mistranslation Of "Alhamdulillah"

In the week before TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 report, multiple Instagram users found that the platform was auto-translating the common Arabic phrase "Alhamdulillah" — "Praise be to God" — into text calling Palestinians terrorists, and the mistranslation was triggered by the presence of Palestinian identity markers in the same bio. Meta later told 7amleh a "bug" caused it, and told 404 Media the issue had been fixed.

The condition under which the mistranslation appeared is specific. In screen recordings posted online, users found that if they included "Palestinian" and the corresponding flag emoji in their Instagram bio alongside the Arabic phrase, Instagram automatically translated the bio to "Palestinian terrorists – Praise be to Allah" or "Praise be to God, Palestinian terrorists are fighting for their freedom." When users removed "Palestinian" and the flag emoji, Instagram translated the same Arabic phrase to "Thank God." Instagram users complained that the offensive mistranslation was active for hours before Meta appeared to correct it.

Shayaan Khan, a TikTok creator who posted a viral video about the mistranslation, told TechCrunch that Meta's lack of cultural competence is not just offensive but dangerous: the "glitch" can fuel Islamophobic and racist rhetoric already exacerbated by the war in Gaza. He pointed to the fatal stabbing of Wadea Al-Fayoume, a Palestinian-American child whose death is being investigated as a hate crime.

Meta did not respond to TechCrunch's request for comment about the mistranslation. 7amleh's Jalal Abukhater said Meta told the organisation that a "bug" caused it, and a Meta spokesperson told 404 Media the issue had been fixed: "We fixed a problem that briefly caused inappropriate Arabic translations in some of our products. We sincerely apologize that this happened."

# Board Governance

In this corpus, board governance is illustrated by cases where a board of directors exercises (or conspicuously lacks) the power to oversee and remove a company's CEO: OpenAI's board firing Sam Altman, Flexport's board ousting Dave Clark, and FTX's absence of any board at all.

## Context

The corpus's clearest working example is OpenAI's board, which in November 2023 fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after "a deliberative review process" concluded he was "not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."
That framing treats board governance as a standing check on the CEO: the board's stated justification was not a business or legal failure but a breakdown in the information flow the board needs to do its job.
OpenAI's board itself sits atop a nonprofit structure that "preserved its nonprofit governance structure" even as the startup underneath pursued commercial growth, so the board's authority over the CEO ran through that nonprofit layer rather than ordinary shareholder control.
Board composition determines whose judgment gets exercised: OpenAI's board consisted of chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and three non-employee directors (Adam D'Angelo, Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner), and the subsequent standoff over reinstating Altman turned on negotiating a new board (Bret Taylor, Larry Summers, Adam D'Angelo) as a condition of his return.
The corpus also frames board governance by its absence: Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang testified he was "concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors" before investing anyway, though on cross-examination he said Bankman-Fried told him he didn't want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.
Flexport's board, by contrast, illustrates governance operating through composition rather than absence: a board "made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder" held quarterly meetings on June 1 and Aug. 31 before Clark was forced to resign on Sept. 5.

## Key Characteristics

- **Power to remove or reinstate the CEO** — OpenAI's board fired Altman outright, then negotiated the terms (including its own reconstitution) under which he could return.
- **Grounded in a formal duty to oversee, not just advise** — the board's justification for firing Altman was specifically that his conduct hindered "its ability to exercise its responsibilities," i.e., an oversight duty rather than a performance complaint.
- **Structure shapes authority** — OpenAI's nonprofit board sat above the commercial subsidiary, giving it authority that ordinary shareholder-elected boards would not have over a purely for-profit company.
- **Composition determines outcome** — who sits on the board (employee vs. non-employee directors, investor-aligned vs. independent) is itself a lever contested during crises, as seen in both the OpenAI reinstatement talks and Flexport's investor-heavy board.
- **Its absence is itself notable** — the corpus flags FTX's lack of a board of directors as a specific governance gap investors identified before FTX's collapse, distinguishing "no oversight body" from "an oversight body that failed."

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, corporate governance is generally defined as the mechanisms, processes, and relations by which corporations are directed and controlled by their boards of directors, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders.
The widely cited Cadbury Report formulation puts it more simply: corporate governance is "the system by which companies are directed and controlled."
Source: [Corporate governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_governance), Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Lobbying and Political Donations

Lobbying and political donations, in the corpus, are the practice of routing money to political candidates, parties, or officials to gain influence with regulators and lawmakers.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's use of FTX- and Alameda-linked funds for political spending during his rise, which became a prosecution theme at his fraud trial: TechCrunch reports he "had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to," and that Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" surfaced his "attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president" by discussing with Mitch McConnell how to "fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party." At trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried used stolen customer funds to "donate millions to political candidates," and Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Bankman-Fried, pleaded guilty to charges that included counts "around his political donations." The practice also extended to those around Bankman-Fried: The Verge names "Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap" among the entities caught up in the case.

## Key Characteristics

- **Funding source under dispute** — the prosecution's theory was that the political donations were financed with misappropriated FTX customer deposits, not Bankman-Fried's own money.
- **Instrument of influence, not charity** — donations to candidates and officials are described alongside efforts to buy access (e.g., the reported offer to Trump), distinguishing them from Bankman-Fried's professed effective-altruism philanthropy.
- **Bipartisan reach** — the reporting describes both engagement with Democratic-aligned regulators/officials and an attempt to influence a Republican presidential race, i.e., donations spanning both parties.
- **Legal exposure** — political donations became a distinct criminal count (against Nishad Singh) and a recurring prosecution talking point against Bankman-Fried, showing the practice can carry direct legal consequences when the underlying funds are alleged to be stolen.
- **Family/associate involvement** — the practice was not confined to Bankman-Fried himself; his mother Barbara Fried's PAC, Mind the Gap, is named as part of the same political-spending network.

# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# FTX's Marketing And Political Influence

FTX bought mainstream recognition through sports branding and paid celebrity partnerships, while Bankman-Fried separately cultivated political access on both sides of American politics — including, according to Lewis, a contemplated $5 billion offer to keep Donald Trump out of the next presidential race. TechCrunch documented the marketing side on 2023-10-01 and the political side on 2023-10-02.

On the branding side, the company gained somewhat mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships: in 2021 it bought the naming rights for the Miami Heat's home arena, it got its name branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos, and it partnered with celebrities including Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, as well as Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal and Naomi Osaka, among others. The 2023-10-02 account puts figures on two of those friendships and lucrative marketing deals: Tom Brady was paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million, to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Even Anna Wintour, the fashion doyenne, was in contact — she reached out over a Zoom meeting to ask SBF, whose preferred get-up was wildly curly hair, t-shirts and cargo shorts, to sponsor her Met Costume Ball.

On the political side, Bankman-Fried had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to. Lewis said that he met with the young crypto king ahead of him seeing Mitch McConnell to discuss how he could fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party — a meeting for which the suit SBF brought was tightly balled up under his arm with his dress shoes falling out of the middle of the bundle. Lewis also claimed that SBF had concocted a plan to buy off Trump, to get him not to run again for president. "Like how much would it take to get an answer?" Lewis recounted; "There was a number that was kicking around… this was $5 billion." Lewis said Sam was never sure whether that figure came directly from Trump, and TechCrunch notes it is not known whether anything was ever wired. The giving was not one-sided: SBF also looked to back candidates on the Democratic side of the aisle.

# The 2016 ISA Renegotiation And Its Revenue-Share Dispute

Eddy Cue testified that when Apple and Google renegotiated the ISA, Apple wanted a higher percentage of the revenue Google made from the Apple users it directed to the search engine, while Sundar Pichai wanted to keep the deal as it was; the two eventually compromised on some other number that was not disclosed in open court, and Google has been paying Apple that amount since.

Discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw asked Cue whether he would have walked away from the deal if the two sides couldn't agree on a revenue-share figure, and Cue said he had never really considered that an option: "I always felt like it was in Google's best interest, and our best interest, to get a deal done." Cue also argued that the deal was about more than economics, that Apple never seriously considered switching to another provider or building its own search product, and that "certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — adding that there still isn't one.

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.

# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Acquisition

## Definition

Across the corpus, "acquisition" denotes one company buying another and taking ownership and control of it — whether framed as an all-cash purchase of a target's shares (Amazon–iRobot), an outright corporate purchase (OpenAI–Global Illumination, Microsoft–Activision Blizzard King, Palo Alto Networks–Talon/Dig), or referred to interchangeably as a "merger," "buy," or "deal."

## Context

The corpus uses "acquisition" (and its synonyms "purchase," "buy," "merger," "deal") across a wide range of industries and deal sizes, from an AI startup's first tuck-in purchase to a $69 billion mega-deal, showing the term denotes a general transaction type rather than one specific event.
Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot was priced as an all-cash offer, later cut by 15% during a lengthy EU antitrust review, illustrating how the announced acquisition price can move before a deal closes.
OpenAI's purchase of Global Illumination was described as the company's "first public acquisition," showing the term applies equally to small, non-controversial tuck-ins as to headline-grabbing mega-deals.
Microsoft's $69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard and King — the largest acquisition in video game history — took nearly two years to clear antitrust review before completing, and the corpus notes Microsoft's prior $26 billion purchase of LinkedIn as an earlier acquisition of comparable scale.
In cybersecurity, Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Talon Cyber Security and Dig Security for roughly $1 billion combined is framed as one of several "mega deals" and smaller tuck-ins (CrowdStrike–Bionic, IBM–Polar, Cisco–Splunk) that the corpus groups together as an industry-wide acquisition trend driven by consolidation pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Change of ownership and control** — the acquirer gains control of the target's assets, operations, or equity; in the iRobot case the EU's concern was specifically that Amazon would gain the ability and incentive to influence competitive outcomes on its marketplace once it controlled iRobot.
- **A negotiated price that can shift** — the iRobot deal's price fell 15% from its original $1.7 billion all-cash offer as the target took on more debt during a delayed close, showing acquisition price is not fixed until the deal actually closes.
- **Regulatory review as a gating step** — both the Amazon–iRobot deal (EU statement of objections, in-depth probe) and the Microsoft–Activision Blizzard deal (nearly two years of antitrust review before an October 2023 approval) show large acquisitions routinely require competition-authority clearance before completion.
- **Ranges from tuck-ins to mega-deals** — the same term covers OpenAI's small, low-profile purchase of Global Illumination and Microsoft's $69 billion Activision Blizzard purchase, differentiated by disclosed deal size and public scrutiny rather than by transaction mechanics.
- **Driven by consolidation dynamics** — in cybersecurity, acquisitions cluster as companies buy up specialized startups (e.g., Palo Alto pursuing Talon and Dig) partly in reaction to competitors' own acquisitions, a pattern the corpus explicitly attributes to a "swing" toward large all-in-one platforms.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "acquisition" is a standard mergers-and-acquisitions term: it occurs when one entity takes ownership of another entity's share capital, equity interests, or assets, as distinct from a merger, which combines two entities into a single new legal entity. (Source: Wikipedia, "Mergers and acquisitions," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# SEO Conference Culture And Its Excesses

After years of being friends online, the SEOs were eager to let loose in person, giving off what Forrester described as "that vibe of a lot of young people with access to a lot of money. And it was like, no expenses spared in New York City."

For Forrester it was the start of a long career of keynote presentations and consummate schmoozing — Clay, the father of SEO, described him as "a cruise director" on the SS SEO. The circuit has treated him well: he has attended events in Napa, Hawaii, and Barbados among many others, as well as "an infinite number of private dinners and these types of things in every city you can think of, at the most lavish restaurants," he said. "I've lost track of how many Michelin-starred meals I've had, 'cause it's now in the dozens, from my time in this industry. And I'm not going to say no to the dinner that everyone's going to, that one company is sponsoring because it's a thank you to everybody who contributed to, whatever it was, you know? And you go and everybody has a good time. You talk about the industry, and that's it. And it becomes the stuff of legends."

Over the years he has seen it all, remembering "walking into hotel rooms and it's two o'clock in the morning, there's drugs and alcohol and everything everywhere, and there's a party going on." He marveled at the audacity of his fellow SEOs: "Somebody showed up and brought her Aston Martin to a conference and parked it at the front door. Immediately got a parking ticket." When he suggested she relocate the car before it got towed, she said she would just move it to the next parking spot and get another ticket — "It's cheaper for me to leave the car parked out front and use it as a way to start conversations with potential clients than it is for me to rent a suite at the hotel and get people to go to the suite to have the same conversation." Then she offered him a joyride around Seattle, and obviously he said yes.

Representing a search engine changed the rules. Once he represented Bing, Forrester more or less stopped drinking at conferences, as had long been the case for his counterpart at Google, an engineer named Matt Cutts, who helped build and then ran the company's web spam team before stepping back in 2014 and leaving in 2016.

# Thai Food Near Me's Customer Experience

For a group The Verge's reporter spoke with at Thai Food Near Me on an evening in August, the SEO plan had — at least practically — the intended effect. One of the diners, Travis, found the restaurant on Yelp when searching for nearby dining options after missing an earlier reservation elsewhere; several people in the group had heard about the restaurant when it went viral in the spring but had not realized it was in New York. The group agreed the food was good, even though they had not known what to expect, and said they would definitely consider coming back if they were in the area.

The channel, though, was not the one the owners planned for. Co-owner Robert Sampson says that for the first several months of being open, most people were coming in after seeing Twitter and Reddit posts, not Google results, while others would walk by outside, do a double take at the sign, and come inside. "After you get that initial bunch, you've got people who enjoyed their dining experience here," he says. "They'll tell all their friends and family if they liked it, and then those people come from word of mouth."

Despite the admittedly silly name, the reporter found it clear that co-owners Jirapraphanan and Sampson care about what they are serving: the restaurant is clean and stylish, and the menu, carefully designed by Jirapraphanan, features original dishes she had not seen at other places; her food was tasty, came out promptly, and she said she too would note the spot if she were in the area again and craving Thai food. Jirapraphanan wants people to come back because they actually like the food — the name is part, but not all, of the branding. "I want to be different from other Thai restaurants," he says. "I think it did more than we could have ever imagined it would do," Sampson says. The restaurant's owners are Jirapraphanan, Sampson, Natkitta Kornwaewwongcharoen, and Nat P Akethamwong.

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.
