# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# SEO Conference Culture And Its Excesses

After years of being friends online, the SEOs were eager to let loose in person, giving off what Forrester described as "that vibe of a lot of young people with access to a lot of money. And it was like, no expenses spared in New York City."

For Forrester it was the start of a long career of keynote presentations and consummate schmoozing — Clay, the father of SEO, described him as "a cruise director" on the SS SEO. The circuit has treated him well: he has attended events in Napa, Hawaii, and Barbados among many others, as well as "an infinite number of private dinners and these types of things in every city you can think of, at the most lavish restaurants," he said. "I've lost track of how many Michelin-starred meals I've had, 'cause it's now in the dozens, from my time in this industry. And I'm not going to say no to the dinner that everyone's going to, that one company is sponsoring because it's a thank you to everybody who contributed to, whatever it was, you know? And you go and everybody has a good time. You talk about the industry, and that's it. And it becomes the stuff of legends."

Over the years he has seen it all, remembering "walking into hotel rooms and it's two o'clock in the morning, there's drugs and alcohol and everything everywhere, and there's a party going on." He marveled at the audacity of his fellow SEOs: "Somebody showed up and brought her Aston Martin to a conference and parked it at the front door. Immediately got a parking ticket." When he suggested she relocate the car before it got towed, she said she would just move it to the next parking spot and get another ticket — "It's cheaper for me to leave the car parked out front and use it as a way to start conversations with potential clients than it is for me to rent a suite at the hotel and get people to go to the suite to have the same conversation." Then she offered him a joyride around Seattle, and obviously he said yes.

Representing a search engine changed the rules. Once he represented Bing, Forrester more or less stopped drinking at conferences, as had long been the case for his counterpart at Google, an engineer named Matt Cutts, who helped build and then ran the company's web spam team before stepping back in 2014 and leaving in 2016.

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# Alameda's $65 Billion Line Of Credit At FTX

Alameda Research held a line of credit at FTX that ultimately reached $65 billion, an effectively unlimited borrowing facility unmatched by anyone else on the exchange and carrying no requirement to post collateral. Caroline Ellison testified that there was no contract and no written terms, and that the credit line was not visible to FTX's auditors; when she raised that with Bankman-Fried, he told her not to worry about it.

The defining features are its size, its informality, and its exclusivity. Gary Wang, who set the line up, testified that it did not start that big: Bankman-Fried asked him to increase it a few times because Alameda kept running into its limits — first "a few hundred million," then a billion, then even that was not enough. It was not clear how Wang arrived at $65 billion specifically, but he said he had discussed the number with Bankman-Fried, and that other customers did not have the same privileges. Ellison said the credit was drawn in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time and was used primarily for trading: the effectively unlimited funds "allowed us to make profitable trades we couldn't have made otherwise."

The boundary case is the source of the capital and Bankman-Fried's disclaimed knowledge of it. Ellison testified that Alameda and FTX were initially "very integrated," run by the same team from the same office, and that when Alameda was scrounging for funds Bankman-Fried told her FTX would be a good source of capital. On the stand, Bankman-Fried denied he knew about the effectively infinite line of credit Alameda received from FTX — an argument The Verge's reporter found peculiar, summarising the take-away as that the CEO of a financial company simply did not pay attention to finances.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Apple's Privacy Stance Versus Google's Default Payments

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

Bellshaw asked Cue whether Apple believes user privacy is important, to which he said, "Absolutely." She then showed a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies, and Cue readily agreed with them: "We've always thought we had better privacy than Google." He said one provision of the ISA was that Google had to allow people to search without logging in, and that Apple has done things in Safari and around its platforms to make it harder for Google or anyone else to track users. Bellshaw never quite said it, but The Verge read the DOJ's implication as this: Google is a privacy menace anathema to everything Apple believes is important to its users, yet Apple gives it that central place because Google pays so handsomely. She then asked Cue to review some of Apple's financial filings and whether it is true that the ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits. Cue's rebuttal was that this is not how Apple looks at it, because the framing doesn't account for all the work Apple did to make its platform so appealing that an agreement like this could work as well as it does.

# Travis Kelce's First Contact Attempt And The Eras Tour Bracelet

The first link between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce was established in 2016 when Kelce played "Kiss, Marry, Kill" on AfterBuzz TV and said he would kiss Swift, and the first real contact attempt came in July 2023, when he tried and failed to give her a friendship bracelet with his number on it at her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

# Google's Denial That Ad Keyword Matching Affects Organic Results

Google's official search liaison Danny Sullivan rebutted the allegation that Google manipulates search to maximise ad revenue by denying the causal link it depends on: in a post on X, he said ad systems do not affect the organic results — the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored.

"Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads," Sullivan said. "A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query." He also defended query interpretation on its own terms: "It's no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning… If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that's not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren't even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help." The Age noted the claim being answered comes from Megan Gray, herself a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google; she admits she may have misinterpreted the evidence but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. The paper granted that some search queries result in more ads than others and that which ads you get can vary wildly by request — the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads — but noted Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. # Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.

# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. # Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

The Verge argued that Thai Food Near Me's name really did help the restaurant — but not through the mechanism its owners intended. # Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# ChatGPT Mobile App Launches And Revenue

ChatGPT's mobile apps, launched for iOS in May 2023 and Android in July 2023, topped 110 million combined installs and reached nearly $30 million in consumer spending, according to a market analysis by data.ai.

The rollout was staged by geography. OpenAI launched the ChatGPT app for iOS free to use, free from ads and allowing voice input, but initially limited to U.S. users; the app syncs history across devices so it knows what a user previously searched via the web interface, and it is integrated with Whisper, OpenAI's open source speech recognition system, for voice input. Within six days it topped 500,000 downloads. OpenAI then announced the app was available on iOS in the U.S., Europe, South Korea and New Zealand, and added 11 more countries — Albania, Croatia, France, Germany, Ireland, Jamaica, Korea, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria and the UK. The app was later expanded to more than 30 further countries: Algeria, Argentina, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Estonia, Ghana, India, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Lithuania, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mexico, Morocco, Namibia, Nauru, Oman, Pakistan, Peru, Poland, Qatar, Slovenia, Tunisia and the United Arab Emirates. A new version brought native iPad support with full-screen mode optimized for the tablet interface, support for using the chatbot with Siri and Shortcuts, and drag and drop for pulling individual messages from ChatGPT into other apps. On Android, OpenAI first put up a "pre-order" page on Google Play and days later released the app live in the US, India, Bangladesh and Brazil; the Android app looks more or less identical to the iOS one in functionality, getting most if not all of the web version's features and syncing conversations and preferences across devices.

Revenue is large but not dominant, and growth has slowed. In September, OpenAI amassed 15.6 million downloads and nearly $4.6 million in gross revenue across its iOS and Android apps worldwide — a record $4.58 million month for the mobile app — but revenue growth dropped from 30% to 20% in September according to market intelligence firm Appfigures. OpenAI's chatbot app far outpaces all others on mobile devices in terms of downloads, yet it is surprisingly not the top AI app by revenue: several other AI chatbots, such as "Chat & Ask AI" and "ChatOn — AI Chat Bot Assistant," make more money than ChatGPT.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# Prediction: AI Marketing Claims Meet Reality

TechCrunch predicts a considerable customer withdrawal from AI tools in 2024 as the benefits fail to justify the costs and risks. The simple fact behind the forecast is that the hype built up in 2023 is going to be very hard for companies to follow through on: marketing claims made for machine learning systems that companies adopted in order to not fall behind will receive their quarterly and yearly reviews, and it is very likely they will be found wanting.

At the far end of that spectrum, the prediction is that we will see lawsuits and regulatory action against AI service providers that failed to back up their claims.

The forecast is bounded rather than blanket: capabilities will continue to grow and advance, but 2023's products will not all survive by a long shot, and there will be a round of consolidation as the wobblier riders of the wave fall and are consumed.
